abstract: Estimating the principal eigenpair of a positive operator from stochastic evaluations gives rise to a noisy form of normalized power iteration: each step applies a sampled operator estimate and then renormalizes. We establish finite-time stochastic-approximation guarantees for this procedure, working in Hilbert's projective metric, which is well-suited to the multiplicative geometry of Perron--Frobenius eigenproblems. Our main application is risk-sensitive average-cost reinforcement learning (RL) with exponential utility. In this setting the Bellman equations are multiplicative, and value functions are characterized by nonlinear eigenvalue problems rather than additive fixed points. We cast both policy evaluation and control in this framework, obtaining risk-sensitive TD- and Q-learning algorithms that learn from a single Markovian trajectory. Under explicit positivity, mixing, and linear function approximation assumptions, we prove finite-time bounds on the recovered eigenvector and eigenvalue with $\tilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity up to problem-dependent constants. The results cover both tabular and linear function approximation regimes, and through the duality between exponential utility and KL-robust control yield finite-time guarantees for KL-robust average-cost RL as well.

title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
abstract: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand. We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings. On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.

title: The Limits of Information-Flow Control Enforcement for Agentic Systems
abstract: Information-flow control (IFC) is a promising approach to enforce policy in agentic AI systems. However, IFC suffers from label creep, a phenomenon where monotonically increasing security labels propagate through a system and progressively limit its utility. Label creep in agentic AI systems can be mitigated using two major strategies: (1) improved system design and (2) label declassification. In this paper, we characterize how far system design alone can mitigate label creep in agentic systems. Specifically, we measure how system topology, scale, and agent composition affect utility loss and security enforcement cost proxies for conservative IFC enforcement in a stateful agentic system simulator. We develop a pipeline to systematically vary these features and measure their impacts on label propagation. Our results demonstrate strong associations between structural graph features and our IFC utility loss metric (up to a Spearman correlation $|ρ|$ of $0.96$) and show that system size and tool allocation substantially affect how labels propagate. These findings identify design choices to reduce IFC utility loss, but they also demonstrate that system design alone cannot fully prevent utility loss due to monotonic label propagation. This motivates the development of label declassification mechanisms that aid these design choices and diminish IFC utility cost.

title: Discrete-Time Zero-Sum Markov Games with Control, Stopping, and State-Dependent Discounting
abstract: We study a discrete-time two-player zero-sum stochastic game with control and stopping, where both players can stop the game, the discount factors depends on the states, and the running and terminal rewards may be unbounded. A contraction argument for the constrained Shapley equation establishes the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium consisting of stationary controls and stopping times. We further provides algorithms for approximating the value and computing an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium. A numerical example with state-dependent discount factors illustrates the results.

title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
abstract: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.

title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
abstract: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.

title: Too Big to Inspect? Ethically Auditing Large Datasets Through Small Samples
abstract: Big techs and researchers increasingly claim that their training datasets are too large to inspect for bias and ethical problems. However, in the race to build ever-large models, they have relied on automated web scraping and no human curation. Datasets built this way absorb the stereotypes, exclusionary norms, and historical prejudices of their sources, and the models trained on them can reproduce and amplify those patterns. Because manually auditing billions of samples is humanly impossible, we need practical, effective methods to identify biases in these datasets. This paper studies the feasibility of ethically auditing large datasets through small samples and proposes a practical method for identifying structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools (AIETs) to random samples. We applied Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels, and Data Cards to a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe. Our results show that evaluating small samples with AIETs can reveal ethical problems, structural biases, and technical inconsistencies. Although industry practice assumes that identifying problems requires analyzing the entire dataset, we show that a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without overwhelming computational or human resources. Demonstrating that a dataset is biased does not require examining every instance: if a bias appears in a random sample, it is a flaw of the creation process. The AIETs' questions acted as provocateurs, evoking different perspectives and analysis methods for the same dataset, but the analysis and its results depended fundamentally on the human factor. We hope these findings contribute to urgent public discussions about ethics, transparency, accountability, and AI regulation by offering a practical pathway for responsibly auditing massive datasets.

title: Detecting and Explaining Robot Policy Failures from Sparse Internal Features
abstract: Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. MIND uses a sparse autoencoder to break down the policy's internal activations into features that can be studied individually. We give meaning to these features by linking their activity to the robot's position, movement, and surroundings, and by steering their activations to examine how they affect the robot's actions. From successful and failed executions, we learn how the features behave on the way to a failure. During execution, MIND flags deviations from these patterns and uses the meaningful features contributing most to the change to describe the problem. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that changes in these internal features help detect and explain failures. By using the same features for detection and diagnosis, MIND connects failure signals to understandable changes inside the policy.

title: Efficient Estimation and Consistent Class Number Selection for Semiparametric Class-Specific Index Regression
abstract: The study introduces a parsimonious semiparametric class-specific index regression that captures heterogeneous covariate--response relationships across latent subpopulations. In such a latent class model formulation, subject-specific indices are used as a complete-data representation of the realized latent labels. We propose a unified framework for estimating model parameters and recovering latent class memberships. For the class-specific index mean model, estimation and latent class recovery are conducted via a pseudo-least-squares criterion with a separation penalty, and a semiparametric information criterion is proposed for consistently estimating the number of classes. Exploiting the response distribution, we develop a Bayes classification rule that maximizes the asymptotic probability of correct assignment and a pseudo-maximum likelihood criterion that yields class index coefficient estimators with asymptotic semiparametric efficiency. This refinement step characterizes latent class membership probabilities via sufficient dimension reduction of the covariate space. Simulations and applications to marketing and biomedical datasets demonstrate superior finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology in parameter estimation, latent class recovery, and class number selection.

title: Basis selection, universal sampling discretization, and sampling recovery
abstract: For every real $N$-dimensional subspace of $L_2$, we construct one orthonormal basis such that, for every $1\le v\le N$, at most $Cv\log(eN/v)$ positively weighted samples discretize the squared $L_2$ norm of all $v$-term combinations. Random rotations also give simultaneous weighted $L_p$ estimates and a sharp $C\log(eN)$ bound for the squared $L_2$ norm of the pointwise maximum. For prescribed coefficient classes, a change of measure yields sampling recovery estimates from $Cv\log^3(2v)$ samples under a lower Riesz inequality and a common square-integrable pointwise bound.

title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. Designed for quorum-based systems, QUASI enables parties to attest to external entities that the statement is valid. Surprisingly, each party need not sign the entire statement: authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for the quorum to attest to the whole. A simple deterministic construction illustrates this possibility. Built purely from hashing and error correction, QUASI achieves small per-party contributions and low attestation generation and verification costs, without relying on SNARKs for aggregation. Our main contribution is a randomized construction achieving reductions of more than $10\times$ in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

title: Yuanbao-Reranker: Document-Grounded Synthesis and Preference Distillation for Text Reranking
abstract: High-precision text reranking is a critical component in modern search, recommendation, and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. We present Yuanbao-Reranker, a family of general-purpose dense rerankers spanning 0.6B, 4B, and 8B parameter scales built upon the Qwen3 backbone. To construct diverse and reliable ranking supervision at scale, we pair answer-first and query-type-guided document-grounded synthesis with a three-stage curation funnel that verifies positive support, eliminates semantic redundancy, and enforces balanced source-by-length quotas. For each curated pair, we screen real retrieval pools with a teacher score margin to filter out potential false negatives and sample Hard, Medium, and Moderate negative tiers, yielding 2.75M $1{:}3$ ranking groups. We train the models by jointly optimizing pointwise relevance cross-entropy and a bounded minimum-gap hinge objective over both positive--negative and negative--negative pairs. This formulation transfers fine-grained teacher preferences across candidate tiers without over-constraining well-separated predictions, supporting both cross-scale and same-scale distillation followed by layerwise adaptive model merging. Across five comprehensive benchmarks spanning Chinese (CMTEB-R), multilingual (MMTEB-R), English (BEIR), long-document (MLDR), and code (MTEB-Code) retrieval, Yuanbao-Reranker consistently leads every parameter tier: the 0.6B variant reaches 70.96 Avg. to surpass 1B--4B active-parameter baselines, the 4B variant reaches 73.63 Avg. to outperform the 8B teacher (72.68), and the 8B variant achieves a state-of-the-art 74.21 Avg., with substantial gains generalizing across distinct first-stage retrievers.

title: Early Signals of Problematic AI Use: The Longitudinal Roles of Motivation and Emotional Engagement
abstract: Longitudinal evidence about the psychological impact of conversational AI use remains scarce. We report a survey study of 114 adults who reported their level of problematic AI use one year after reporting their motivations (for escape, social, entertainment, and instrumental reasons) for engaging with AI. We found high levels of AI motivation of all types predicted later problematic AI use, especially when participants turned to AI for managing their feelings and overcoming difficulties. Our findings imply that AI motivation could be used as an early warning signal of potential problematic use, especially if individuals engage with AI for emotional purposes over time.

title: A comparative analysis of semileptonic $B_{(s)}\to D_{(s)}$ and $B_c\to(η_c,B,B_s)$ decays in the light-front quark model
abstract: We present a global analysis of the semileptonic transitions $B_{(s)}\to D_{(s)}$ and $B_c\to(η_c,B,B_s)$ by comparing five potential-model implementations of the QCD-motivated light-front quark model. We use the same fully Bakamjian--Thomas-based prescription for the weak current in all five models and keep their respective spectroscopic parameters fixed. We examine how confinement, radial mixing, and the treatment of hyperfine interactions jointly affect the form factors, differential decay rates, branching fractions, and lepton-flavor ratios. The internal Lorentz prefactors use the same free quark--antiquark kinematics as the on-shell constituent spinors in the weak-current kernels, while the physical meson masses determine the external kinematics. For each model and decay channel, the two independent extractions of $f_-(q^2)$ using the $(+,\perp)$ and $(+,-)$ current-component combinations agree within numerical accuracy. We perform a direct analytic continuation of the spacelike overlap integrals in the $q^+=0$ frame using a mass-weighted contour in complex transverse momentum space. This yields the form factors throughout the physical timelike region, including zero recoil, without parametrizing their $q^2$ dependence. Form factors and differential decay rates are presented as equal-weight model averages with pointwise minimum--maximum bands. The light-lepton-averaged ratios range from $0.282$ to $0.301$ for $R(D)$ and from $0.287$ to $0.303$ for $R(D_s)$.

title: Sharp Logarithmic-Product Bounds for List Replicability of Sign Matrices
abstract: List replicability measures how many accurate hypotheses suffice to contain the output of a learning rule with arbitrarily high confidence. We prove that every nonempty class of $m$ binary concepts on $n$ domain points has list replicability at most $805\ln(2m)\ln(2n)$. This resolves the logarithmic-product conjecture of Blondal, Hatami, Hatami, Lalov, and Tretiak. Hanner matrices give lower bounds of the same order, for square matrices and for explicit families with unequal logarithmic aspect ratios. The upper bound is obtained by constructing nested acyclic sets in the faces of a cube. A critical-point estimate supplies highly connected regions, weighted cell attachments keep the sets compatible across faces, and a cubical carrier theorem converts them into accurate finite covers and learning rules. Appending one constant coordinate turns list replicability into an exact geometric quantity, the face width, and graph-orientation classes satisfy exact product formulas. In particular, there are explicit classes with list replicability $4k+1$ and equivariant index $3k$, so the additive gap between the two is unbounded. We also develop entropy-tilting and two-sided Gibbs constructions, give combinatorial upper bounds adapted to structured matrices, compute exact values on classical families, and study the index of Paley matrices.

title: Directional Ergodic Theorems, Ergodicity, and Weak mixing for $\mathbb Z^2$-actions
abstract: In this paper, we study Birkhoff and von Neumann type ergodic theorems for $\mathbb Z^2$-measure preserving systems along irrational directions. This leads us to a further investigation of directional ergodicity and weak mixing. Additionally, we show that our framework (dynamical definitions) is equivalent to the spectral definitions of directional ergodicity and weak mixing introduced by Robinson, Rosenblatt and Şahin \cite{RRS2023} for $\mathbb Z^2$-actions. We note that in their recent paper \cite{RS2026}, Robinson and Şahin established the equivalence between dynamical and spectral directional weak mixing for $\mathbb Z^2$-actions using an approach fundamentally different from the one employed in the present paper.

title: SimDuoReal: Object-Centric Bimanual Policy for Emergent Dexterity
abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and hand control, yet specifying such coordination manually is challenging and often task-specific. In this work, we explore whether complex bimanual dexterity can emerge from a simple object-centric learning objective. We train reinforcement learning policies under a shared object-centric reward, varying their training environments rather than tuning separate rewards for each behavior. We find that the policies discover pre-grasp manipulation, grasping and regrasping, in-hand adjustment and handover to reach object-pose goals without hand-designed motion sequences. We then refine the experts on transition states and use DAgger and reinforcement learning to distill them into a single policy that composes these behaviors for diverse bimanual tasks. On real hardware, the same policy succeeds in 61 of 80 trials (76.3\%) across four tasks with unseen objects and no task-specific fine-tuning. In simulated barcode scanning, our policy achieves 85.0\% success, compared with 60.4\% for two single-arm policies without handover. These results suggest that this objective provides a simple and scalable interface for learning general bimanual dexterity, shifting the burden from manually designing robot coordination to specifying what should happen to the object.

title: Tail-risk-aware Agent Safety: Constraining Tail Risks Across Multi-step LLM Agent Workflows
abstract: LLM-based agents extend LLMs with tool calls, memory, planning, and retrieval to act in external environments, but they are vulnerable to attacks at different workflow steps. Existing defenses, including prompt engineering and post-training alignment, primarily improve LLM-only safety and often overlook risks that arise from multi-step execution. External verification adds guardrails to check each step separately, but it typically ignores how risks can propagate across steps. We argue that we should consider risk transitions across dependent steps through the agent workflow, rather than separate verification on a single step. In this paper, we propose \textbf{T}ail-risk-aware \textbf{A}gent \textbf{S}afety (TAS), a tail-risk-aware safety framework that models agent workflow safety as a sequence of dependent safety states and constrains the rare but extreme risks (i.e., tail risk) with a shared budget. TAS first models safety-state transitions sequentially along the workflow as an MDP to trace risk propagation, then measures a tail-sensitive risk to target rare but high-cost risks (i.e., tail risk), and constrains the risk with a shared budget to derive a step-wise safety strategy. By constraining tail risk rather than the overall average, TAS suppresses rare high-cost failures while preserving utility in normal cases. Experiments show that TAS achieves better performance compared with eleven baselines across three benchmarks.

title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn settings. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over it before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our evaluation, nine LLMs achieve overall pass rates from 42.86% to 59.59% on 490 scenarios. Performance varies substantially across challenge types: models perform well on Stateful Multi-Constraint Following but remain considerably less reliable on Scope Creep and Goal Shift. These results reveal persistent limitations in reasoning over evolving user requirements across turns.

title: Frequency-Structure Complementary Modeling for Hyperspectral Image Fusion
abstract: Existing methods mainly rely on convolutional aggregation or attention-based spatial-spectral interaction. However, conventional feature-domain attention does not explicitly characterize variation patterns along spatial-token and learned latent-channel coordinates, while spatially shared local operators lack the flexibility to adapt neighborhood aggregation to heterogeneous structures. To address these limitations, we propose a Frequency-Structure Complementary Modeling Network (FSCM-Net), which couples frequency-aware dependency learning with structure-adaptive local refinement. Specifically, a Spatial-Spectral Frequency Calibration Attention (SSFCA) module constructs spatial-token affinities from Fourier-interacted query-key representations and builds latent-channel affinities after input-conditioned frequency filtering along learned channel coordinates. The latent-channel response is then calibrated by a learned shared gain and combined with the spatial-token response. Complementarily, a Structure-Coherent Dynamic Feature Fusion (SC-DFF) module combines regularized structure-tensor cues from MSI features with context-modulated HSI detail representations to generate channel- and position-dependent aggregation kernels. This design makes local HSI refinement responsive to smooth regions, edges, and textures while maintaining spectral fidelity. The two modules are progressively integrated within a multiscale encoder-decoder to coordinate representation-level interaction and structure-adaptive reconstruction. Experiments on two simulated benchmarks and one real remote-sensing dataset demonstrate favorable performance against representative fusion methods in spatial detail reconstruction and spectral preservation.

title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
abstract: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

title: Birational Geometry of K-Moduli Spaces of Genus Four Curves
abstract: We study the wall-crossings for K-moduli spaces of (3,3)-curves on $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$. Together with the boundary polarized Calabi--Yau moduli space, these spaces interpolate between the GIT moduli space of (3,3)-curves and the Baily--Borel compactification of the moduli space of K3 surfaces arising as cyclic triple covers of $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$ branched along such curves. As applications, we describe the corresponding birational models in the Hassett--Keel--Looijenga program and realize the K-moduli space of degree one del Pezzo surfaces through explicit wall-crossings.

title: S2HAND: Accuracy-Preservation Trade-Offs for Hand Specialization in Whole-Body Pose Models
abstract: Unified whole-body pose estimators jointly predict body, face, and hand landmarks, but often degrade on small, blurred, or occluded hands. Attaching a standalone hand specialist introduces extra detection overhead, coordinate alignment, and wrist-stitching artifacts. We introduce S2HAND, a hand-specialized Sapiens2-5B framework that preserves the native 308-keypoint output interface. Specifically, S2HAND-MT adapts a lightweight 0.87M-parameter pose branch to route 40 finger heatmaps while strictly preserving the shared Transformer, auxiliary task heads, and the other 268 body, foot, and face heatmaps. S2HAND-Pose further fine-tunes three Fisher-selected Transformer blocks (267.13M parameters), trading exact preservation for stronger hand recovery: it lifts macro AUC from 57.83% to 65.73% across HInt TEST, COCO WholeBody VAL, and FreiHAND EVAL, and surpasses HInt-adapted Hand5/HRNet and stitched Hand5 systems on all five Native Pipeline benchmarks. On COCO, S2HAND-Pose improves hand AP by 12.89 points and body-plus-foot AP by 0.19 points. Across a 512-image multi-task audit, it maintains 99.60% foreground segmentation agreement with the public checkpoint, with quantified normal and pointmap drift. Its 2D coordinates also lower 3D mesh error in frozen Pose2Mesh transfer, while our optional TailGuard re-cropping module cuts S2HAND-MT's severe failure rate on NewDays from 13.45% to 10.43%. S2HAND thus resolves the whole-body hand bottleneck with either exact non-hand preservation (MT) or empirically audited trade-offs (Pose).

title: Momentum-Resolved Kondo Hybridization of Nonsymmorphic Dirac-Derived Bands in CeAgBi$_2$
abstract: How symmetry-constrained conduction states acquire heavy-quasiparticle character is a central question in correlated quantum materials. Combining angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, Ce $4d \rightarrow 4f$ resonant photoemission, and first-principles calculations, we investigate the nonsymmorphic Kondo lattice CeAgBi$_2$. We identify quasi-two-dimensional Bi-square-net-derived bands consistent with calculated Dirac crossings and nodal lines. Resonant photoemission resolves a nearly dispersionless Ce 4$f$ band near the Fermi level, establishing Kondo heavy-quasiparticle states. Its pronounced momentum-dependent spectral weight at intersections with the identified Dirac-derived branches provides direct spectroscopic evidence for their participation in $c$-$f$ hybridization. Complementary measurements on independently cleaved samples and an effective hybridization model connect these branches to the Kondo heavy-quasiparticle spectrum. The combined results support preservation of nonsymmorphic Dirac-band connectivity under Kondo renormalization, showing how symmetry-constrained conduction states become constituents of correlated heavy quasiparticles.

title: Beyond Query Similarity: Safety-Conditioned Cache Routing for LLM Response Reuse
abstract: Semantic response caching reuses a cached response for a semantically similar query to improve LLM inference efficiency. However, query similarity alone can lead to unsafe reuse when safety conditions change. Existing approaches improve cache safety through stricter similarity checks, context-aware validation, or response verification, yet they may still miss safety conflicts between the cached response and the new request or introduce unnecessary verification overhead. We argue that safe and efficient semantic caching requires a reuse policy that makes the cached response's safety conditions explicit and uses them to guide the reuse decision with a balance between safety and utility. In this paper, we propose SafeCache, a safety-aware framework that separates candidate retrieval from safety approval and formulates semantic response reuse as a safety-conditioned routing problem. SafeCache matches each cached-response condition against the new request and aggregates the per-condition mismatches into an overall risk score. A separate contradiction guard prevents explicit conflicts from being diluted by strong matches. It further estimates matching uncertainty and calibrates the routing policy under a required unsafe-reuse target and a verifier-call budget to choose among direct reuse, selective verification, or regeneration. Experiments show that SafeCache achieves the better safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated baselines, enabling safer response reuse at comparable cache utility.

title: Time-Delay Recovery in AGN Reverberation Mapping via Mutual Information
abstract: Active galactic nuclei exhibit complex, nonlinear multiwavelength variability that standard cross-correlation techniques, sensitive only to linear covariance, may fail to capture fully. We apply time-lagged Mutual Information (MI) lag estimation, via the Kraskov-Stoegbauer-Grassberger $k$-nearest-neighbour estimator ($k = 5$) with a 150-iteration Random Subset Selection bootstrap, to the light curves of four Seyfert galaxies (Mrk 509, NGC 5548, NGC 4151, and NGC 4593) monitored across eight energy bands by Swift. In the UV/optical regime the MI estimator successfully reproduces the inter-band disc reprocessing lags established by the interpolated cross-correlation function, with performance degrading toward the optical where low variability amplitude produces poorly defined MI peaks. In the X-ray bands, where the physical X-ray/UV coupling is known to be weak, the estimator fails to recover consistent lags across the sample, with the notable exception of NGC 4593. Contextualising these outcomes within the multifractal characterisation of our previous work, we discuss how MI performance relates to the multifractal spectral width $Δα$ of each band, and we propose $Δα$ as a candidate diagnostic for anticipating where MI-based reverberation mapping is likely to succeed or fail in multiband datasets of active galactic nuclei.

title: Dynamic Molecular Transformation Mediated Crystallization Regulation and Interface Passivation in Tin Based Perovskite Solar Cells
abstract: Tin-based perovskites are promising candidates for lead-free photovoltaics but suffer from labile Sn$^{2+}$ coordination, rapid crystallization, and severe interfacial defects. Here, we develop a dynamic molecular transformation using 1-acetylpiperazine (PX) to regulate crystallization and interface chemistry simultaneously. During nucleation and growth, the carbonyl group coordinates with Sn$^{2+}$ to stabilize precursor complexes, moderate supersaturation, and enable controlled crystal growth. Upon annealing, PX undergoes in situ molecular transformation, suggested to form amidinium-functionalized species that preferentially occupy surface A-site vacancies, forming a passivation layer and suppressing nonradiative recombination. This coupled bulk-to-interface evolution yields compact, highly crystalline films with improved optoelectronic quality. Devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 15.18% and retain 94.1% of initial efficiency after 500 h of continuous illumination. This work demonstrates a dynamic molecular engineering approach integrating crystallization control and interface passivation, providing a pathway toward efficient and stable lead-free perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Nonexistence of positive solutions stable outside a compact set for the Lane--Emden system in a half-space
abstract: We prove that, in every dimension and for all positive exponents, the Lane--Emden system in a half-space with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions admits no positive classical solution stable outside a compact set.

title: Dissipative properties of isoscalar collective excitations in heavy nuclei
abstract: The dissipative properties of isoscalar collective motion in heavy nuclei are studied within a kinetic model of collective excitations in finite Fermi systems with a free moving surface. The model includes both the one-body damping produced by the interaction of nucleons with the dynamic surface of nucleus and the Landau damping mechanism. In this paper, we study the damping and dissipative properties of the isoscalar dipole collective modes and the isoscalar vortex octupole mode, which are formed due to dynamic effects of the nuclear surface. To study the damping mechanism of the considered collective modes, a multipole strength function is used in various approximations. It is shown that the damping of the considered isoscalar collective modes is due to a one-body damping mechanism. An analytical expression for the dissipation coefficient at finite frequency for the collective variable describing multipole oscillations of nuclear surface is obtained. It was found that the dissipation coefficient in the energy region of the considered isoscalar collective modes does not exceed the wall formula friction coefficient derived in the one-body dissipation theory. This result confirms the understanding of friction in the wall formula as a macroscopic limit of the one-body nuclear dissipation.

title: Mental Imagery That Matters: Curing Latent Collapse in Multimodal Reasoning
abstract: Mental simulation, the ability to reason by constructing and updating internal visual states, is central to flexible human cognition, but remains elusive in current multimodal large language models. Latent multimodal reasoning offers a promising route toward this capability by interleaving text with continuous visual latent blocks, allowing models to maintain internal visual workspaces without decoding them into pixels. In this paper, we ask whether these latent visual states actually matter. Through a direct perturbation analysis across representative latent-reasoning MLLMs, we find that they often do not: dropping, replacing, or shuffling generated visual latents has only minor effects on the model's own final-answer probability, while equivalent perturbations to the linguistic reasoning trace are substantially more damaging. We call this failure mode Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): the model appears to perform interleaved visual reasoning, but routes most answer-relevant computation through text. We further diagnose that MSC follows naturally from existing training objectives: visual alignment can make generated latents resemble helper-image embeddings, but it does not require the decoder to rely on them; subsequent text-only supervision further leaves the semantic role of the latent pathway unidentifiable. To address this, we introduce AnchorSim (Anchored Mental Simulation), a contrastive distillation framework that trains models to make their generated visual latents consequential. Across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks, AnchorSim improves performance, while diagnostic re-evaluation shows that visual perturbations now meaningfully affect predictions. Our results expose a fundamental failure mode of latent multimodal reasoning and demonstrate that mental simulation must be anchored to model behavior in order to matter.

title: Efficient and Accurate Zero Shot Generation of Symmetric Protein Complexes
abstract: Symmetric organization is a fundamental principle of biomolecular complex assembly. The same principle underlies engineered applications, from vaccine platforms to nanomaterials, making symmetric de novo generation a core capability for computational protein design. We establish a theoretical foundation equating generation of an assembly with underlying symmetry group $G$ to generation within a quotient space over $G$. This directly allows $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant models to generate symmetric structures with minimal distribution shift. With this insight we introduce ZeUS ($\textbf{Ze}$ro-shot $\textbf{U}$nified $\textbf{S}$ymmetrization), a framework that converts any pretrained $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant backbone generative model into an efficient generator of symmetric assemblies with no retraining. ZeUS operates on a single $\textit{canonical subunit}$ and utilizes $\textit{phantom subunits}$ to preserve internal model operations, reducing memory and runtime cost by $\mathcal{O}(|G|)$ for finite groups $G$, compared to a full-complex forward pass. We implement ZeUS for IPA-based models (FrameDiff, FoldFlow) and axial-attention-based RFdiffusion, showing high generation efficiency with minimal degradation to generation quality. We then apply ZeUS to generate symmetric complexes of over $10{,}000$ residues with exact, untruncated attention, a scale previously intractable with any model.

title: Governed Self-Improvement for a Local-First Security Analyzer: Baseline Measurements and a Preregistered Evaluation Protocol for Tantular Cyber
abstract: Local-first security tools let organizations analyze code without sending it to third-party services, but the small language models they can run locally are weaker than hosted ones and are hard to improve without breaching the privacy guarantee that motivates them. We present Tantular Cyber, an open-source, read-only repository security analyzer that keeps deterministic scanner findings authoritative and confines a locally served language model to advisory explanations in Bahasa Indonesia. We report its measured v0.3.0 baseline on a synthetic, ground-truth benchmark: combining Semgrep with an interprocedural call-graph scanner yields precision 0.843 and recall 0.915 (Semgrep alone: 0.818 and 0.766). The advisory layer is the weak point: 57% of explanations met an evidence-grounding check, against 95% for a different 8B model under identical prompts. A forensic re-scoring of retained outputs shows that every grounding failure cites a code identifier absent from the evidence shown, and that a prompt change which appeared to raise grounding from 0.56 to 0.72 did so partly by citing nothing. We document two evaluation-validity hazards we encountered: silent model-file migration during a run and non-reproducible published figures. Building on these lessons and on constraint-aware evaluation from security operations research, we propose a governed self-improvement loop (code-free feedback, curated data, a cheapest-first intervention ladder from prompts to LoRA and weight-space edits, hard gates, and human release approval) and preregister the protocol by which its first cycle will be judged. We report no results for the loop itself.

title: Extendability of general prime $K3$ surfaces without Gaussian maps and classification of prime Fano threefolds
authors: with an appendix written jointly with Anand Deopurkar
abstract: In arXiv:2409.03960 an approach to the question of extendability of projective varieties via degeneration to ribbons was introduced, and in arXiv:2503.12661 it was used to give a new proof of optimal results on the extendability of general non-prime $K3$ surfaces and the classification of non-prime Fano threefolds. In this article we treat the prime case. We give a new proof of the optimal results on the extendability of general prime $K3$ surfaces of every genus, of the classification of prime Fano threefolds of Picard rank one due to Fano, Iskovskikh and Mukai, and of the irreducibility of their Hilbert schemes. This involves degenerations of $K3$ surfaces to ribbons on embedded rational normal scrolls, called $K3$ carpets. We compute exactly the cohomology of the twisted normal bundle of these $K3$ carpets, instead of computing coranks of Gaussian maps of the canonical curve sections. The key challenge is to analyze the coboundary map of the sequence relating the normal bundle of the $K3$ carpet to the normal bundle of the scroll. We give a deformation theoretic interpretation of this map. Given such a $K3$ carpet and its hyperplane section, which is a canonical ribbon, we show that the coboundary map corresponds to the obstruction to lifting a first order deformation of the underlying scroll fixing the underlying rational normal curve to a first order deformation of the $K3$ carpet fixing the canonical ribbon. To compute the obstruction, we use a result on extensions of non-split ribbons on any curve to a unique $K$-trivial carpet in a canonical way.

title: Multifractality in sputtered crystalline and amorphous transition metal nitride thin films
abstract: In this work, we present evidence for multifractal growth in Titanium and Niobium nitride thin films on different substrates. Self-similar multifractal structures such as dendrites and multi-branched snowflake-like structures are reported. The fractal dimensions are controlled by a combination of processing parameters and conditions at the film-substrate interface. Significantly, fractal growth is observed not only in crystalline films on crystalline and amorphous substrates but also on amorphous films on crystalline substrates. The 2D Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (2D MFDFA) carried out on the scanning electron micrographs, clearly reveals the multifractal nature of the nitride thin films. The statistical moments were varied between -5 to +5. The Hausdorff dimensions for the TiN films are in the range of 1.65 to 1.79 while it is 1.64 to 1.74 for the NbN thin films. It is proposed that the observed multifractality is due to a competition between morphological instabilities and Diffusion-Limited Aggregation

title: Current Closure and Gamma-Ray Signatures of Spark-Gap and Current-Sheet Activities in Radiative Black Hole Magnetospheres
abstract: We investigate the evolution of an axisymmetric black hole magnetosphere using general relativistic particle-in-cell simulations, focusing on its global current structure, variability, and radiative effects. We include inverse-Compton (IC) scattering of ambient photons and subsequent two-photon pair production, and compare simulations with and without synchrotron-curvature (SC) radiation reaction. Starting from an axisymmetric vertical magnetic field, the system develops a polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet that together sustain the global poloidal current. For the parameters explored in this study, we observe that the spark gap oscillates upon the onset of SC cooling, whereas the current sheet is less sensitive to radiative cooling. Time-dependent electric fields in the return-current layer trigger magnetic-field rearrangement followed by magnetic reconnection. Cross-correlation analysis finds no significant correlation between the two regions' variability, suggesting dynamical independence. We further perform post-processing ray-tracing calculations to evaluate the radiative efficiencies of the IC and SC processes. High-energy particles dominate the bolometric luminosity, which reaches up to 1 percent of the Blandford-Znajek luminosity for SC emission and 0.1 percent for IC emission. The relative IC luminosity to SC is higher at lower viewing angles because particle momenta are more anisotropic near the pole than near the equator, due to efficient acceleration along the local magnetic field lines. Together with energetic estimates, these results suggest that both regions can contribute to high-energy emission in active galactic nuclei, with spark-gap photons reaching the sub-TeV regime.

title: Applied bifidelity material response model construction and uncertainty quantification with a sampling hypernetwork
abstract: Multifidelity modeling offers a practical route to accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce but lower-fidelity data are comparatively abundant. This work develops a bifidelity Langevin sampling hypernetwork framework that constructs probabilistic neu- ral response models by learning a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than a single deterministic fit. The method combines a flexible shared-latent data representation for low- and high-fidelity responses, enabling parameter sharing and transfer learning between the fidelities. We introduce several methodological enhancements to improve the robustness and efficiency of this ap- proach, including stability-promoting drift models, staged and conditional training strategies, adap- tive initialization of Langevin trajectories, and training procedures designed to better exploit corre- lations between fidelity levels. These additions improve convergence behavior, reduce the sampling effort required to obtain representative posterior ensembles, and provide more reliable predictive uncertainty in data-limited regimes. The resulting framework makes more effective use of available multifidelity data while preserving interpretability through the learned posterior structure, yielding improved predictive performance, better uncertainty characterization, and a more stable workflow for constructing uncertainty-aware surrogate models. The method is demonstrated on experimental, high-fidelity simulation and illustrative synthetic data.

title: Deploying Physically and Epistemically Compliant Agents by Distilling Belief-Space Task and Motion Planners
abstract: In this work, we train agents to act under uncertainty according to specified, belief-dependent rules. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can in theory train agents to follow rules if encoded into well-designed rewards, but in practice, RL fails to perfectly optimize these rewards, leading to ineffective or noncompliant agent behavior. Belief-space planners by construction produce behavior in line with developer specification, but require hand-programming online planners and belief-state estimators, adding significant engineering complexity at scale. We combine the two: we plan offline to generate a dataset of sample trajectories and then distill the plans into a policy that acts on raw observations. We propose two changes to planner distillation that address problems specific to history-based policies: Dual Averaging, a loss that combines per-timestep predictive loss and average loss on task changes, and $ρ$-Optimal Reinforcement, a feedback mechanism that reinforces the policy's own successful rollouts when these are near-optimal. We provide a sufficient condition under which static search problems with noiseless observation models is complete, and show that maximum-likelihood-observation planning implies this condition in static search with continuous beliefs. We create a challenging new domain, Scavenger, where an agent needs to gain information in order to succeed. We evaluate our distilled policy in two versions of Scavenger, one where information is provided visually and one where it is provided as a command in natural language. In either case, the learned policy attains a success rate above 90% in Scavenger, compared with at most 5% for RL. We also find that distilled planners transfer with greater than 60% success to following unseen and intentionally vague commands and greater than 75% success to following floorplans larger than those seen in training.

title: Faint Thermonuclear Transients from the Double Detonations of Common White Dwarfs
abstract: The double detonation model is a viable channel to explain many observed Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), with thin helium shelled white dwarf (WD) progenitors of 0.9--1.1 M$_\odot$ reproducing normal SNe Ia observables. Recent work has also shown that all C/O WDs $\leq$ 1.0 M$_\odot$ can sustain a helium shell detonation that triggers a detonation of the underlying core. As WDs of lower masses (0.5--0.7 M$_\odot$) far outnumber those at higher mass, it is important to explore their double detonation outcomes. To that end, we conducted multidimensional double detonation simulations of low mass C/O cores with very thin helium shells, finding explosion outcomes that differ non-trivially from those at higher masses. Not surprisingly, their cores are incompletely burned with low yields of radioactive elements. Though still formally unbound in isolation, some of the ejecta could remain bound to a nearby companion. In addition, the offset initiation of the core detonation wave and its failure to burn through the entire core lead to a very asymmetric distribution of $^{56}$Ni that creates dramatically viewing angle-dependent light curves and spectra. We find that the peak bolometric luminosities for the same explosion vary up to nearly 2 magnitudes over the sky, and that the spectra and light curves from these models are within the range of faint SNe Iax. In particular, our 0.50 M$_\odot$ models agree well with the photometry of SNe Iax 2008ha and 2024vjm.

title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.

title: HexIt: Learning Hexahedral Block Decomposition with Expert Iteration on Combinatorial Maps
abstract: Decomposing a polyhedral solid into a few well-shaped hexahedral blocks is a long-standing open problem in mesh generation. We cast it as a sequential decision problem on a 3-dimensional generalised map: an agent splits edges, faces and volumes with three insert operations until every cell is a hexahedron and the mesh passes a quality threshold, and a policy that convolves over the map's involutions chooses each insert. A successful decomposition takes over a hundred decisions, and a uniformly random policy never finds one. We clone a policy from constructed decompositions and improve it by expert iteration. On held-out chamfered solids that share no boundary topology with the cloning data, the final policy solves an expected $94.4\%$ in $20$ samples, and expert iteration raises the best-of-20 solve rate on large chamfered solids from $0.203$ to $0.355$. At matched compute, PPO, GRPO and VinePPO updates all make the cloned policy worse.

title: Magnetosonic Solitons Driven by a Moving Charged Source: Two-Fluid Modeling and PIC Validation
abstract: We develop and validate a one-dimensional electron-ion two-fluid model, self-consistently coupled to Maxwell equations, for magnetosonic structures generated by a moving charged source. The model is independently benchmarked against kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to assess its ability to reproduce electrostatic and electromagnetic responses. In the zero-magnetic-field limit, the electrostatic precursor structures are validated using the Korteweg--de Vries amplitude--width invariant. For a finite magnetic field, the frequency and propagation speed of the far wake are consistent with the low-frequency fast-magnetosonic branch, providing a linear benchmark for the electromagnetic response. The model reproduces the transition from a wake-dominated regime to localized forward precursors as the source velocity exceeds the magnetosonic speed, and to source-locked pinned structures at higher velocities. Independent PIC simulations recover the principal features of these regimes, supporting the validity of the two-fluid description for the parameters considered. By retaining separate electron and ion dynamics, electron inertia, and charge-separation effects, the validated model provides a framework for investigating source-driven plasma-wave structures across a broader range of plasma conditions and source-magnetic-field geometries, with potential applications to interpreting plasma-wave signatures associated with moving charged objects in space plasmas.

title: Multi-Objective Adaptation After Deployment: A Position on World Models for Remote Robot Teams
abstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. By predicting policy outcomes under updated estimates of current conditions, world models could enable teams to re-evaluate existing policies without physically executing each candidate, provided predicted performance changes reflect those realized on deployed systems. We identify research priorities for model-based policy re-evaluation, validation of predicted against realized performance, and incorporating shared information into world models to support coordinated team adaptation.

title: High-order long-time stable methods for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations
abstract: We present in this paper two scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) correction steps for constructing long-time stable schemes for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. A main feature is that the same correction steps apply to any linear predictor satisfying the order and spatial regularity requirements in Assumption~P. Their construction and stability analysis are independent of the particular form of the predictor and require no energy estimate for it. The first correction uses a damped, shifted kinetic-energy variable to obtain a uniform-in-time $L^2$ bound in two and three dimensions, together with a weighted dissipation estimate. In two dimensions, the second correction combines a higher-energy auxiliary variable with a scalar relaxation to yield a uniform-in-time $H^1$ bound. Under the stated assumptions, these estimates hold on arbitrary positive time grids, without restrictions on step sizes or adjacent step ratios. We also derive eventual absorbing bounds; for the two-SAV scheme, these apply to the admissible initial class associated with fixed parameters. The generalized BDF schemes require one constant-coefficient Helmholtz solve per velocity component and one pressure Poisson solve per step; the second correction adds no field solve. Numerical experiments exhibit second-, third-, and fourth-order convergence for the tested BDF schemes and illustrate the long-time stability and efficiency of adaptive time stepping.

title: Bulgarian solitaire with distinguishable cells
abstract: Classical Bulgarian solitaire tracks only the sizes of the stacks. We ask how the lengths of its periodic orbits change when individual cards are distinguished. To study this question, we introduce four actions $T_1,T_2,T_3,T_4$ on partitions with labeled cells. The actions differ in whether the top or bottom cell is removed from each column and in the order in which the removed cells are arranged to form a new column. We determine the exact sizes of the periodic orbits for all four actions. The main work lies in the analysis of $T_2$, for which we develop a coloring algorithm on Ferrers diagrams. The coloring encodes the cycle structure of the permutation of the labels induced by one full period of the underlying partition.

title: An introduction to discrete dynamics in condensed sets: orbits, periodic loci, and arithmetic examples
abstract: We formulate discrete dynamics internally in the topos Cond of condensed sets. For an endomorphism $f\colon X\to X$, we construct orbit quotients, backward histories, preimage trees, and periodic loci as objects evaluated on profinite parameter spaces. The framework recovers global-section dynamics, fully faithfully embeds compact Hausdorff systems, characterizes the invertible extension, and is compatible with inverse limits. It organizes $p$-adic congruence towers and shows, for a Cantor-type non-Archimedean Julia set, that classical periodic points can be dense although the internal periodic locus is not isomorphic to the compact condensed Julia set.

title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

title: Lower Bounds Above $\sqrt{3}$ for Online Makespan Minimization on Four Identical Machines
abstract: For deterministic online makespan minimization, $m = 4$ identical machines is the smallest case whose optimal competitive ratio is open: it is known only to lie between $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205$ and $26/15 \approx 1.73333$. We prove a lower bound of $14383/8304 \approx 1.73206$ using a single branching layer, and refine the construction with a second, mirrored branching layer to obtain $14350/8283 \approx 1.73246$, closing about a third of the gap. Our constructions are the first branching adversaries for $m = 4$ machines, and the first explicit lower bounds for online makespan minimization in which the adversary presents jobs in non-monotone order of size.

title: Split and Bridge: Multimodal Generation via Diffusion Bridging
abstract: Visual data are often expressed through multiple complementary modalities (e.g., images and segmentation masks), each capturing different aspects of the same underlying structure. Most existing multimodal methods adopt a top-down paradigm, learning a shared latent variable through joint training from scratch, which limits scalability. We propose Split and Bridge (SnB), a bottom-up framework for multimodal generation that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time. Rather than learning a unified latent space, SnB generates coherent multimodal samples by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point and then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. This design enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models without joint training, making it scalable and easily adaptable. Across standard benchmarks (PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ) and more complex settings (PIE-Bench++, ROCO), SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence. We show that SnB naturally extends to downstream zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Our results demonstrate that bottom-up generation provides a practical framework that complements existing top-down multimodal approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB

title: Transverse quasiparticle heat transport in p-wave magnetic Josephson junctions
abstract: We study transverse heat currents carried by Bogoliubov quasiparticles in $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions under a longitudinal temperature bias. We find that such a junction supports a transverse spin heat current while the net transverse heat current vanishes. This effect stems from the $p$-wave magnetism, which shifts the two spin sectors oppositely in transverse momentum space and thereby causes them to carry opposite heat currents. A weak Zeeman field lifts the compensation between the two spin-sector contributions, thereby generating a finite net transverse heat current. The directions of both currents can be switched by reversing the sign of the $p$-wave magnetic splitting or tuning the superconducting phase difference, while both currents vanish in the absence of $p$-wave magnetism. These findings highlight $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions as a versatile platform for switchable transverse heat transport and controllable spin caloritronics.

title: Spatial Representation Distillation and Knowledge Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Understanding three-dimensional physical structure has become essential for vision-language-action models (VLAs). However, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric inputs at inference time or adopt a single visual pathway, potentially compromising the visual-semantic knowledge inherited from pre-trained models. We present SPARK-VLA, Spatial Representation distillation and Knowledge routing for VLAs, a preserve-specialize-route framework for spatially adapting VLAs without requiring external 3D inputs or experts at inference. SPARK-VLA consists of two key components: (1) spatial representation distillation, which transfers 3D understanding from a frozen 3D expert to a LoRA-adapted visual branch by aligning attention responses while preserving the original visual pathway, and (2) a lightweight knowledge router, which selectively forwards action-relevant visual tokens to the language model using routing supervision derived from action-loss gradients. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation, SPARK-VLA achieves strong performance with only a 0.5B language backbone and approximately 53M trainable parameters, providing an effective and parameter-efficient approach to 3D-aware VLA learning. Code is available at https://github.com/park-jungin/spark-vla.

title: Uniqueness and stability of Appleton's solitons
abstract: We prove that Appleton's noncollapsed steady gradient Ricci solitons on complex line bundles over positive Kähler--Einstein manifolds are the unique such solitons arising from his metric ansatz. We then show that the four-dimensional examples on $O_{\mathbb{CP}^1}(-k)$, $k \geq 3$, are strictly linearly stable. By a result of Deruelle, this implies dynamical stability under the Ricci flow.

title: DiSARM: Diverse and Surprising Association Rule Mining with Large Language Models
abstract: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) aims to discover informative patterns in large datasets. For transactional data, Association Rule Mining (ARM) is an established approach that facilitates EDA by efficiently generating candidate patterns. Beyond efficient mining, identifying informative rules has also been extensively studied through both objective and subjective interestingness measures. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for assessing subjective interestingness using world knowledge. Nevertheless, relying solely on LLMs raises concerns about scalability and statistical reliability. Building on prior ARM research, we propose a hybrid framework, DiSARM, that leverages the world knowledge of LLMs to assess the subjective interestingness of rules, while maintaining statistical reliability and promoting diversity among the selected rules. Across three transactional datasets, experiments demonstrate that DiSARM effectively combines statistical reliability with surprise and diversity, offering a promising approach to ADE from transactional data.

title: Self-organization of magnetic islands and zonal magnetic fields driven by slab microtearing modes in the absence of magnetic shear
abstract: Self-organization in collisional microtearing turbulence is investigated using gyrokinetic simulations in a slab geometry without equilibrium magnetic shear. Unlike magnetically driven conventional tearing instabilities, microtearing instabilities are driven by the electron temperature gradient. Electron temperature fluctuations are found to contain most of the gyrokinetic free energy. Although magnetic perturbations contribute little to the free energy, the magnetic field structure plays a crucial role in the nonlinear evolution of microtearing turbulence. Zonal magnetic fields emerge spontaneously through the nonlinear interaction between magnetic perturbations and electron temperature fluctuations. These zonal fields provide an effective magnetic shear that enables magnetic islands to form despite the absence of equilibrium magnetic shear. The electron temperature profile is flattened within the islands. This flattening reduces the instability drive and is expected to promote turbulence saturation.

title: Good Looks and the Academic Job Market: Measuring Attractiveness with Vision Embeddings
abstract: We introduce a new approach to measure physical attractiveness---the relative vision embedding (RVE) score. The score maps a face to a vector in the embedding space of a pre-trained deep vision model and measures its proximity to a reference set of celebrity faces. It requires no additional training or fine-tuning, no hand-crafted features, and no human raters; it is continuous, inexpensive, scalable, and fully reproducible. Using publicly available photographs with human attractiveness ratings, we show that the RVE scores correlate strongly with human ratings and that rankings are consistent across several off-the-shelf vision models. We apply the measure to administrative hiring data from a research-oriented economics department, complemented by hand-collected photographs of the job applicants. Higher RVE scores are associated with better job-market outcomes, though the association is not robust across all specifications. In contrast, the association with reference-letter length and sentiment is strong and robust: candidates with higher RVE scores receive longer letters written in more favorable language, and this sentiment gradient is steeper for female candidates. The pattern is consistent with appearance affecting academic hiring in part through letters of recommendation.

title: ESTRA: Enabling Extreme Attention Sparsity for Training-Free Video Diffusion Acceleration
abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.

title: Extended No-Go Theorem and Its Verification in Spin-Selective Transport through Chiral Cyclodextrin Assemblies
abstract: The classical two-terminal single-channel no-go theorem relies on time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and scattering-matrix unitarity. In open systems, omitted channels or environment leakage break unitarity, so TRS and the symplectic reciprocity symmetry TRS\(^{\dagger}\) are no longer equivalent, invalidating the classical premises. We prove that if the two-terminal single-channel scattering matrix satisfies TRS\(^{\dagger}\) plus central inversion symmetry, transmission remains no spin selectivity; this result provides an important complement to the classical no-go theorem in nonunitary regime. When these conditions are violated or the single-channel constraint is lifted, spin-selective transport occurs. In charge transport through devices based on chiral \(γ\)-cyclodextrin molecular assemblies, we verify separately the classical no-go theorem in unitary case and its supplementary version together with its multichannel corollary in nonunitary case: when the conditions for the corresponding no-go theorem hold, the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) of the assembly disappears, whereas when they are violated, CISS emerges. These results extend the no-go theorem to nonunitary scattering systems and establish an effective theoretical framework for studying CISS in real molecular assemblies.

title: The Truth Beneath the Tokens: Prompt-Space Recovery of Knowledge Edits in Language Models
abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.

title: Grip, Trace, Write: Force-Aware Imitation and Reinforcement Learning for High-DoF Robotic Handwriting
abstract: Most robotic handwriting rigidly mounts the pen and reduces writing to trajectory tracking. A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention.
