Third, when OOD prediction error exceeds ID error, the AUROC of distance-based and density-based detectors correlates with the size of that gap. Collectively, these findings indicate that reliable OOD detection in scientific domains requires representation learning strategies that explicitly preserve OOD relevant signal, particularly for tasks where current GNN architectures encode no extractable signal at all.

title: Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation
abstract: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

title: AI and Mathematical Work on Mastodon: Attention, Topics, and Target-Specific Evaluations
abstract: How does a mathematical community discuss AI on a federated social platform? We study 24,920 public posts from January--September 2026 by 272 accounts in a fixed roster of 1,002 Mastodon accounts whose profiles indicate mathematical research or study. LLM-assisted extraction identifies 1,191 AI-for-mathematics posts by 101 accounts. Their share of all posts rises from 1.1\% in January to 11.5\% in September, with contributing accounts increasing from 10 to 59. We represent discussion through linked target--aspect--stance triples, separating what is discussed from the property assessed and the author's evaluation. From July to September, capability and usefulness decline as a share of related discussion, while social and institutional concerns increase; changing contributors account for much of the latter shift. Among 38 accounts evaluating both technical quality or utility and communication, credit, or verification procedures, the procedural negative-component fraction is 19.4 percentage points higher on average (95\% account-bootstrap interval: 3.8--35.1). Matching targets within posts gives a similar direction. Repeated extraction varies substantially at the level of individual triples, although replacing the repeated sample preserves the aggregate contrast. Around OpenAI's October 6 mathematics release, related-post share rises from 9.6\% to 13.6\%, and contributing accounts increase from 13 to 28. Post-release discussion includes appreciation of the results' potential mathematical value and applications alongside criticism of promotion centered on result counts, limited methodological disclosure, and verification arrangements.

title: A Benchmark and Layered Evaluation Protocol for Evidence-Grounded Shared Belief Updating in Connected Robotics
abstract: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.

title: Aggregation-Induced Calibration Failure in Sum-Based Label Expansion for Multi-Label Facial Expression Recognition: A Diagnostic Study
abstract: Label-space expansion - predicting a larger joint space and summing back to the original labels - is a natural design for multi-label facial expression recognition, but its failure modes have not been characterised. We evaluate Condition-Aware Label Expansion (CALE) on a self-built dataset (30,240 training images, 3,460 multi-label test images), on seven backbones, and on the public RAF-DB and RAF-ML benchmarks. The central finding is that the aggregation rule, not the representation, decides whether the method works. With a fixed threshold of 0.5, the aggregate score spans 28x across five backbones at 10% of the training data (0.24 to 6.79) and collapses to a 1.9x range at full data, while threshold-free mAP stays within 1.28x over the same backbones, which localises the fault to the summation step. The mechanism is the uncalibrated aggregation rule, which adds the main-branch score to half the sum of the three non-main branches; we verify it by measuring main- and non-main-branch activations. Two plain seven-dimensional sigmoid baselines (BCE, ASL) reach mAP 0.5055 and 0.5175; ASL exceeds three of the five CALE configurations and falls within 0.03 of the best. On single-label FER the gain over a seven-dimensional baseline is nominally significant (paired t-test, p = 0.0436) but does not survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p_BH = 0.2055) or a Wilcoxon test (p = 0.1250). We conclude that sum-based label expansion requires threshold calibration at the deployment data scale, or a learned aggregation, before it can support multi-label decisions.

title: Compact branch sets and injectivity of proper branched coverings
abstract: In this paper, we show that a proper continuous open discrete map from the open unit ball $B^n$ onto a domain in $\R^n$ with $n\geq5$ is a homeomorphism whenever its branch set is compact. This answers Vuorinen's question affirmatively in every dimension $n\ge5.$ In dimension four, we also show that, under the additional assumption of quasiregularity, the map is a quasiconformal homeomorphism. Together with the three-dimensional theorem of Kauranen, Luisto and Tengvall, these results answer the quasiregular question posed as Problem~7.66 in the collections of Barth--Brannan--Hayman and Hayman--Lingham in every dimension $n\ge3$.

title: Prop-WRF: Proposal-Guided Wireless Radiance Field for Scalable Multi-Frequency Outdoor Channel Frequency Response Prediction
abstract: Sparse-directional wireless radiance fields (WRFs) enable complex channel frequency response (CFR) prediction from receiver locations and multipath direction priors. However, in large-scale outdoor environments, long sampling intervals make it difficult to concentrate a limited sampling budget around valid virtual anchors (VAs), degrading prediction accuracy and training stability. This paper proposes Prop-WRF, a proposalnetwork-guided WRF for CFR prediction across multiple subcarriers. A lightweight proposal network learns VA occupancy densities through online distillation from the main network and iteratively guides resampling toward likely VA locations. The main network then predicts complex radiance over the refined intervals and synthesizes CFRs using an analytical propagation model. By introducing frequency encoding only into the radiance branch, a single model jointly learns shared VA geometry from observations across subcarriers while representing frequencydependent complex radiance. A stage-wise hybrid normalized loss and an interval-weight regularizer further strengthen weakchannel supervision and suppress spurious VA peaks. In addition, a multipath simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) front end refines receiver states and path associations to construct geometrically consistent training priors. Simulations show that Prop-WRF improves CFR prediction accuracy and training stability over conventional sparse-directional WRF baselines in larger environments.

title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation
abstract: Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.

title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
abstract: Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.

title: Joint LSFC and Nakagami-m Estimation From Downlink SINR in GZF-Precoded CF-mMIMO
abstract: Accurate characterization of the instantaneous signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) is important for reliability-sensitive cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems. This paper proposes a joint estimation method for link-specific large-scale fading coefficients (LSFCs) and a common Nakagami-$m$ shape parameter using power and downlink SINR measurements. A tractable SINR distribution is first derived under global zero-forcing (GZF) precoding, Nakagami-$m$ fading, and link-level fractional power control (FPC). Based on the derived probability density function (PDF), a model-driven neural network (NN) is developed to solve the resulting maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) problem. Simulations show that the reconstructed SINR distributions obtained with the estimated parameters closely match the empirical distributions. With $2 \times 10^{5}$ samples, the proposed method achieves an LSFC root-mean-square error (RMSE) of approximately 1.0 dB and an $m$ RMSE of approximately 0.085.

title: Computing Classical Partition Functions via Cycle-Space Sampling
abstract: We present a method for computing thermodynamic properties of classical spin systems by reformulating the partition function as a sum over even subgraphs of the interaction graph. Starting from the high-temperature expansion, we show that the expansion coefficients are determined by the weight distribution of the null space of the binary incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and that this statement holds verbatim for multi-spin interactions once the graph is replaced by a hypergraph. We introduce a Monte Carlo scheme based on the $1/t$ Wang-Landau algorithm that performs a random walk directly in this null space. Because the weight distribution is temperature independent, a single estimate yields the zero-field partition function, and the thermodynamic quantities obtained from its temperature derivatives, at arbitrary temperature. We validate the approach against exact finite-size results on the two-dimensional triangular-lattice Ising model, apply it to the three- and four-dimensional hypercubic Ising models where no exact solution is available, and to the two- and three-dimensional Baxter-Wu models, whose three-spin interactions place them outside the reach of Pfaffian methods. For the two-body models we compare against conventional Wang-Landau sampling in energy space; for the Baxter-Wu models we validate against exact enumeration at the smallest size in each dimension.

title: An operator theoretical approach to weak solvability of a porous medium equation with Neumann boundary condition
abstract: This paper is concerned with the Neumann problem for the porous medium equation, \[ u_t - Δa(u) = f \quad \mbox{in}\ Ω\times (0, T), \qquad \nabla a(u) \cdot ν=0 \quad \mbox{on}\ \partial Ω\times (0, T), \qquad u(\cdot, 0) = u_0 \quad \mbox{in}\ Ω\] in a smoothly bounded domain $Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ $(N \in \mathbb{N})$, where $T \in (0,\infty)$, $ν$ is the outward unit normal vector to $\partial Ω$, and where $f$ and $u_0$ are given. A typical example in mind is $a(u)=|u|^{p-2}u$ with $p \in [2, \infty)$. The main interest is weak solvability of the problem in the case that $u_0 \in H^1(Ω)^*$, $f \in L^2(0,T; H^1(Ω)^*)$. Under the condition that the mean value of $f(t)$ vanishes for almost all $t \in (0,T)$, existence of weak solutions is established by an application of abstract results from operator theory, for instance, properties of Gâteaux derivative. The key of the proof lies in the approximate equation \[ [(\varepsilon I - Δ)^{-1} u_\varepsilon]_t + a(u_\varepsilon) = (\varepsilon I - Δ)^{-1} f, \quad \varepsilon \in (0,1), \] where the map $\varepsilon I - Δ$ from $H^1(Ω)$ onto its dual space is regarded as the Riesz isomorphism of $H^1(Ω)$ equipped with an appropriate topology.

title: Identifiable but Hard to Estimate: Rotation in Equally Spaced Overcomplete ICA
abstract: How many observations are needed to estimate a common rotation in two-dimensional overcomplete independent component analysis? We study equally spaced mixing columns with known source count, common source law, and column norm. For a fixed non-Gaussian fourth-order Gram-Charlier source law, the rotation is identifiable modulo the column spacing. Yet the sample size for fixed relative angular accuracy grows exponentially with the source count. We characterize this sample size, up to absolute constants, by the reciprocal of the squared Hellinger distance between two rotations separated by half the column spacing. An explicit radially weighted phase estimator attains this scale uniformly over the rotation family, using the observation radius to prevent cancellation in the mean of an angular harmonic. We also determine the exact exponential decay rate of single-observation total variation for the same pair. This gives bounds on the sample size exponent; its exact value remains open. Finally, a noisy binary-source example shows how an exact zero line of the observed characteristic function can have an exponentially small normal derivative.

title: The Dusty Circumstellar Structure of the Yellow Hypergiant IRC +10420: Constraints from the SED and Near-Infrared Imaging Polarimetry
abstract: The yellow hypergiant IRC +10420 is a post-red supergiant evolving toward higher temperatures. We model its circumstellar dust with the radiative transfer code RADMC-3D, including polarized scattering, constrained by the spectral energy distribution (SED) from 0.4 $μ$m to 1.3 mm and by the K' (2.2 $μ$m) imaging polarimetry of Shenoy et al. (2015), assuming a pole-on view. The model consists of an equatorial structure (a flared inner disk of 0.3 $μ$m grains at 300-3000 au, a ring at 3000-16,000 au whose surface density peaks at $\approx 10^4$ au, and a thin mid-plane disk of 300 $μ$m grains) embedded in a spherical envelope of 0.15 $μ$m grains with $ρ\propto r^{-2.3}$. It reproduces the SED within 0.07 dex and the total- and polarized-intensity profiles; the fractional polarization peaks at 15% at 1.7 arcsec (observed: 14%). The rising surface density of the ring produces the polarized-intensity plateau, and 0.5 $μ$m grains at its outer edge the decline beyond 2 arcsec; grains of $\gtrsim 0.7$ $μ$m are excluded. A thin disk of large grains suggests a settled mid-plane. Stellar temperatures of 7000-8500 K fit equally well. Of the total extinction ($A_V \approx 6.9$ mag), 5 mag is interstellar. Most of the $7.4 \times 10^{-2}$ $M_\odot$ of dust is equatorial; the envelope implies a mass-loss rate of $\approx 10^{-5}$-$10^{-4}$ ($ψ$/100) $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. Because equatorial dust redirects starlight poleward, the pole-on SED overestimates the luminosity by $\approx 1.5$; at the Gaia distance, $L_\star \approx 3.3 \times 10^5$ $L_\odot$. Subtracting a scaled stellar PSF removes most of the nebular light within $\approx 1$ arcsec.

title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

title: Distributionally Robust Rational Inattention
abstract: We study a rational inattention model in which a decision maker chooses a stochastic choice rule while facing ambiguity about the prior distribution over states. Ambiguity is modeled through a distributionally robust formulation in which the prior belongs to an uncertainty set defined by a general phi-divergence. Our main result establishes an exact Lagrangian dual representation of the resulting max-min problem as a finite-dimensional concave optimization problem. This characterization yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the emergence of robust consideration sets and a tractable one-dimensional dual representation for the Cressie-Read family of divergences. We further connect the model to robust risk measures: Average Value-at-Risk arises from a particular non-smooth divergence, while Kullback-Leibler ambiguity is linked through Lagrangian duality to the entropic-risk multiplier representation. We then develop two extensions. The first allows the attention-cost technology and prior ambiguity to be governed by distinct phi-divergences, while the second introduces a deeper layer of ambiguity over the decision maker's baseline prior. Both extensions preserve the finite-dimensional structure of the model and encompass standard Kullback-Leibler robust rational inattention specifications as special or corresponding multiplier cases.

title: DeltaForge: A Post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts VLA for Multi-Domain Autonomous Driving
abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.

title: OverlapAdvisor: Modeling and Adapting Computation-Communication Overlap for Distributed MoE Serving
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference with expert parallelism (EP) relies on All-to-All communication, making computation-communication overlap strategies critical for achieving high performance. However, no strategy is universally optimal. Across 103 production configurations, varying input lengths, and four hardware platforms, we observe that the fastest strategy shifts based on model shape, EP degree, input length, and hardware. Since no strategy dominates more than 80.6% of configurations, configuration-aware selection is necessary. In this work, we propose OverlapAdvisor, which models overlap stages using two granularities to capture computation-communication dependencies. OverlapAdvisor builds a unified performance model, accounting for deviations from peak compute, memory, and communication performance across workloads and hardware. This model enables launch-time, configuration-aware strategy selection within two serving engines. We conduct experiments on four MoE models (30B-235B) against three baselines, utilizing SGLang and vLLM. At the kernel level, OverlapAdvisor achieves 1.16x average and 1.59x maximum speedups, with a prediction MAPE of 3.3%-15.9%. In SGLang and vLLM, it improves end-to-end throughput up to 31.7%. Its granularity-guided optimizations further achieve median speedups of 1.10x for DeepEP-v1 and 1.22x for FlashMoE.

title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization
abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Angular Rotational Counter (ARC), a novel approach to represent objective functions that can be decomposed as a weighted sum of Boolean functions. ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register used in much of the previous literature. We mathematically establish and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all possible solutions and derive the relationship between the resulting measurement probabilities and the objective. This design was applied to construct a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata and state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost function, which is a special case of the quadratic assignment problem. We evaluate this oracle design on 26 benchmarks and compare it with corresponding Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics. Across these benchmarks, the oracle with ARC produces a mean reduction in the qubit count of 20.8%, gate count of 89.3%, circuit depth of 92.4%, and quantum cost of 90.6%. These results demonstrate substantial reductions in circuit cost for the evaluated benchmarks and establish rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in optimization based on quantum search algorithms.

title: Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval from Modular Forms
abstract: We present new information-theoretic protocols for $s$-server, doubly-efficient private information retrieval (PIR) in sublinear server time and one extra bit of space on the servers, for every constant $s \geq 2$. On an $n$-bit database, each of the $s$ PIR servers first builds and stores a preprocessing data structure consisting of $n+1$ bits (which is unique to each server, and after which the server may discard the original database). Then, each server answers a PIR query in time $T_s(n)$, by reading at most $T_s$ bits of its data structure and sending them to the user. In the two server setting ($s=2$), our PIR protocols achieve $T_2 = n^{0.82}$, matching the server time of the state-of-the-art schemes of Henzinger and Ragavan (EUROCRYPT 2026) while shrinking their storage from $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ to $n+1$ bits. With $s \geq 3$ servers, our PIR protocols retain the $n+1$ bits of storage and additionally improve on the server time of all prior information-theoretic $s$-server schemes with $n^{1+o(1)}$ storage: for example, achieving $T_3 = n^{0.74}$ and $T_{10} = n^{0.61}$ (previously $n^{0.79}$ and $n^{0.75}$). Asymptotically, as the server count $s$ grows, we shrink the number of servers required to achieve a given server-work exponent from $s^{3.9}$ to $s$. Our results draw inspiration from matching-vector techniques (Efremenko, STOC 2009), which we generalize to handle degree-two computations in the exponent. Using this generalization, we build doubly-efficient PIR from the new intermediate abstraction of Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions. Then, we construct such Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions via a connection to modular forms and complex analysis: if a Fourier-sparse cone-delta function does not exist, then there exists a modular form which has too many roots, contradicting the valence formula.

title: GPU acceleration of the numerical-atomic-orbital DFT code OpenMX with GEMMul8: performance and numerical agreement on consumer and HPC GPUs
abstract: We integrate GEMMul8, a library that emulates FP64 matrix multiplication on INT8 Tensor Cores, into the GPU version of the numerical-atomic-orbital first-principles code OpenMX 4.0. The GEMMul8 configuration is compared against the cuBLAS FP64 configuration within each of two environments, a consumer GeForce RTX 5080 and an HPC-oriented H100 PCIe, for the four computational paths formed by collinear (CL) or noncollinear (NCL) spin and band or $Γ$-point-cluster solvers. In fixed-work measurements that completed 25 SCF iterations, the diagonalization section of a 384-atom CL band calculation on the RTX 5080 is accelerated by a factor of 2.1 and the total run time by 1.8; a 512-atom CL cluster calculation, which uses only real matrix products in contrast to the CL band calculation, still gains a factor of 1.5 in the diagonalization section. On the H100, GEMMul8 provides little additional acceleration of the diagonalization section. In an accuracy test on a 216-atom Si system in which one atom was displaced by 0.05 angstrom, all 24 configurations were converged using an SCF convergence criterion of $10^{-8}$; every configuration converged at the same iteration within each path, and the differences between GEMMul8 and cuBLAS are at most $2\times10^{-12}$ Ha in the total energy and $7\times10^{-12}$ Ha/Bohr in force components.

title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed. We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.

title: Are UFOs Real? Introducing Unified Factored Organizers
abstract: Implicit in much research in deep learning is the assumption that if a network achieves low loss, then it must have learned a good representation of its training data. Recent work by Kumar et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.11581) questions this assumption, arguing that networks trained with conventional gradient descent achieve low loss despite learning fractured entangled representations (FER), leaving related concepts disconnected and unrelated concepts entangled inappropriately. Kumar et al. further show that dramatically better representations are possible: a network evolved through an open-ended, human-in-the-loop process learned unified factored representations (UFR) that capture the regularities of the domain far better than a counterpart with nearly identical outputs trained with conventional gradient descent. Inspired by UFR, this paper introduces unified factored organizers (UFOs), networks trained to model regularities in the representations of other networks. A network can then be trained both to achieve low loss on its task objective and to align its representations with the model learned by the UFO. Networks trained with UFOs are shown to learn qualitatively superior representations in an image-regression domain where representations are easily interpretable. To provide quantitative evidence for the impact of UFOs on representation learning, a transformer is trained with and without UFO regularization to grok a modular arithmetic problem set. When combined with weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 10x relative to weight decay alone. Without weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 100x relative to an unregularized baseline. If UFOs are real, they suggest a new paradigm where loss functions themselves are trained to learn an effective model of good representation.

title: Can Hindsight Critics Guide Delayed Actors?
abstract: Sensory delays create temporal misalignments between the state of the environment and the observations available to an agent, turning Markovian control problems into partially observable ones. In this work, we inquire whether such misalignments can be mitigated during training by using hindsight to recover aligned state-action transitions. We introduce Hindsight Critics, an asymmetric extension of the Soft Actor-Critic for reinforcement learning under partial observability. The critics are trained on hindsight-aligned transitions whereas the actor learns from the resulting privileged value estimates despite only having access to delayed observations. Comparisons against delay-aware and unaware baselines on the DelayBench suite show that Hindsight Critics can partially compensate for observation delays without requiring modifications to the agent's observations during deployment.

title: Separable social welfare evaluation without completeness
abstract: In this paper, we study incomplete social evaluation of utility vectors to capture situations in which there is disagreement in society about the degree of inequality aversion. We characterize multi-prioritarian criteria using efficiency, equity, impartiality, separability, and a condition called continuous divisible completion condition. We also provide uniqueness results and investigate comparative inequality aversion.

title: Schur multiplier exponents of finite $p$-groups: bounds and critical-class phenomena
abstract: The Schur exponent conjecture is a long-standing conjecture in group theory, which asserts that $\operatorname{exp}(\mathrm{M}(G))\mid\operatorname{exp}(G)$ for every finite group $G$, where $\mathrm{M}(G)$ denotes the Schur multiplier of $G$. In this article, we prove that the Schur exponent conjecture holds for finite $p$-groups $G$ of nilpotency class at most $2p-2$ when $p$ is an odd prime. Our approach is to establish upper bounds on the exponent of $γ_{s+1}(G)$ for $s\in\mathbb{N}$. Using this approach, we further establish exponent bounds for Schur multipliers, nonabelian exterior squares, and tensor squares of $G$ of arbitrary nilpotency class, improving some existing bounds. Moreover, we show that Moravec's Bogomolov multiplier exponent conjecture holds for finite $p$-groups of nilpotency class at most $2p-1$. Havas conjectured that, for every prime $p>3$, there exists a finite $p$-group of exponent $p$ and nilpotency class $2p-1$ for which the Schur exponent conjecture fails. We show that the Schur exponent conjecture still holds for finite $p$-groups of nilpotency class at most $2p-1$ generated by at most three elements. For four-generator groups of exponent $p$ and class at most $2p-1$, we prove that $\mathrm{M}(G)\cong C_{p^2}^{\,b}\times C_p^{\,a}$ for some $a\ge0$ and $b\in\{0,1\}$.

title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
abstract: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.

title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
abstract: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence. Finally, campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's expenditure schedule: unlike a matched numerical bounded-confidence population receiving interventions at the same times and locations, the LLM population exhibits a payoff structure with no pure-strategy equilibrium.

title: Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk
abstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.

title: Action Representation for Spatial Generalization in Robot World Models
abstract: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.

title: A Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem for marked graphs
abstract: The classical Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem characterizes graphs with least eigenvalue at least $-2$ in terms of generalized line graphs, exceptional graphs, and root systems. In this paper, we establish a marked graph extension of this theorem. For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and a binary vector $\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^n$, we completely characterize all marked graphs $\mathbf{G}=(G,\mathbf{b})$ such that $λ_{\min}(A(G)+\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}^\top-J_n)\ge -2$, where $J_n$ denotes the all-ones matrix of order $n$. Using representations by finite root systems, we show that every irreducible marked graph satisfying the above inequality is represented by either the root system $B_n$ or the exceptional root system $E_8$. This leads to a complete structural characterization in terms of irreducible marked graphs, namely induced subgraphs of extended generalized line graphs, the marked graph $(2K_1,\mathbf{0})$, and exceptional graphs with all vertices marked. In the special case $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{j}$, our characterization reduces to the original Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem. The root system $B_n$ and extended generalized line graphs play the roles occupied by $D_n$ and generalized line graphs in the classical theory. We further apply the characterization to graphs whose second largest eigenvalue is at most $1$, showing that every $-2$-markable graph satisfies this spectral condition.

title: Integrating Deep PPG Representations and Digital Biomarkers for Aortic Stenosis Detection with Peri-TAVI Assessment
abstract: Access to echocardiography is often limited, delaying recognition of progressive aortic stenosis (AS). A brief, low-cost physiological measurement obtained during routine care could help identify patients who may warrant earlier imaging. Here, we present PulseAS, integrating deep photoplethysmography (PPG) representations, waveform biomarkers and clinical information for high-grade AS screening. Three complementary analyses assessed (1) validation and transfer across cohorts differing in geography and ethnic composition, (2) score-based enrichment of AS and pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) cases, and (3) preoperative and postoperative pulse changes. Using 15-s recordings, separate patient-level cross-validation in EDU (n = 1,209) and MIMIC-III (n = 2,970) yielded AUROCs of 0.818 (PulseAS-XGB) and 0.838 (PulseAS-L2), respectively. In external validation from MIMIC-III to EDU, PulseAS-XGB achieved an AUROC of 0.716, improving to 0.813 after local adaptation. The highest-scoring 10% captured 45.2% of all high-grade AS cases in EDU and 41.3% in MIMIC-III, and 56.9% of pre-TAVI cases in EDU. Notably, in the EDU TAVI subgroup, PPG waveforms showed earlier systolic peaks and narrower systolic contours following intervention. These findings support clinical-PPG risk stratification in new populations and warrant prospective evaluation of echocardiographic prioritisation.

title: Distribution-Free Symmetry Detection in Multi-Reference Alignment at Low SNR
abstract: Symmetry can reveal the structure of a signal, but detecting it becomes difficult when observations are noisy and randomly transformed. We study how to infer symmetry directly from multi-reference alignment data with additive isotropic Gaussian noise of known variance, without aligning the observations or knowing how the transformations were sampled. For cyclic symmetry, we identify a simple statistical signature that yields tests with exact finite-sample error guarantees. We demonstrate their performance even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. Dihedral symmetry presents a deeper challenge: we show that, for some signals, invariant moments below a sharp order threshold cannot distinguish reflectional from purely rotational symmetry. For generic signals, however, this distinction emerges much earlier. We use these insights to develop tests for dihedral symmetry with asymptotic error control under explicit nondegeneracy conditions. Together, the results clarify what we can learn about symmetry from noisy, unaligned data and suggest a path toward symmetry inference in cryo-EM.

title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
abstract: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.

title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes
abstract: Log-optimal e-variables at fixed horizons, also called numéraires, have been conjectured to ``almost'' form an e-process for exponential-family null hypotheses. A related open question is whether an e-process can attain the optimal e-power at every horizon up to a bounded loss. Given a final horizon, we study the minimax regret of e-processes relative to the numéraires at all times up to it. For the Gaussian location null and the composite alternative of Gaussian distributions with a smaller variance and an unknown location, we show that the minimax regret in the worst case over the location grows like the iterated logarithm of the final horizon. A single e-process attains this rate at every horizon. This growth answers the question negatively. It also refutes the conjecture if ``almost'' means a regret bounded uniformly over horizons. For this Gaussian location problem, we thus exhibit the frontier precisely: the minimax regret is bounded if and only if the alternatives have at least the variance of the null.

title: Beyond Head Importance: Collective Computation in Video Transformers
abstract: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.

title: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers with Graph Computing Accelerators
abstract: Solving large sparse linear systems by Gaussian elimination is a challenging computational task due to the introduction of non-zero elements, or fill-in. Practitioners use heuristics such as the nested dissection reordering algorithm to try to reduce fill-in. In practice, reordering codes do not achieve the same parallel scaling as factorization, nor can they exploit AVX instructions or GPUs. Thus, reordering can be the primary runtime bottleneck in large-scale computer-aided engineering applications. We consider the use of a novel accelerator, the UpDown system, to accelerate the METIS multilevel nested dissection reordering algorithm. The UpDown system is designed for a broad class of graph computing and irregular algorithms. We report results for small-scale UpDown systems that will be available commercially in 2027, using validated simulation and FPGA emulation platforms. Our findings indicate that small UpDown systems can speed up METIS by two-orders of magnitude versus a single CPU. Compared to ParMETIS on hundreds of MPI ranks, we anticipate the same small UpDown systems offer speedups of 4 - 7, providing the potential to significantly speed finite element simulations

title: Tropical Gaussian Anticoncentration: Optimal Instance-Dependent Bounds for Online Learning in Extensive-Form Games
abstract: We study the minimax regret of full-information online decision making in extensive-form games. For prediction with expert advice, the optimal regret is $Θ(\sqrt{T\log K})$, where $K$ is the number of experts, or equivalently, the number of normal-form actions. For treeplex strategy spaces, existing efficient algorithms, including KOMWU and online mirror descent with the weight-one dilated entropy regularizer, achieve regret $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of reduced normal-form strategies. We prove that this logarithmic dependence is minimax optimal in the worst-case full-information reward model. The main difficulty is that pure plans in a treeplex are not independent experts: their rewards are correlated through the recursive structure of decisions and observations. To capture this correlation, we introduce tropical Gaussian formulae, recursive Gaussian expressions built from maxima and normalized sums which preserve the variance. The index count of such a formula matches the number of reduced normal-form continuation plans in the corresponding subtree. Our main analytic result shows that every log-balanced tropical Gaussian formula with index count $N$ has Gaussian width $Ω(\sqrt{\log N})$. While a direct approach struggles to recover this lower bound, our proof uses a spherical entropy profile to measure scale-dependent separation among the Gaussian directions, and then applies Turán's theorem and Sudakov minoration to obtain the width lower bound. Applying this result to treeplexes gives an oblivious hard distribution with valid transition outcome and Rademacher terminal rewards, establishing a regret lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$. This matches known upper bounds up to universal constants and shows that the DilEnt/KOMWU dependence on the reduced normal-form complexity is unavoidable.

title: Velocity gradient tensor reconstruction from tracer orientations via Jeffery dynamics
abstract: The velocity gradient tensor is a local quantity, but methods that obtain it by spatial differencing of the velocities of spherical tracers amplify measurement noise. We propose a method that reconstructs the velocity gradient tensor from the orientations of non-spherical tracers such as flakes and rods. Based on the Jeffery-type equation, we show that, for incompressible flow, all components of the velocity gradient tensor are uniquely determined from the orientations of four tracers and their time derivatives in the neighbourhood of a reference point (orientation-based method). The method uses neither tracer positions nor spatial differencing. It therefore requires orientation measurements only near the reference point, without requiring measurements throughout a three-dimensional region, and measurement noise is amplified only through temporal differencing. Consequently, the minimum achievable error scales as $σ^{1/2}$ with the noise level $σ$, compared with $σ^{1/3}$ for the positional PTV-plus-differencing approach (position-based method). Numerical tests further show that the vorticity is reconstructed more accurately than by the position-based method, whereas the strain rate is reconstructed with comparable accuracy. Finally, applying the method to spherical Couette flow, we find that the reconstruction fails where the neighbouring tracers align, which renders the inversion ill-conditioned, and that this degeneracy appears as the characteristic light-and-dark pattern familiar from flow visualization.

title: Work needed to lift a mass in Schwarzschild spacetime
abstract: We determine the work needed to lift a mass from $r_2$ to $r_1$ in Schwarzschild spacetime in three ways. First we use a winch and a light rope. Then we use a photon collision. Finally we let the mass decay into photons and reconstruct it at the higher radius. All three methods give the same local work at $r_1$, $W_1=mc^2[1-N(r_2)/N(r_1)]$, where $N(r)=\sqrt{1-r_s/r}$. Thus, independently of $r_1$, the work tends to $mc^2$ as $r_2$ approaches the horizon. The rope example also gives a useful general-relativistic version of a simple machine: a rope in equilibrium need not have equal local forces at its two ends. The redshift factor plays the role of the lever arm. For a real rope the energy conditions prevent the tension from decreasing with height, so this lever advantage is confined to the idealization. The examples are intended as teaching material for undergraduate relativity courses.

title: Presentations of inverse Artin monoids of type $D_n$ via cluster mutations
abstract: Let $D_n^\varepsilon$ denote the Dynkin diagram of type $D_{n+1}$ with the endpoint $\varepsilon$ of its long branch frozen, and let $\mathcal{M}(D_n^\varepsilon)$ be the mutation class of any orientation of this diagram under mutations at mutable vertices. For each $Γ\in\mathcal{M}(D_n^\varepsilon)$, we define an inverse monoid $M_Γ$ by generators and relations determined by $Γ$. We prove that $M_Γ\cong M_{μ_k(Γ)}$ for every mutable vertex $k$. Consequently, every quiver in this mutation class yields a presentation of the inverse Artin monoid of type $D_n$. Our argument establishes mutation invariance for the presentations of inverse Artin monoids of both types $A_n^\varepsilon$ and $D_n^\varepsilon$.

title: When Does Physics Beat Data? Data-Efficient Traffic State Estimation with Amortized PINNs
abstract: Traffic state estimation (TSE) reconstructs traffic density at unmonitored locations from a sparse set of sensors. Data-driven models work well when sensors are dense but degrade sharply as coverage thins. We show that imposing the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards conservation law as a physics-informed prior makes TSE more data-efficient. On four real corridors (NGSIM, I-80, PeMS04, PeMS08), physics-informed estimators generalise to held-out sensors where data-driven models, including classical and deep kriging, overfit the observed ones. On the two shock-rich corridors the effect is a clear crossover: as more sensors are held out, data-driven models collapse while the physics-informed estimator degrades gracefully, leading the no-physics network by about 26-38% at 85-90% held out and the strongest classical kriging by about 10-21% at 90%. A matched smoothness prior does not reproduce the gain, and an extended Kalman filter on the same LWR model is outperformed on the shock corridors, so the advantage comes from how the conservation law is imposed. Finally, one loss-conditional PINN removes the per-corridor loss-weight search, matching a 20-point search at about 5x lower cost.

title: Interplay of Scalar and Pseudo-Scalar Mesonic Channels in $Λ\barΛ$ Spin Correlations
abstract: The spin correlation of $Λ\barΛ$ hyperon pairs produced in heavy-ion collisions is investigated through scalar and pseudo-scalar mesonic channels that mediate the creation of $s\bar{s}$ pairs. Because a $J=0$ meson forces $L=S$ while parity requires $(-1)^{L+1}=+/-1$, the two vertices project the pair onto distinct total-spin states: a scalar ($0^+$) vertex selects the $L=S=1$ configuration with a spin weight of $+1$, whereas a pseudo-scalar ($0^-$) vertex selects the $L=S=0$ configuration with a weight of $-3$; these weights are the traces of the correlation tensor, corresponding to $P_{s\bar{s}}=+1/3$ and $-1$, respectively. Implementing this framework within the three-flavor Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model at the Random-Phase-Approximation level, we compute the scalar and pseudo-scalar spectral weights. Our results show that the pseudo-scalar channel dominates, resulting in a negative net correlation fraction throughout. And the spin correlation also depends on the opening angle: strongest spin correlation at around $θ=0$ while weakest at $θ=π$. Furthermore, we show that the collision-energy dependence of the momentum-integrated spin correlation along the freeze-out line is sensitive to the trajectory's path relative to the chiral phase boundary. Trajectories passing near the crossover region exhibit a non-monotonic structure, providing a sensitive probe for the location of the chiral phase transition.

title: Ejecta fate and deposition in the Didymos-Dimorphos system after the DART impact
abstract: Kinetic impact is a promising technique for asteroid deflection in planetary defense. The NASA Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos, the satellite of the binary asteroid (65803) Didymos, at 6.1449 km s^{-1} in 2022. Observations revealed changes in both the orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos and the heliocentric orbit of the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The ESA Hera spacecraft will arrive at the system at the end of 2026 to investigate the post-impact surfaces. Here, we present an analytical model, based on Maxwell's Z model, to predict ejecta behavior following the DART impact. The model provides the relationships among ejection velocity, ejection angle, and ejecta mass, allowing the momentum enhancement factor beta to be estimated for both Dimorphos and the Didymos-Dimorphos system. We show that the observed beta can be reproduced when 0.3-1% of the impact kinetic energy is converted into ejecta kinetic energy and the effective strength of the target is less than 100 Pa. The escaping mass is estimated to be 0.3-3.0% of the mass of Dimorphos. The globally averaged and minimum ejecta thicknesses on Dimorphos are estimated to be 2.0 m and 0.5 m, respectively, indicating that the entire surface was resurfaced by ejecta deposition, although boulders larger than 1 m were only partially buried. The model also predicts the momentum partition parameter kappa_p to be as low as 0.6, suggesting that the mass and the bulk density of Dimorphos may be revised upward. These predictions provide quantitative constraints for interpreting forthcoming Hera observations.

title: The shape and velocity of black hole coronas
abstract: The first highly significant detection of the polarization of the X-rays from the Black Hole X-ray Binary Cygnus X-1 revealed surprisingly strong polarization parallel to its radio jet. The observation is now commonly interpreted as resulting from the Comptonization of some lower frequency seed photons in a laterally extended corona. The emitting plasma is likely moving along the jet axis with a sizable fraction beta of the speed of light, amplifying the polarization degree. In this letter we address the question of how laterally extended the corona actually needs to be to account for the observations, and we calculate the required outflow velocities of velocity-stratified coronas as a function of the stationary-frame aspect ratio h=H/2R of cylindrical coronas of height H and radius R. We find that models with h lesser equal 0.8 and beta=0.5-0.9 at the top of the corona can give both the observed photon index of Gamma=1.6 and the observed 4% polarization parallel to the symmetry axis. We do not find suitable solutions for larger h. Given the constraints on h, we discuss the likely size of the corona, emphasizing that compact coronas close to the black hole are preferred as they can tap more efficiently into the gravitational energy and the rotational energy of the black hole, and are less exposed to their own emission reprocessed in the optically thick portion of the accretion flow.

title: Design of a hybrid tendon-linkage finger with coupled and adaptive motion
abstract: Dexterous robotic fingers require coordinated joint motion and adaptability to object contact, while independently actuating multiple joints increases the complexity of the transmission mechanism. This paper presents a hybrid tendon--linkage robotic finger with four mechanical degrees of freedom driven by three actuators. The MCP abduction/adduction joint is driven through a bevel gear, while MCP and PIP flexion/extension are driven by separate bidirectional tendon transmissions. The DIP joint is not independently actuated but is coupled to the PIP joint through a four-bar linkage with a torsional spring and mechanical stopper. The tendon routing also introduces mechanical coupling between the MCP and PIP joints. Kinematic analysis was conducted to describe the coupled and adaptive motions, and experiments were performed to evaluate the joint motion characteristics. ArUco-based measurements showed that the coupled motion closely matched the theoretical prediction, whereas the adaptive motion was partially limited by interference between linkage components. The fabricated finger demonstrated different contact postures with cylindrical, cuboid, and irregularly shaped objects, and the mean peak fingertip force was 4.56 N. The proposed mechanism provides both coupled motion and contact-dependent adaptation without requiring an additional actuator for the DIP joint.

title: Multi-Modal Agricultural Document Understanding at the DAGRI Task
abstract: Agricultural documents, such as prefectural technical reports and crop calendars, are critical knowledge resources. However, their complex table layouts, significant variations in document length, and dense multi-modal elements pose substantial challenges for automated understanding. To address these issues, the NTCIR-19 DAGRI (Data Analytics for aGRicultural Information) task introduced three subtasks focusing on different dimensions of document intelligence. In the Table Information Extraction (TableIE) task, we developed a multi-stage pipeline combining structure-preserving parsing via MinerU, region-adaptive segmentation for long documents, and a dual-modal (vision-text) extraction strategy for complex work schedules. This approach achieved first place with an exact match score of 0.6566. For Multi-Table Multi-Hop Question Answering (MTMH-QA) over interrelated JSON tables, we adopted an agentic search framework utilizing DCI-Agent to iteratively explore directories via bash commands, reinforced by a cross-model validation mechanism. This yielded a revised accuracy of 0.8444, initially ranked first. In the Figure and Table Question Answering (FiT-QA) task, which requires comprehending single large composite images, we implemented a dual-modal VLM pipeline enhanced by deterministic answer normalization, securing the highest BLEU score. Together, our system effectively addresses regional structural variations, dynamic cross-file evidence discovery, and multi-modal alignment, providing a robust framework for complex agricultural document understanding.

title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

title: OmniSynth: A Meta-Evaluation Framework for Benchmarking the Quality of Missingness-Inclusive Synthetic Health Data
abstract: Synthetic data are an emerging solution to the reproducibility crisis in machine learning for health, driven by data privacy restrictions surrounding electronic health records. Yet no consensus exists on how to evaluate synthetic health data quality, existing metrics functionally overlook missingness despite its prevalence in clinical data, and benchmarking frameworks have never been empirically validated. We introduce OmniSynth, a modular Python benchmarking suite that evaluates synthetic tabular data across fidelity, missingness similarity, utility, and privacy - the first framework to explicitly evaluate missingness as a distinct dimension of synthetic data fidelity. OmniSynth further proposes a meta-evaluation procedure that stress-tests evaluation performance under controlled degradation scenarios, providing a systematic characterization of how an evaluation framework behaves across datasets, sample sizes, and variable types. Applying this procedure to OmniSynth in two health datasets (Pima Indians Diabetes; MIMIC-IV-ED), we found that scores responded monotonically to degradation, three of four novel missingness metrics captured induced missing data patterns, and individual metric contributions to the scoring system were empirically justified.

title: Critical Slowing Down and the Crossover to Quantum Scrambling in Holographic CFTs
abstract: We investigate critical relaxation dynamics and their connection to quantum information scrambling in the conformal field theory dual to a Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter (RN-AdS) black hole. Employing the holographic dictionary, we formulate the thermodynamics in terms of boundary CFT variables and study the stochastic evolution of the reduced horizon radius using Langevin and Fokker-Planck formalisms. We demonstrate pronounced critical slowing down in the dual CFT, characterized by an enhancement of the autocorrelation time and stochastic fluctuations, accompanied by a suppression of the lowest nonzero Fokker-Planck eigenvalue. The autocorrelation time exhibits a universal power-law divergence, $τ\sim|ε|^{-Δ}$, with $Δ\simeq 2/3$, consistent with the analytical prediction and previous bulk gravitational results. Going beyond the conventional single-parameter analysis, we incorporate variations of the CFT central charge and identify a combined scaling variable involving temperature and central charge, demonstrating that the leading relaxation dynamics retain the same critical exponent along different trajectories in the two-dimensional parameter space. Finally, we explore the interplay between thermodynamic relaxation and quantum information scrambling by comparing the relaxation timescale with the fast-scrambling timescale. The comparison reveals a crossover between thermodynamic relaxation and quantum scrambling for which we derive the corresponding crossover scale analytically and find that, in the large-central-charge limit, it behaves as $\hatε\sim(C\ln C)^{-3/2}$. We also verify this numerically using the full nonlinear free-energy landscape. Our results connect critical dynamical scaling, finite-central-charge effects, and quantum scrambling within the holographic CFT framework.

title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
abstract: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Cross-Lingual Multi-Jurisdiction Patent Drafting from Patent Cooperation Treaty Applications
abstract: Securing patent protection across countries requires drafting claims separately for each national patent office, in the relevant language and according to its legal and stylistic conventions. Patent claims can therefore differ across languages and jurisdictions because of translation, target-office drafting practices, and prosecution-stage changes. We formulate cross-lingual patent drafting as generating plausible candidate claim sets for a specified target language, jurisdiction, and prosecution stage from a source claim set in another language. The task models jurisdiction- and stage-specific transformations beyond content-preserving translation. We construct a large-scale Japanese-English dataset by linking Japan Patent Office (JPO) and United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) records through 884,179 Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)-derived patent families. Across six released configurations, these families yield 4,067,168 directional claim-set instances; four core configurations form the main benchmark. Commercial machine translation and zero- and few-shot prompting capture part of the task, while supervised adaptation provides the strongest overall baseline, showing that task-specific patterns can be learned from linked cross-jurisdictional claim sets.

title: When Answer Decodability Is Not a Decision: Separating Final-Answer and Imminent-Emission Signals in Chain-of-Thought
abstract: Answer probes applied to chain-of-thought hidden states are often read as evidence that a language model has already decided its final response. This reading overlooks a competing signal, the candidate the model is about to mention. We introduce emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before any fit. On correct DecisionDepth (DD) rollouts in which a distractor is mentioned before the final answer, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. This pattern is not universal. In a pre-specified evaluation of Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled on held-out MMLU questions, using a full-prefix attention reader over every thinking position, both targets are decodable and the final answer is read far more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). Model, task, positions, and reader change together between these settings, and an attempted matched comparison on DD produced no valid statistics because the imminent-mention probe did not train reliably, so we do not identify what reverses the order. On DD, planted-signal controls show that the reader recovers an injected final-answer signal at one tenth of full dose. Answer-candidate decodability is therefore target-relative and protocol-dependent: a strong answer readout does not by itself establish when a model commits, and a probe that fails to train is not evidence that the information is absent. ECDP is a practical control for distinguishing imminent text emission from evidence of a settled decision.

title: Developing a Street View Imagery Processing Pipeline for Building-Level Vacant House Assessment
