Finally, we resolve two unary merge-model hardness questions left by the bounded-alphabet study \citep{kastreva2026}: standard unary bottom-up tokenisation is APX-hard, and unary optimal pair encoding is strongly NP-complete, strengthening the previously known weak hardness.

title: Sufficient conditions for spanning trees with bounded total excess in tough graphs
abstract: Let $G$ be a connected graph and $T$ a spanning tree of $G$. The toughness of $G$ is defined by $t(G)=\min\Big\{\frac{|S|}{c(G-S)}:S\subseteq V(G), c(G-S)\geq2\Big\}$ for $G\neq K_n$. A graph $G$ is said to be $t$-tough if $t(G)\geq t$. The size, the adjacency spectral radius and the signless Laplacian spectral radius of $G$ are denoted by $e(G)$, $ρ(G)$ and $q(G)$, respectively. The $k$-excess of a vertex $v$ in $T$ is defined as $\max\{0,d_T(v)-k\}$. The total $k$-excess $\mbox{te}(T,k)$ is defined by $\mbox{te}(T,k)=\sum\limits_{v\in V(T)}{\max\{0,d_T(v)-k\}}$. A tree $T$ is called a $k$-tree if $d_T(v)\leq k$ for every $v\in V(T)$, namely, the maximum degree of a $k$-tree is at most $k$. It is obvious that $T$ is a spanning $k$-tree if and only if $\mbox{te}(T,k)=0$. This paper investigates a generalization of spanning $k$-trees using a concept called total $k$-excess and puts forward three lower bounds based on $e(G)$, $ρ(G)$ and $q(G)$ in a connected $\frac{k}{k(k-2)+b+3}$-tough graph $G$ to guarantee that $G$ has a spanning tree $T$ with $\mbox{te}(T,k)\leq b$, where $k\geq3$ and $b\geq0$ are two integers. As corollaries, we obtain three sufficient conditions for a connected $\frac{k}{k(k-2)+3}$-tough graph to has a spanning $k$-tree.

title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

title: UniOMA: Unified Optimal-Transport Multi-Modal Structural Alignment for Robot Perception
abstract: Achieving generalizable and well-aligned multimodal representations remains a core challenge in robot learning. While recent approaches have attempted to align modalities by modeling conditional or higher-order statistical dependencies, they do not explicitly consider the structural coherence across modalities. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal alignment method that augments existing contrastive losses with a geometry-aware Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) distance-based regularization. To this end, we encode intra-modal geometry for each modality and reduce cross-modal structural discrepancies through a dynamically learned GW barycenter, thereby encouraging structural consistency in addition to instance-level contrastive alignment. We apply this optimal-transport-based alignment strategy to robot perception tasks involving underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals, where modality data often exhibit varying sample densities. Extensive experiments on five robotic benchmarks show that our method improves structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across a wide range of downstream tasks, including robot and environment state prediction. Moreover, our GW-based regularization can be seamlessly integrated into most InfoNCE-like objectives.

title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics
abstract: This study focuses on regression estimation and variable selection based on target data, while incorporating information from coefficient estimates obtained in related studies. A weighted combination of these estimates may agree with some target effects but differ from others. We propose Transfer Regression with Adaptive Credibility Estimation (TRACE), a Bayesian method requiring only fitted coefficients and sample sizes from source studies. TRACE learns simplex-constrained source weights shared across variables. Separate latent indicators determine target inclusion and whether each coefficient is guided by the weighted source estimate. We develop an approximate collapsed variational expectation-maximization algorithm with robust source-weight initialization. Under suitable conditions, consistency of variable selection, transfer decisions, and source-weight estimation is established. These results hold at every prespecified fixed iteration in fixed dimension and at global mean-field optima of the exact collapsed variational objective as the dimension grows. Simulations show that TRACE achieves competitive variable-selection performance under different patterns of source heterogeneity. An application to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project illustrates its use in cross-tissue gene-expression prediction.

title: QCC-WM: Linking Macro-State Dynamics and Visual Generation via Quotient Causal Construction
abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.

title: Boosting bottom-up milling of glass with GHz laser bursts
abstract: Burst-mode laser processing has gained increasing attention in material machining due to its potential to enhance processing efficiency and quality. However, most studies have focused on conventional top-down machining strategies, while investigations of bottom-up milling (BUM) remain limited. In this work, we optimize processing parameters for high-efficiency glass milling using a bottom-up approach with GHz bursts. The results show that the highest BUM efficiencies are achieved when employing high pulse counts ($\geq$ 20). To the best of our knowledge, we report the highest glass milling efficiency, reaching more than 250 $μ$m$^3$/$μ$J for both soda-lime glass and fused silica. Furthermore, increasing the burst repetition rate while maintaining a parameter set associated with high milling efficiency enables a material removal rate larger than 8 mm$^3$/s.

title: Edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--Širáň graphs $H_q$ for every prime power $q\geq 3$
abstract: Motivated by Hamilton cycle problems and applications to collective communication, we study edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--Širáň (MMS) graphs. The MMS graph $H_q$ (indexed by a prime power $q$) is a highly symmetric graph arising from finite fields. For every prime power $q\geq 3$, we prove that the MMS graph $H_q$ contains $\big\lceil\frac{q-1}{2}\big\rceil$ edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles. This resolves a problem of Li, Wang and Zheng, who established the result for prime $q$ and for $q=4$. Our construction uses graph lifts over finite fields and joins the components of lifted Hamilton cycles by adding edges within vertex fibres. The resulting cycles can be constructed using $O(|E(H_q)|)$ finite field operations, comparisons, and elementary list operations. As an application, these cycles provide edge-disjoint spanning rings for parallel ring-all-reduce algorithms on MMS networks.

title: DForkTree: Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Fork-Aware Block Diffusion Draft Trees
abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by having a lightweight drafter propose future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash predict an entire block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees directly from their per-position distributions. Each distribution implicitly assumes that the drafter's own greedy continuation is accepted, whereas a draft tree improves over a chain only on branches that leave this greedy path. Once a path forks, the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its top candidates often miss the true token. Re-running the drafter from the fork token largely restores its accuracy, showing that the errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than from limited model capacity. In this paper, we introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. It adjusts the drafter's scores with pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and a layer-wise GPU search recovers the exact optimal tree under these scores. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, by up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.

title: Gorenstein modules over Thompson's group
abstract: Let $k$ be any commutative ring of characteristic $0$. We construct an example of a countably presented Gorenstein projective module over the algebra of Thompson's group $F$ with coefficients in $k$, that is not Benson cofibrant. In particular, we provide a negative answer to a conjecture proposed by Dembegioti and Talelli. The construction uses a general method that produces totally acyclic complexes of flat modules and is based on the computation of the (co-)cohomology of $F$ by Brown and Geoghegan.

title: Induced packing treewidth III. Branch decompositions
abstract: The notion of induced packing treewidth aims to unify classes defined by forbidden induced subgraphs or induced minors with classes defined by the existence of certain structured tree decompositions. In this paper, we introduce induced packing branchwidth, a branch-decomposition analogue of induced packing treewidth. For a graph $H$, the induced $H$-packing branchwidth of a graph $G$, denoted by $\branchpi_H(G)$, is the minimum, over all branch decompositions of $G$, of the largest number of pairwise anticomplete induced copies of $H$ that cross one displayed cut. For $H=P_2$, it equals sim-width. We prove several structural properties of graphs of bounded $\branchpi_H$, for various choices of $H$, including $χ$-boundedness, polynomial degree-boundedness, and metric properties.

title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform
abstract: The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber--Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.

title: Avoiding short progressions in Euclidean Ramsey theory II
abstract:
Recently, Currier, Moore, and Yip developed a general framework for constructing colorings avoiding prescribed monochromatic arithmetic progressions in Euclidean Ramsey theory. Writing $\ell_m$ for an $m$-term arithmetic progression with unit spacing, they proved $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,\ell_{20})$ and $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{6889})$ for every $α>0$. We refine and simplify their framework, proving $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{22})$ for every $α>0$. We further establish $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{21})$ except possibly for four values of $α^2$, and $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{17})$ for all but finitely many $α>0$. Our approach also recovers several earlier results and avoids some technical arguments used in previous works.

title: Law-Invariant Operators for Stochastic Mechanics
abstract: A central objective in stochastic mechanics is to separate deterministic physical behavior from the probability laws governing uncertain inputs. While classical spectral approaches achieve this separation in linear settings, nonlinear responses introduce interactions beyond conventional second-order variability response functions (VRF). Inspired by the spirit of VRFs, this work establishes that, for a fixed physical system, uncertainty propagation is described by a law-invariant operator mapping input realizations to responses, governed by the underlying physics and the deterministic parameters of the system. Different probability laws affect the input sampling and resulting response statistics, but not the mapping operator. We establish this law invariance under complete, invertible coordinate transformations and develop complementary, Fourier, fixed-reference polynomial-chaos (PCE) and finite element method (FEM) transfer formulations. Fourier captures nonlinear cross-frequency interactions and recovers the classical VRF in the appropriate linear limit, PCE describes coupling among stochastic modes, while FEM expresses the deterministic inverse-stiffness action. Neural approximations of these deterministic operators are investigated through analytical and finite-element benchmarks, examining cross-law generalization, the influence of training distributions and stochastic excitation, and the prediction of response fields and statistics. The results demonstrate the potential for reusing learned physical operators across different stochastic laws without retraining, while highlighting the importance of adequate training coverage and the challenges of accurately estimating low-probability events.

title: Release Sooner, Expose Less: Offloading MoE Dispatch in NCCL-EP under Dual-Batch Overlap
abstract: Dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides mixture-of-experts (MoE) communication behind another microbatch's computation, but only after dispatch send releases the GPU. The time dispatch send holds the GPU therefore stays exposed, while network progress after release can be hidden. We evaluate GPUDirect Async - Kernel Initiated (GDA-KI) Free Flow, an NCCL-EP research configuration that leaves WQE construction on the GPU but moves send progression to a host thread. On a GB300 NVL72 system, GDA-KI Free Flow reduces dispatch-send time relative to default GDA-KI at every operating point in the evaluated parameter sweep. An experiment that inserts a GPU delay between dispatch send and receive shows that offload increases the in-flight interval. Depending on the load, 32-96 microseconds of computation or other independent work between send and receive hides the deferred progress, leaving less exposed time than default GDA-KI. In disaggregated vLLM serving with DBO, GDA-KI Free Flow lowers median TPOT by 15-25% relative to NCCL-EP default GDA-KI and by 16-42% relative to DeepEP v1.

title: Naturalness in the Past from a Time-Dependent Supersymmetry Scale
abstract: We consider the possibility that electroweak naturalness may be epoch dependent. In no-scale supergravity, a rolling quintessence modulus can control the supersymmetry-breaking scale, allowing superpartners to be much lighter in the early universe while remaining heavy today. Fifth-force and varying-constant effects can be suppressed via correlated modular weights in the visible-sector Kähler metric and modulus-dependent superpotential Yukawa couplings, while radiative stability of the quintessence potential requires additional tuning of the field-dependent vacuum energy. The resulting effective theory has distinctive implications for early-universe phase transitions, relic abundances, and gravitational waves.

title: TRIAD: Multimodal Retrieval across Abstraction, Constraints, and State
abstract: Multimodal retrieval increasingly supports agentic systems, where user requests can involve cross-level relations, combine multiple constraints, and evolve across dialogue turns. In these settings, a highly similar result may still violate the user's requirements, while retrieved content may directly inform downstream actions without human screening. We introduce TRIAD, a multimodal retrieval benchmark for evaluating how well retrieval systems satisfy these complex, evolving requests. TRIAD comprises three tracks: abstraction, testing bidirectional retrieval between visual instances and concepts at different hierarchical levels; constraints, testing the joint satisfaction of positive and negative conditions; and state, testing the integration of requirements across dialogue turns and the updating of earlier conditions when users revise their requests. The benchmark contains six subsets, each with 1,000 queries and a fixed pool of 1,000 candidates per query, evaluated using a common multi-positive mean average precision (mAP) protocol. Simpler reference tasks and hard negatives grouped by the requirements they violate help characterize specific retrieval difficulties. We evaluate 20 configurations of 17 systems and find that no system leads across all six subsets. Performance declines with hierarchical distance, and negative-only queries generally underperform positive-only queries with the same number of constraints. Across paired tasks expressing the same final intent, multi-turn retrieval yields lower mAP in 39 of 40 configuration-domain comparisons. The benefits of explicit reasoning also vary across models and tasks. These findings highlight the gap between retrieving similar content and satisfying a complete request.

title: Completions of vector metric spaces and the diagonal property of order convergence
abstract: A vector metric space carries a distance with values in an ordered vector space $E$; a sequence converges if its distances to the limit are dominated by a sequence decreasing to zero in $E$. We show that, for Archimedean $E$, every $E$-valued vector metric space has a completion if and only if order Cauchy sequences in $E$ converge and $E$ has the diagonal property of order convergence (SDP): for every double sequence $(a^k_n)$ with $a^k_n\downarrow_n0$ there are indices $n_k$ and $e_k\downarrow 0$ with $a^k_{n_k}\le e_k$. In vector lattices this is the classical diagonal property of Kantorovich, equivalently the strong Egoroff property. We show that its standard characterisations remain valid in Archimedean ordered vector spaces, and that it holds if and only if convergence in every $E$-valued vector metric space satisfies the iterated limit axiom. For an ordered Banach space with a closed normal cone, all completions exist if and only if the norm is $σ$-order continuous; if the cone has an interior point, all vector metrics are then scalar. By a theorem of Veksler and of Hager and van Mill, for compact Hausdorff $K$ either $K$ is an almost $P$-space and $C(K)$-valued vector metrics are scalar, or there are countable $C(K)$-valued vector metric spaces without completion. A product of ordered vector spaces with (SDP) and nonzero cones has (SDP) if and only if there are fewer than $\mathfrak b$ factors, extending a result of Hager and van Mill for $\mathbb{R}^A$. We also prove permanence results for direct summands and uniformly dense vector lattice covers of pre-Riesz spaces.

title: Reconstructing Flash-Evoked Potentials in the Human Brain and Tracking Cortical Activity Using Spatiotemporal Filtering: Numerical Simulation Study
abstract: Electroencephalographic source reconstruction of visual evoked activity is challenging because distributed, temporally evolving, and overlapping cortical sources generate scalp potentials. We present a controlled simulation framework for flash visual evoked potentials (FVEPs) based on a coupled Jansen--Rit neural mass network and a realistic finite-element EEG forward model. The framework generates a sequential activation pattern across early visual, parietal, and frontal regions and enables direct comparison of reconstructed activity with known ground truth. Standardized Kalman filtering (SKF), change-rate SKF (CrSKF), conventional Kalman filtering (KF), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) beamforming are compared using parcel-wise time courses, temporal lags, and assessments of spatial focality and Earth Mover's Distance. In the inverse comparison, SKF and CrSKF preserve the principal temporal progression more consistently than KF and LCMV, while CrSKF produces smoother temporal estimates. The results also demonstrate parcel-wise leakage and reduced separation of closely spaced components, emphasizing the need to interpret temporal ordering together with spatial reconstruction quality. The proposed framework provides a reproducible test environment for evaluating dynamic EEG inverse methods under controlled noise conditions.

title: An Agile Homomorphic Encryption and ML-KEM Scheme for Privacy-Preserving Health Data Processing
abstract: The storage and processing of health data raise serious privacy concerns; therefore, the data must be encrypted. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows computations on encrypted data, which makes it a very promising technology in this context. However, although the efficiency of FHE algorithms has improved in recent years, they remain very complex. The security of several prominent FHE schemes is based on variants of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, which is also the basis of Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), the new post-quantum standard for asymmetric encryption. In this paper, we propose an agile cryptographic scheme -combining ML-KEM and BGV -that allows efficient implementations in an embedded use case. We describe the parameter selection for the proposed scheme and show its feasibility with a proof-of-concept implementation.

title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.

title: VNA-Only Calibration of Waveguide Thermistor Mounts with Self-Consistent Determination of the Thermistor-Port Impedance
abstract: A method is presented for determining the calibration factor and the effective efficiency of waveguide thermistor mounts from vector-network-analyzer reflection data alone, without a microcalorimeter, extending the three reflection-coefficient method of the coaxial case. In waveguide the thermistor is coupled to the line through a matching structure and the reference impedance of the thermistor port, $Z_0$, is not known a priori; it is inferred through a power-consistency relation between pairs of states, under the convention that it is real. The method reproduces the factory certificates (U = 2 %) of four K486A mounts within 1.0 % rms and the PTB-traceable values (U = 0.85 to 0.98 %) of a fifth within 0.34 % rms; its expanded measurement uncertainty is 0.5 to 1.16 % (k = 2) for the best specimen and below 2 % for the five. A mount with its waveguide-to-coaxial adapter is calibrated directly, without characterizing the adapter, from the model factor of the mount and the geometric factor measured through the adapter. The scattering matrix implied by the solution is not passive; a minimum-norm correction of the thermistor impedances along the two directions invisible to the calibration factor - the ratios of the efficiencies of the three states - brings it to the floor of passivity, where the efficiency depends on the load only through its mismatch factor, leaves the result unchanged, and gives the sensitivity of the efficiency to the bias resistance in closed form: below $4\times10^{-5}$ $Ω^{-1}$ in band mean, proportional to the mismatch of the operating state and to the loss of the mount.

title: Adapting Multi-Stage Distributed Real-Time Systems Design to Vehicular Edge Computing
abstract: Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) aims to support computation-intensive applications in intelligent transportation systems while meeting stringent latency requirements. When processed remotely, applications require access to different resource types in a specific sequence, forming a multi-stage processing pipeline. This structure closely resembles multi-stage distributed applications executing across heterogeneous resources, making established multi-stage distributed real-time scheduling techniques well suited for modeling VEC systems. The resulting model accommodates diverse resource configurations and access patterns. Building on this model, we propose a joint mapping and scheduling approach that accounts for vehicle mobility and real-time constraints. The proposed heuristic extends optimal priority assignment for multi-stage systems to the VEC setting, to construct feasible schedules while minimizing local-device energy consumption and ensuring that offloaded jobs meet their deadlines. Extensive simulations show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms both a baseline based on the same delay-composition framework and a deadline decomposition-based approach.

title: Kagome Flat Bands from Self-Assembled Water on Non-van der Waals 2D Materials
abstract: The properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials are governed not only by their intrinsic electronic structure but also in particular by their surface chemistry and interactions with the environment. The surfaces of non-van der Waals (non-vdW) 2D materials are intrinsically reactive and may require chemical stabilization under realistic experimental conditions. Here, we perform a systematic first-principles study of water passivation of non-vdW 2D materials and demonstrate that molecular water adsorption is energetically and dynamically favored for a wide range of systems. Rather than dissociating, water molecules frequently remain intact and form adsorbed ordered surface overlayers. These overlayers can adopt a kagome lattice geometry, leading to the emergence of flat electronic bands directly at the valence-band edge. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals a strong intermolecular coupling between neighboring water lone pairs within this kagome topology, while the locked molecular orientations simultaneously produce an electrostatically frustrated surface potential. These findings establish water not only as a stabilizing agent but also as an active element for electronic structure engineering of non-vdW 2D surfaces.

title: Ultralight scalar field domain walls and Galileo GNSS atomic clocks
abstract: In this article, we study the impact of an Earth-sized ultralight scalar field domain wall (DW) on the European Galileo Global Navigation Satellite System constellation and the feasibility of a related detection. In particular, a set of statistical procedures is developed and implemented to characterize the statistical properties of the background noise for a subnetwork of $N$ Galileo satellite clocks, including a false-alarm rate estimation and a detection efficiency analysis. These methods allow to implement a coincidence analysis and establish a preliminary statistical framework for a robust and controlled search for domain-wall crossings in clock data, and for deriving constraints on the associated fundamental particle physics parameters. The activity is addressed from the point of view of the scientific objectives of the Galileo for Science (G4S$\_2.0$) project.

title: Magnetic moments of the $Σ_c$ and $Σ_b$ baryons from external-field QCD sum rules
abstract: We compute the magnetic moments of the $Σ_c$ and $Σ_b$ isotriplets with external-field QCD sum rules. The heavy-quark propagator is kept with its full mass dependence and with its couplings to the photon, to soft gluons and to both simultaneously, and the magnetic sum rule is normalized by the mass sum rule of the same interpolating field, which removes the residue and gives the baryon masses within a few percent. The quark-condensate magnetic susceptibility $χ$, which otherwise dominates the uncertainty, is fixed by the proton magnetic moment computed with the same interpolating field; the neutron moment then follows to about $5\%$. Uncertainties from the QCD inputs are evaluated with a Monte Carlo analysis, and those from the interpolating field, the Borel window, the scale of the heavy-quark mass, the calibration and the normalization are added. With $\overline{\rm MS}$ heavy-quark masses we obtain $μ_{Σ_c^{++}}=2.37\pm0.65$, $μ_{Σ_c^{+}}=0.50\pm0.15$, $μ_{Σ_c^{0}}=-1.39\pm0.37$, $μ_{Σ_b^{+}}=2.16\pm0.65$, $μ_{Σ_b^{0}}=0.55\pm0.16$ and $μ_{Σ_b^{-}}=-1.06\pm0.32$ in nuclear magnetons; at this order the results depend sizably on the heavy-quark mass scheme. The moments are carried by the light diquark; the heavy-quark contribution, whose separation depends on the interpolating field, is $-0.13\pm0.02\,μ_N$ for $Σ_c$ and $+0.013\pm0.003\,μ_N$ for $Σ_b$.

title: TANSAR: Editable and Attributable Correlation Matrix Memories under Correlated Keys, with Rule-Constrained Multi-Hop Knowledge Editing
abstract: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.

title: AudioCodex: Streaming Autoencoders for Live Audio
abstract: We introduce AudioCodex, a fully causal autoencoder for live generative audio applications that compresses stereo audio into compact continuous latent sequences at ~10 Hz. It combines a Mean Flow magnitude autoencoder with latent hypersphere projection, bounded-noise augmentation, representation alignment, and adversarial phase recovery to learn representations that support both efficient downstream generation and high-quality reconstruction. Through extensive ablations, we show that AudioCodex outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of generation-reconstruction trade-off, whilst remaining strictly causal in both encoding and decoding. This work paves the way towards truly real-time interactive and streaming generative audio applications.

title: Vector metrics with values in pre-Riesz spaces I: transfer of order convergence along vector lattice covers
abstract: Vector metric spaces in the sense of Çevik and Altun take values in a vector lattice, but their axioms use only the order of the value space. We develop the theory for vector metrics with values in an Archimedean pre-Riesz space $E$, i.e.\ an ordered vector space admitting a bipositive order dense embedding $i$ into a vector lattice $Y$. We ask when an $E$-valued vector metric $d$ and the vector-lattice-valued metric $i\circ d$ have the same convergent and Cauchy nets and sequences. Relatively uniform convergence transfers along every cover. For nets, $\mathrm{o}_3$-convergence transfers if and only if the cover has an intrinsic domination property. This property holds for pervasive covers, by a result of Kalauch and van Gaans, for uniformly dense covers and in finite dimensions; it fails for an example of Kalauch and van Gaans. Sequential convergence transfers under a countable domination property implied by uniform density, but not under pervasiveness. For uncountable $Γ$, the vector lattice $\mathbb{R}\mathbf 1\oplus c_{00}(Γ)$ is pervasive in its Dedekind completion $\ell^\infty(Γ)$ without the transfer, while for countable $Γ$ the transfer holds; the difference is explained by order separability. In finite dimensions, with a closed generating cone, all these convergences coincide with norm convergence in every cover. For $C^1[0,1]$-valued integral metrics, positivity of the kernel on the diagonal forces all order convergences to coincide with $L^1$-convergence. For the Volterra kernel $(t-s)_+$, by contrast, $L^1$-convergence, relatively uniform convergence and order convergence are pairwise different, and we describe each explicitly.

title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
abstract: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

title: Safety-Constrained Intelligent Control of a 2-DOF Robotic Manipulator Using Control Barrier Functions
abstract: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.

title: Reconstructing hourly traffic on every street of a capital from a sparse counting network: a graph neural network applied to Paris
abstract: Micro-scale air quality models require hourly traffic data on every road segment, whereas permanent counters cover only a small part of the network. A graph neural network (GNN) was developed to reconstruct hourly traffic flows on the 32,163 road segments of Paris intra-muros from the 1,573 segments equipped with a counter (4.9%). The model adapts the Graph Neural Network for Urban Interpolation (GNNUI) to a real, sparse counting network. Flows are decoded on the edges of the junction graph (one edge per segment, both directions summed), a traffic climatology serves as an offset in a zero-inflated negative-binomial likelihood, and training proceeds by masking counters. Eight-fold spatial cross-validation, with counters sharing a published series merged before splitting, distinguishes interpolation at a withheld counter in an instrumented district (R${}^2$ = 0.89, error of a quarter of the mean flow) from extrapolation to a district without counters (R${}^2$ = 0.74, a third of the mean flow). These scores hold on main axes where counters are located, while relative errors are about 50% on the few counted local streets. Ablations show that the climatology offset tends to help extrapolation. Road attributes, time cycles and the live state of the counting network matter most, while weather inputs have no significant effect. The masking rate is the only inherited hyperparameter with a clear effect. When evaluated on January--August 2026 (outside the training period), the frozen model stayed around the error band of previous years.

title: Lipschitz inner rates of normal surface singularities
abstract: In this article, we connect the local Lipschitz geometry of a normal surface singularity with a rational homology sphere link to the analytic semigroup $S_{an}(\tilde{X})$ associated with a convenient resolution. Under certain restriction, we provide an explicit computational characterization of the Lipschitz rate $q_v$ associated with an irreducible exceptional curve $E_v$ in terms of the semigroup. We also show that removing the restriction we get examples when $q_v$ cannot be determined from the semigroup. Interestingly enough, this phenomenon already happens for rational singularities. Indeed, we exemplify that the inner rates of rational singularities are not topological.

title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 1: single and double rf systems
abstract: In the first part of this lecture, the main characteristics of synchrotron motion, namely, synchronous particle and phase, bucket area and emittance, are introduced. The equations of longitudinal particle motion in a single rf system of a proton synchrotron are rederived and the phase equation is analyzed for small and large amplitude particles. The particle motion below and above transition energy is also considered. The main applications and operation modes of a double rf system are discussed in the second part of the lecture. The intensity effects and beam instabilities are the subject of the following lecture.

title: AutoVLA-D: Learn a Trajectory-Geometric Condition from Reasoning for Autonomous Driving VLA
abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.

title: PCTac: Mechanochromic Photonic-Crystal Tactile Sensor for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Modern visuotactile sensors primarily sense contact by imaging the deformation of a compliant interface. Using techniques such as photometric stereo, they can recover detailed contact geometry, often represented as surface normals or depth. However, force-related information typically still needs to be inferred indirectly through calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings. Mechanochromic photonic-crystal (PC) materials offer an alternative physical encoding mechanism: contact loading changes their periodic microstructure and spectral response, directly transforming local stress into a spatially resolved structural-color field. Despite this potential, PC materials have rarely been explored as visuotactile sensors for closed-loop robot learning. We present PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic PC fingertip that uses a dense hue field as its tactile observation. Loading characterization demonstrates a repeatable relationship between the applied normal load and the observed hue response. We further integrate this representation directly into a Diffusion Policy and evaluate it on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Across 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68 successes (75.6\%), compared with 60 (66.7\%) for PCTac RGB, 57 (63.3\%) for Wedge RGB, and 29 (32.2\%) for vision-only. PCTac Hue also achieves the highest observed success rate on each evaluated task, including Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, where it achieves 16/30 successes versus 13/30 for tactile RGB baselines and 1/30 for vision-only. These results demonstrate the potential of mechanochromic structural color as a compact, load-sensitive tactile representation for robot learning and closed-loop manipulation. Project page: https://bey0ndt1me.github.io/PCTac-page/.

title: Retweeting patterns reveal partisan asymmetries in information sharing and signal state-level electoral outcomes in the 2020 US presidential election
abstract: As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political ecosystems and relates to offline voting remains unclear. Here we reconstruct partisan information ecosystems from more than 500 million tweets generated during the 2020 US presidential election, integrating information diffusion across media outlets, influencers, and social peers. Contrary to the conventional expectation that broader information exposure promotes moderation, we find that retweeting a wider range of political information is associated with stronger political polarization. We further show systematic asymmetries in political information ecosystems: the Republican ecosystem is highly concentrated and ideologically biased, whereas the Democratic ecosystem is more dispersed and primarily organized around relatively moderate left-leaning sources. Finally, we demonstrate that several shared retweeting signatures robustly map onto state-level electoral outcomes despite cross-state heterogeneity. Our findings reveal asymmetric political information ecosystems as a key organizing principle of online political communication and identify collective retweeting patterns as a scalable signal of real-world voting behaviours.

title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Artificial intelligence models for clinical prediction are proliferating across neurosurgery, but their aggregate discriminative performance, distribution along the care pathway and methodological quality are unclear. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed these studies in neurosurgery and its subspecialities along with their risk of bias appraisal. We performed a PRISMA search for peer-reviewed original studies using AI to predict a clinical outcome in neurosurgical populations. Metrics were pooled using random effects modelling. Each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and was assigned an evidence level. Clinical prediction task sub-stratification analysis was performed. Risk-of-bias was assessed using PROBAST. 1063 studies were included. Across 451 studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86, ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity. Performance varied by clinical pathway stage, highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks. Only 51 studies were using prospective data with external validation, whereas 619 rested on internal validation alone or no validation. 89 percent studies were at high risk-of-bias, driven by the analysis domain. AI models report high performance across all the neurosurgical subspecialities, concordant across AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity and robust to risk-of-bias stratification. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest at decision-facing post-operative stage. However, the literature is dominated by optimism-prone, internally-validated and poorly calibrated models with extreme heterogeneity. External validation, calibration analysis and reporting guidelines adherence remain prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

title: On a soliton with a non-normalisable zero mode
abstract: We consider the holomorphic baby Skyrme model, which we propose as a simple tractable example of a soliton with a non-normalisable zero mode. The $1$-soliton has the same structure as a lump of fixed size. The size modulus of the sigma model becomes massive, while the phase modulus remains massless. The latter is non-normalisable in the $(0+1)$-dimensional sense because of the soliton tail. A suitable way to treat it is to consider the radial $(1+1)$-dimensional effective action on the half-plane. The soliton core sets the boundary condition for the effective model, which we evaluate with the WKB approximation and also numerically. We discuss the analogue of the effective moduli space approximation with a $1+1$ model and a boundary term at a certain cutoff scale. This may serve as a prototype for more complex systems featuring non-normalisable zero modes such as certain kinds of monopoles in $3+1$ dimensions.

title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 2: intensity effects and beam instabilities
abstract: In this lecture, dealing with intensity effects, the equations of longitudinal motion with induced beam voltage are analyzed. This allows us, first, to describe the single-bunch potential well distortion and the loss of Landau damping. Then the linearized Vlasov equation is used to derive step-by-step the Lebedev equation. This matrix equation is then applied to find the thresholds, growth rates and spectra of an unstable multi-bunch beam. The lecture is concluded by a discussion of possible beam-instability cures.

title: Diversification Across Predictors: Heterogeneous Ensemble Learning for Cross-Sectional Return Prediction
abstract: Cross-sectional stock return prediction remains challenging due to extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, high-dimensional factor spaces, and non-stationary predictor effectiveness. Individual model classes exhibit complementary failure modes in this regime: neural networks overfit noise due to high variance, while linear models underfit nonlinear structure due to high bias. We propose a heterogeneous ensemble framework that extends the financial principle of diversification to the predictor level. Through a bagging procedure combining linear predictors with nonlinear predictors, each model functions as a distinct specialist whose prediction errors exhibit low cross-covariance, enabling error cancellation upon aggregation. We formalize this mechanism via bias-variance-covariance decomposition, establishing an exact mathematical correspondence between portfolio diversification and predictor aggregation. On CSI300 daily-frequency Alpha158 factor datasets, the proposed ensemble achieves a Rank IC improvement exceeding 13\% over standalone neural networks and surpasses tree-based state-of-the-art methods including XGBoost and Double Ensemble, as measured by both predictive accuracy and portfolio-based evaluation metrics.

title: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of early-type stars. Testing Stokes parameter inversions with theoretical magnetohydrodynamic models
abstract: Zeeman-Doppler imaging (ZDI) is widely used to reconstruct magnetic fields in early-type stars from time-series spectropolarimetric observations, yet its accuracy has not been systematically validated against physically self-consistent, complex magnetic field models. We aim to assess the reliability and limitations of modern ZDI techniques applied to fossil fields of early-type stars. We generated synthetic spectropolarimetric data from three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of fossil magnetic fields. The resulting Stokes profiles - individual lines and least-squares deconvolved (LSD) profiles - were inverted with contemporary ZDI codes using Stokes IQUV and IV data. We compared the reconstructed maps with the input MHD surface fields and quantified deviations in field strength, vector orientation, and harmonic energy decomposition. For Stokes IQUV inversions, ZDI recovers field vector components and strength with better than 10% accuracy, while Stokes IV inversions degrade to 15-20% for the most complex geometries. The field inclination is recovered to within 10 deg, with errors increasing to 15-20 deg in the same cases. Full Stokes inversions reproduce poloidal and toroidal energies to within a few percentage points. LSD-based inversions yield accuracy comparable to, and sometimes better than, that achieved with ZDI using individual Fe II lines. Imposing a current-free poloidal constraint, which the input field satisfies, only helps where the unconstrained Stokes IV inversion performs poorly. Cross-talk between magnetic and abundance reconstructions is weak, with spurious inhomogeneities at or below 0.1 dex on average. Modern ZDI robustly reconstructs fossil magnetic fields in early-type stars, including their smaller-scale non-dipolar features, particularly when full Stokes information is available.

title: Semantic-Aware Communications in Industrial IoT:What Can Be Tested Today, and What Is Missing?
abstract: Classical networks treat every bit as equally important, which wastes time and energy in factories and requires extra traffic engineering for critical traffic. Semantic communications send only what a task needs, but how can they be tested under realistic conditions? This paper examines what can be tested today in 6G industrial IoT, that is, networks of factory machines, robots, and sensors, and what is still missing. It introduces semantic importance, a score attached to each message that states how much the message matters, and uses it in a context-driven design to derive eight testing needs. Existing simulators, emulators, testbeds, codecs, and learning frameworks are assessed against these needs, which reveals five gaps. We propose a toolchain of four components built around the ns-3 simulator for simulated and emulated scenarios.

title: More Than Just Style: Benchmarking Personality Influence in Large Language Models
abstract: In addition to the effects of explicit input prompts and instructions, large language model outputs are influenced by underlying behavioral preferences similar to human personality tendencies. These tendencies can affect how models interpret situations and make decisions. However, their influence is difficult to disentangle from the effects of model capabilities and instructions. Therefore, we introduce SPACE, a benchmark framework combining a controlled evaluation protocol with complementary datasets for personality verification, capability assessment, and hierarchical situational tasks. Controlled comparisons across guidance conditions help distinguish personality influence from measured capability changes and immediate instruction effects. Experimental results demonstrate that although prompting can shift generation style, models' internal personality tendencies are persistent and not readily overridden by opposing instructions. Furthermore, these underlying tendencies have an observable influence on LLM task performance, highlighting the need for greater attention to these characteristics and potential applications. Training code and SPACE benchmark specifications are available at https://github.com/Niklauseik/SPACE-training.

title: AutoBuddy: Evaluating Proactive, Always-On Agents on Task Discovery and Execution in a Simulated Workplace
abstract: As LLM agents become more autonomous, they are increasingly expected to run as always-on assistants on a user's behalf, identifying work to be done and completing it without being asked. Yet existing benchmarks usually give the agent its task, whereas in knowledge work the requests sit in the user's workspace and the agent must first recognise which obligations exist. We study proactive task discovery and execution, in which an agent must infer a user's pending tasks from their workspace and complete them in the systems where the work lives. This setting poses two challenges. For the agent, the tasks are buried in a large volume of mail, chat, documents and records. For evaluation, a benchmark needs a simulated organisation whose people, events and documents are mutually consistent, so that tasks arise realistically and their correct outcomes are known. We introduce AutoBuddy-Bench, a simulator that addresses these challenges. It models an organisation's employees, projects, business systems and event history as a temporal graph, renders it into realistic workspace artefacts, derives ground-truth tasks from the events that create obligations, and computes each task's outcome from the world state; execution is judged by the agent's changes to the workspace. To evaluate current LLMs, we build AutoBuddy, a reference agent with interchangeable backbone LLMs: it identifies tasks from the workspace, grounding each in its source records, and executes each in a separate session with write access. Varying only the backbone, we find a systematic shift in where tasks are lost: weaker models fail mainly at discovery, intermediate models identify tasks but often stop short of carrying them out, and the strongest models fail mainly during execution, most often on business-system operations. Discovery precision is only weakly related to execution quality, suggesting the two are distinct capabilities.

title: HFR distorted-wave photoionization of Te III: a preliminary benchmark for large-scale atomic data production to model nebular-phase kilonovae
abstract: The shortage of photoionization cross sections for heavy elements remains an obstacle to non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) modeling of nebular-phase kilonova ejecta, where hydrogenic prescriptions have often been adopted in the absence of ion-specific calculations. We present a first preliminary benchmark of direct photoionization cross sections for doubly ionized tellurium, obtained using the distorted-wave (DW) approximation within the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method implemented in the Cowan codes, in which a semi-empirical adjustment based on the observed energy levels is performed. For the photoionization from the ground level of Te III to the ground level of Te IV, comparison with Dirac R-matrix data shows encouraging agreement in the magnitude and overall decrease of the non-resonant background in the lower photon-energy region, approximately below 4 Ry (autoionizing resonances are absent from the present direct treatment). These preliminary results support HFR distorted-wave calculations as a promising and computationally tractable approach for large-scale production of photoionization cross sections, with lanthanides and actinides as longer-term targets, in light of their importance to kilonova modeling and of the severe lack of atomic data for these species.

title: Orbits along primes in totally minimal systems
abstract: In this paper, we show that every totally minimal system admits a point whose orbit along the primes is dense. Moreover, assuming the Dickson-Hardy-Littlewood conjecture, we show that in any totally minimal distal system, the orbit along the primes of every point is dense.

title: Linear disjointness and values of Mahler M-functions
abstract: We prove that the algebra generated by the values of Mahler M-functions at algebraic points admits a decomposition as the tensor product, over Q, of a countable family of linearly disjoint algebras. Consequently, the study of linear and algebraic relations among such values reduces to the corresponding problem within each of these smaller algebras. Our proof relies on recent advances of the authors on Mahler's method in several variables. As an application, we obtain a complete description of the algebraic relations among the values of the Fredholm series and their derivatives at nonzero algebraic points. This fully resolves an old problem originating in Mahler's work.

title: Physics design of a dual-ring light source toward MHz-rate free-electron laser radiation
abstract: Combining the high peak brilliance and short pulse duration of free-electron lasers (FELs) with the high repetition rate of diffraction-limited storage rings (DLSRs) is a promising direction for accelerator light sources. In this paper, we propose a dual-ring light source concept that, at MHz repetition rates, delivers pulses with a pulse durations and peak power intermediate between those of FELs and DLSRs. Such a light source can be realized as an upgrade of an existing DLSR by adding an isochronous ring equipped with transverse gradient undulators (TGUs) and connecting the two rings via bunch compression and decompression systems. We present the conceptual layout and show that bunch compression shortens the electron bunches to ps-scale durations; multi-turn radiation in the isochronous ring raises the repetition rate to 1.36 MHz from a single TGU; and the long TGUs enhance the brilliance, delivering $10^{7}$--$10^{9}$ photons per pulse across the soft and hard X-ray range, an increase of 2--4 orders of magnitude over the original DLSR. The dual-ring light source thus provides a cost-effective route to MHz FEL operation based on existing storage-ring infrastructure, combining the high repetition rate of a DLSR with the short pulses and high brilliance of a linac-driven FEL.

title: Low-lying states of $^{115}$Cd modeled as a valence neutron coupled to $^{114}$Cd
abstract: $^{114}$Cd has historically been regarded as an ideal quadrupole vibrator due to its near-canonical level spacings, though this interpretation is disputed due to electromagnetic transition data from the two- and three-phonon states. In this paper we investigate whether, with the extension of including the single-phonon octupole state, the model is still useful in describing the coupling of a neutron to a cadmium-114 core to model the lowest- energy cadmium-115 states, as the triplet states have small to no influence in the calculation. The results thus provide supporting evidence for the tentatively-assigned $J^π$ values of the lowest-energy $^{115}$Cd states. A more- rigorous derivation than often used for the vibrational B(Eλ) is used, in conjunction with the $^{115}$Cd structure calculation, to provide a theoretical prediction of the $^{114}$Cd octupole deformation.

title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
abstract: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

title: Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
abstract: Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.

title: Data-Driven Conservation Laws for Newtonian Systems: Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Eisenhart-Duval Geometry
abstract: We introduce a Physics-Informed Neural Network approach for the data-driven reconstruction of the symmetries and conservation laws of Newtonian dynamical systems, based on the geometrization of the dynamics through the Eisenhart-Duval lift. Within the Eisenhart-Duval lift, the symmetry conditions reduce to the linear Killing or Conformal Killing equations of the extended metric. We combine a Hamiltonian neural network, which reconstructs the potential function from the data, with a random-feature neural network, which solves the symmetry conditions for the collineations of the extended geometry. From the learned vector fields we construct the Lie algebra and, through Noether's theorem, the corresponding conserved quantities, while the derivation of the curvature invariants for the extended geometry provide allow us to perform an independent consistency test. We apply the method to the one-dimensional Ermakov-Pinney equation and to the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, with and without a quartic perturbation, by using different level of noise in the phase-space data. For the Ermakov-Pinney equation, the three Killing vectors of the flat extended plane, and the corresponding nonlocal conservation laws, are recovered for, while for the harmonic oscillator, the ten conformal Killing vectors which form the $so(3,2)$ Lie algebra are determined for noise levels up to $10\%$. When the quartic term is added, the broken symmetries are identified as approximate symmetries.

title: Singularities in leaf closures on complex surfaces
abstract: We prove a geometric and dynamical criterion excluding minimal sets contained in the regular locus of a holomorphic foliation on a compact complex surface. In particular, we prove that every Jouanolou foliation of degree at least two has no exceptional minimal set. We also give an explicit lower bound, growing linearly with the degree, for the number of singularities in every regular leaf closure of a Jouanolou foliation. This bound persists under small perturbations, as does the existence of a nonempty open saturated set whose leaves accumulate at all singularities. Under finite pullback unramified over the singular set, the bound is multiplied by the degree of the normalised component over the base leaf. Together with a general persistence theorem, this yields nonempty analytic open sets of foliations on every smooth projective surface with arbitrarily large uniform lower bounds on the number of singularities in their regular leaf closures. On double-plane K3 surfaces, we obtain foliations with ample canonical bundle and explicitly describe and count their singularities.

title: Observer-based parameter estimation in a Darcy model towards dam internal seepage monitoring with validation on real data
abstract: This paper addresses internal seepage monitoring in hydraulic infrastructures through the estimation of physical parameters in a distributed model. A physics-based approach relying on Darcy's law is adopted to describe the spatiotemporal evolution of hydraulic head within the structure. To enable real-time applicability, a Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to derive a reduced-order model of the underlying partial differential equation. An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is then designed to perform online estimation of the hydraulic diffusivity, a key parameter related to the structural state. The proposed method is validated directly on real measurement data through a twofold approach. First, the estimated parameter is compared with the value obtained via offline batch optimization performed on the same dataset, showing consistent results. Second, the ability of the resulting model, parametrized by the estimated diffusivity, to reconstruct the observed measurements is assessed, to evaluate its suitability for seepage monitoring.

title: From oxygen to lead: testing a common QGP description with high-$p_\perp$ probes
abstract: The observation of suppression and finite high-$p_\perp$ elliptic anisotropy in O+O and Ne+Ne raises the question of whether a common quark--gluon plasma (QGP) description can simultaneously account for both observables across systems from oxygen to lead. We present predictions using event-by-event bulk evolution constrained by soft-sector observables and coupled to DREENA radiative and collisional energy loss, with the same microscopic parameter set for O+O, Ne+Ne, Xe+Xe, and Pb+Pb. The calculation reproduces the observed ordering of suppression and predicts elliptic anisotropies of comparable magnitude across the four systems in 10--20$\%$ collisions. We predict a modest centrality dependence of $v_2^{\mathrm{SP}}$ and a more pronounced decrease of $v_3^{\mathrm{SP}}$ toward peripheral light-ion collisions, in contrast to the corresponding trends in larger systems. In light ions, we predict that $v_2^{\mathrm{SP}}/(1-R_{AA})$ is nearly independent of momentum at high $p_\perp$. We further predict that the differential ratio $v_2\{4\}/v_2\{2\}$ depends only weakly on momentum at high $p_\perp$, with magnitudes and centrality trends broadly comparable to those of the measured soft-sector ratios, suggesting that the soft-sector fluctuation pattern persists in hard--soft correlations. Predictions for D and B mesons extend the comparison to probes of different flavors. Taken together, these system-size, harmonic, fluctuation, and flavor dependences provide experimental tests of how far a common QGP description extends.

title: PTC-IoU: CPU-Friendly Detection Quality Estimation for Edge Video Analytics
abstract: An edge video analytics system must estimate the quality of local detections since there are no ground-truth labels available during runtime. Detectors usually provide confidence scores for their results, but these scores can not reveal every missed object or misplaced bounding box. So a quality estimator is necessary to provide a decision signal indicating which frame has potential detection failures that need to be escalated to a more powerful model in the cloud. Neural network based estimators add workload to the GPU already running detection, while CPU capacity may remain available. We present Predictive Temporal Consistency IoU (PTC-IoU), which moves this workload to CPU by compacting detection boxes histories to support deterministic result scoring. Comparing to neural counterparts, experiments on representative edge hardware, Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, show that our method reduced per-frame estimator latency from 10.3 ms for neural counterparts to 2.2 ms (4.7x faster), increased pipelined throughput by 13.6%, and cuts estimator energy consumption by up to 95%, while maintaining competitive final detection quality verified on multiple datasets.

title: REAL: Reward Modeling through Evidence-Linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in Generated Speech
abstract: As modern text-to-speech systems become increasingly intelligible and natural, evaluation is shifting from detecting gross synthesis failures to identifying subtle departures from lifelike human delivery. Because large-scale listening tests are costly and slow, speech reward models can serve as scalable automatic judges for comparing generated utterances, curating data, and supporting iterative TTS development. Existing speech reward models can predict scores or pairwise preferences and may generate natural-language rationales, but their supervision is typically defined at the utterance or pair level. The connection between local acoustic phenomena and the final preference therefore remains implicit. We introduce REAL, a framework for Reward modeling through Evidence-linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in generated speech. Its central idea is to supervise not only the final pairwise preference but also a structured account of its supporting observations, linking local audio spans to perceptual phenomena, affected dimensions, and the overall judgment. Specifically, REAL-Jury constructs these evidence-linked reports through timestamp alignment, multi-model analysis, and dispute-oriented deliberation. REAL-Judge learns to generate them from paired audio inputs. REAL-Eval assesses preference prediction in two tiers, from salient perceptual differences to subtle distinctions among strong TTS systems. Instantiated with MiMo-Audio, REAL-Judge improves pairwise preference accuracy over its backbone by 16.01 and 11.41 percentage points on the two tiers, respectively, and outperforms the open-source speech reward models SpeechJudge and UniSRM on both tiers.

title: BDBBQ: A Human-AI Collaborative Benchmark for Bengali Social Bias in LLMs
abstract: Despite growing attention to social bias in large language models (LLMs), existing bias benchmarks provide limited coverage of culturally grounded evaluation in Bengali, particularly within Bangladesh's sociocultural context. To address this gap, we develop a bilingual extension of BanglaBBQ comprising 61,312 question-answering instances across 12 social categories in English and Bengali. The benchmark incorporates balanced answer permutations, contrasting question framings, and both ambiguous and disambiguated contexts to systematically examine model performance and stereotype-aligned bias across languages. We validate the dataset through structural checks, 220 statistical tests, and expert annotation of 150 instances by four annotators, achieving strong inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' \k{appa}=0.8349). We evaluate eight LLMs across 490,496 instances and identify five key findings. First, disambiguated contexts yield substantially greater accuracy improvements in Bengali (+36.59 percentage points) than in English (+17.71). Second, all evaluated models exhibit lower accuracy in Bengali, although Mistral-Nemo shows the smallest cross-lingual accuracy gap (5.12 percentage points). Third, stereotype-aligned bias exhibits language and model dependent variation, increasing in Bengali for Gemma 2 9B but decreasing for Mistral-Nemo. Fourth, higher accuracy does not necessarily correspond to lower stereotype-aligned bias. Finally, bias varies considerably across social categories, with Qwen 2.5 7B exhibiting stronger stereotype alignment in Bengali for Politics and Physical Appearance. These findings demonstrate that cross-lingual performance and social bias are distinct dimensions of LLM behavior and underscore the importance of culturally grounded, language-sensitive benchmarks for evaluating fairness beyond English-centric settings.
