The remaining one, the [90,8,65]_7 code, is obtained from the first by appending two coordinates. The parameters and all weight counts were obtained by exhaustive enumeration, and a short program that repeats these computations is included.

title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

title: A Statistical Analysis of Lopsidedness in Disk Galaxies
abstract: We present a statistical analysis of Fourier lopsidedness in disk galaxies based on a deduplicated compilation of 606 unique objects: 442 have a measured m = 1 amplitude (A1), and 302 of these also have a measured m = 2 amplitude (A2), with no entry carrying A2 alone. The sample is a factor of approximately 3 larger than earlier homogeneous A1-A2 datasets. Our main results are: (i) Both A1 and A2 follow log-normal distributions (KS D = 0.046 and 0.048) which are strongly preferred over Rayleigh or exponential forms, pointing to a multiplicative amplification process rather than random-phase superposition. (ii) The m = 1 and m = 2 modes are correlated as A2 = 0.29 A1 + 0.11 (Spearman rho = 0.501, p less than 10^-19). (iii) A1 rises monotonically with morphological T-type from approximately 0.07 in E/S0 to approximately 0.37 in Sm/Im galaxies (Kendall tau = 0.234, p approximately 10^-12). (iv) A1 anti-correlates with gas rotation velocity (Spearman rho = -0.432) and, in a stellar-mass cross-matched subsample of 246 galaxies with independent stellar-mass estimates, with stellar mass (rho = -0.395). The weaker lopsidedness of massive, fast-rotating disks indicates that the observed m = 1 amplitude is regulated by internal dynamics rather than set by tidal perturbations alone. (v) The TNG50-1 simulation, analysed through the TNGGalaxyLab Fourier pipeline, reproduces the observed A1-stellar-mass anti-correlation with a nearly identical Spearman coefficient, although its median A1 is approximately 1.4 times lower, an offset consistent with the heterogeneous target selection of the observational compilation.

title: Metric-Aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization for Explainable Deepfake Detection
abstract: Deepfake detectors are commonly evaluated on real/fake classification alone, but real-world applications require explanations of the visual evidence behind each prediction. Joint vision-language models struggle with authenticity assessment, producing "real" narratives for manipulated images. To address this, we propose a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline as our submission to the ACM Multimedia 2026 Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge, with methods trained and evaluated on the XPlainVerse benchmark. A vision-foundation-model ensemble first classifies the image, then a Qwen3-VL-8B model generates a decision-conditioned explanation of the visual evidence. For fake images, a second Qwen3-VL-8B compresses that text into a short non-expert summary without using the image. We further apply metric-aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both explainers against the challenge criteria. Under matched conditions, GRPO raises complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves grounding (entity and evidence F1); our submission ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall.

title: Dwarf galaxy simulations with stellar-core mass- and metallicity-dependent core-collapse supernova explosion energies
abstract: Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are a critical source of thermal and kinetic energy and chemically enriched material in galaxies. Leveraging recent advances in CCSN modelling, we implement a novel core-mass- and metallicity-dependent prescription for stellar explodability and CCSN explosion energies, $E_\mathrm{expl}$, in the SPHGal galaxy evolution code. It accounts for black hole (BH) formation via SN failures and via partial fallback of ejecta mass, and adopts an explosion-progenitor connection calibrated to three-dimensional CCSN simulations, such that $E_\mathrm{expl}$ varies between $<0.1$-$2\, \mathrm{B}$. We ran simulations of isolated low-metallicity galaxies with variations in the input stellar feedback models. With the new explodability prescription nearly three times more BHs form compared to the canonical CCSN-model, but the reduced number of successful CCSNe has minimal impact on galactic star formation owing to the low fraction of failed CCSNe. While BH formation contributes to removal of matter from the galactic baryon cycle, the latter remains driven by galactic outflows, and most compact remnant mass is stored in white dwarves. The most significant change is instead brought about by the new average-$E_\mathrm{expl}$ that amounts to $\sim33$\% of the $1\,\mathrm{B}=10^{51}\, \mathrm{erg}$ traditionally assumed in sub-resolution CCSN-models. This reduction results in increased and less bursty star formation, reduced outflows and mass-loading factors, increased star cluster formation efficiency, and enhanced chemical enrichment and metal-recycling in star-forming regions. These results stand in contrast with outflow-launching and baryon cycle modelling in lower-resolution galaxy simulations in which canonical (i.e., $1\, \mathrm{B}$) CCSN feedback is typically assumed to produce galaxy models that match observed scaling relations.

title: A first application of split conformal prediction for dose prediction in knowledge-based radiotherapy planning
abstract: Radiation therapy treatment planning is a labour-intensive process prone to inter-expert variability. Deep learning (DL) dose prediction can accelerate this process, but most DL models do not quantify their reliability. In this study, we construct prediction intervals for DL-based radiotherapy dose prediction using split conformal prediction (CP), a model-agnostic and distribution-free method for uncertainty quantification that provides finite-sample coverage guarantees. We propose patient-level nonconformity scores obtained by aggregating voxelwise scores. Specifically, we formulate a maximum aggregation construction, which guarantees simultaneous coverage of the true dose in all voxels of a future patient with at least a user-defined probability, and a quantile-based construction, which guarantees, with the same probability lower bound, that a future patient attains a prescribed minimum level of voxel coverage. We also investigate groupwise calibration for region-specific guarantees and predictive uncertainty scaling for locally adaptive prediction intervals. The methods are evaluated on head-and-neck cases using a deep ensemble model. The proposed constructions achieved empirical coverage consistent with the nominal levels. Maximum aggregation led to conservative prediction intervals, whereas quantile aggregation produced narrower intervals. Groupwise calibration and uncertainty scaling reduced interval widths in some anatomical regions, while providing region-specific guarantees and local adaptivity. This is the first application of split CP to radiotherapy dose prediction. The explicit patient-level coverage guarantees offer a more interpretable characterisation of prediction reliability than raw uncertainty estimates. Split CP could help clinicians assess the reliability of model predictions and identify cases requiring further review.

title: Cascading Contingency Analysis of Modern Power Systems Using a Stochastic Hybrid Systems Framework
abstract: This paper presents a cascading contingency analysis and risk assessment framework that incorporates probabilistic mode transitions motivated by stochastic hybrid system (SHS) concepts together with power-flow-based stress evaluation. A two-stage modeling approach is adopted in which sensitivity-based analysis is first used to identify candidate cascading transitions, followed by DC power flow re-evaluation to accurately capture post-contingency stress redistribution, islanding behavior, and load shedding. A probabilistic propagation model is constructed using mode-dependent transition probabilities derived from line loading conditions. A Cascading Risk Index (CRI) is introduced to quantify the expected load shedding accumulated over cascade progression. Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus system demonstrate that the proposed framework captures diverse cascading routes under multiple initiating outages and identifies critical propagation patterns that are not revealed by N-1/N-2 screening. The results highlight the importance of SHS modeling in assessing cascading risk and providing a scalable framework for resilience evaluation in modern power systems.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

title: Nucleation of water ice under weak ionization via clustering on negative ions
abstract: Water-ice grains are shown to form spontaneously in a cold, weakly-ionized laboratory plasma with trace water admixture when neutrals and ions are cooled below $\sim$200 K. These conditions serve as an analog of ice nucleation in cold astrophysical and atmospheric environments. The ice grains form without the presence of particulate impurities, and do not form in the absence of ionization, indicating that nucleation is induced by ions. Time-resolved ion mass spectrometry provides separate detection of clusters of water molecules on both positive and negative ions. Hydrated negative ions, mainly $\mathrm{OH^-(H_2O)_n}$, grow to $\sim$200 amu, while hydrated positive ions, mainly $\mathrm{H^+(H_2O)_n}$, remain small and short-lived. As the temperature is reduced from room temperature toward 200 K, negative ion clusters grow in size and then drop sharply in abundance, consistent with the onset of rapid growth into macroscopic ice grains below a critical temperature. This indicates that hydrated negative ions are key precursors to ice nucleation in cold, weakly ionized environments, such as the Earth's mesosphere and protoplanetary disks, providing a concrete pathway for ice formation in environments where the nucleation mechanism has remained unresolved. This negative ion pathway is estimated to dominate over ice deposition on pre-existing dust grains in protoplanetary disk locations where there is sufficient UV to partially dissociate water molecules, and in addition, where negative ions such as OH- can form readily through electron attachment at low temperature.

title: Sharp regularity results for variational integrals asymptotic to the $p$-Dirichlet integral
abstract: We consider the regularity for minimisers of $\int_ΩF(Du) \mathrm{d}x$ where $F(z) \approx |z|^p$ in suitable senses at infinity. Depending on the strength of this asymptotic condition, we discuss various regularity results, and by means of counterexamples we show they are sharp. An effort is made to obtain results without assuming unnecessary regularity of $F$ while covering the full range $1<p<\infty$.

title: Assessing Alignment in Automatic Piano Transcription Datasets: A Benchmark for Scoring Methods
abstract: Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) relies on paired audio--MIDI datasets, implicitly assuming near-perfect temporal alignment. However, widely used piano datasets have been shown to contain alignment errors that may bias model evaluation and training. We propose a framework for evaluating audio--MIDI alignment scoring methods through controlled temporal, pitch, and structural MIDI corruptions. We also introduce STI, a scoring method built on AMT models, and benchmark it against existing alignment scoring approaches. Our results show that STI, together with methods based on CENS and spectrograms, achieves the strongest overall performance, with STI exhibiting the highest sensitivity to fine-grained temporal misalignments, the main alignment error in AMT datasets. We then apply the best-performing methods to widely used piano AMT datasets and identify trends in their relative alignment quality. These results support more informed dataset curation, model training, and AMT evaluation.

title: Dimensional Crossover and Correlated Spin Dynamics in the Chain-Like van der Waals Antiferromagnet AgCrP$_2$S$_6$
abstract: We report a comprehensive investigation of the magnetic properties and spin dynamics of the chain-like van der Waals antiferromagnet AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ using magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and $^{31}$P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). The magnetic susceptibility exhibits a broad maximum near 250 K, characteristic of strong short-range antiferromagnetic correlations in a low-dimensional system. A classical Fisher-chain analysis gives an effective intrachain exchange scale $J/k_B\approx 140$ K, while a quantum $S=3/2$ nearest-neighbor-chain calculation yields $J/k_B\approx 114$ K. A constrained AF-FM zig-zag-chain calculation is also compatible with the susceptibility, supporting a dominant quasi one dimensional antiferromagnetic exchange scale of order 100 K. $^{31}$P NMR measurements provide microscopic insight into both static and dynamic spin correlations. The $K-χ$ relation displays two distinct linear regimes separated near $T^\ast\approx 250$ K, with different slopes indicating a change in the effective transferred hyperfine couplings. Below $T_{N}$, the relaxation follows $1/T_1\propto T^5$, consistent with magnon-mediated relaxation in the ordered state. The temperature dependence of the internal hyperfine field yields a critical exponent $β\approx 0.36$, consistent with three-dimensional universality. Together, these results establish AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ as a quasi-one-dimensional $S=3/2$ antiferromagnet embedded in a layered van der Waals host, in which local probes directly resolve the crossover from correlated intrachain spin dynamics to anisotropic three-dimensional magnetic order. More broadly, AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ provides a useful van der Waals platform for studying dimensional crossover, correlated spin dynamics, and hyperfine-coupling evolution in low-dimensional antiferromagnets.

title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions
abstract: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.

title: The active chiral random walk
abstract: We introduce a minimal and intuitive lattice model for an active chiral particle which exhibits persistence, reversal, and chirality in its dynamics. It is fully defined by a small set of microscopic parameters that provide transparent control over the resulting dynamics. By coarse-graining, we extract continuum equations and closed-form expressions for the velocity autocorrelation, off-diagonal directional correlation, mean-squared displacement, and long-time diffusion and odd diffusion coefficients. The complex parameter $λ=q_p+\mathrm{i}q_c$ thereby encodes the microscopic information on persistence ($q_p$) and chirality ($q_c$) of the walker. In a weak-turning limit, microscopically realized by infrequent reorientation events, the continuum description can be mapped onto well-established models of active matter. Outside this limit the discrete model exhibits finite-step dynamics, such as anti-persistent motion, that are not captured by a smooth angular-diffusion description. The model therefore provides a compact, exactly solvable, and readily tunable framework in which a small number of transparent microscopic parameters control chiral active transport.

title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples
abstract: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.

title: Phase transitions in the hard-wall large deviations for the Gaussian free field
abstract: We study the probability that the Gaussian free field on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $d\ge3$, stays above a level $-h_N$ throughout the lattice $N$-blow-up of a bounded Lipschitz domain, when $h_N$ is close to the entropic-repulsion height $\sqrt{4g_0\log N}$. Two mechanisms compete: a collective upward displacement of the field, whose cost is governed by capacity, and the suppression of the remaining local violations, whose cost is their expected number, both of which are of order $N^{d-2}/\log N$ exactly in the window $h_N(β)^2=g_0(4\log N+\log\log N+2β)$. We obtain a sharp asymptotic rate expressed through a variational problem combining a Dirichlet energy with an exponential potential inside this critical window. Outside this window we obtain the asymptotics at the appropriate moving speeds: capacity alone governs the cost as $β\to-\infty$, and the expected number of violations as $β\to+\infty$. As an application, we derive lower-deviation bounds for the cover level of a macroscopic body by random interlacements, which determine the order of decay at the transition.

title: On the symplectic cohomology of orbifold divisor complements
abstract: This article studies the symplectic cohomology of Liouville domains whose contact boundaries admit a periodic Reeb flow, with a particular focus on affine varieties which arise as orbifold divisor complements. We describe a computation of the transverse Conley-Zehnder indices which allows for a simple computation of the positive equivariant symplectic cohomology in cases when the inertia orbifold of the compactifying divisor has only even cohomology. This is then applied to the classification of orbifold compactifications of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Moreover, we study the action of multiplication by the principal orbit on V-shaped symplectic cohomology and prove that if the compactification $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{D})$ is positively monotone, then this class induces a periodic structure on symplectic cohomology, reducing the problem of computing an infinite-dimensional group to a finite-dimensional repeating portion. We combine the index computations and this periodic structure to compute the symplectic cohomology of various Milnor fibers of surface singularities, the rational homology balls $B_{p,1}$ as well as complements of star-shaped configurations of rational curves in K3 surfaces, which includes the Milnor fibers of the exceptional unimodal singularities.

title: Regularity of minimisers for the $p$-distance functional
abstract: We consider regularity of minimisers of the $p$-distance functional $\mathcal{F}[u]=\int_Ω\mathrm{dist}(Du,K)^p \mathrm{d}x$ where $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{N \times n}$ is a compact set. We distinguish the scalar and vectorial cases, and consider geometric conditions on $K$ where regularity can be improved.

title: A Lightweight Differentiable Method for Real-Time Skin Rendering and Digitization
abstract: Inverse rendering for skin typically relies on offline path tracing to estimate physical properties, which fail to map directly to the approximate shaders utilized in interactive applications, such as game engines. We bridge this gap by directly estimating subsurface scattering parameters tailored for real-time rendering pipelines. We introduce a differentiable Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) framework that enables the joint optimization of spatially varying base textures and scattering distances. To account for local variations in skin thickness, we estimate these parameters across distinct facial regions, generating a blended profile map ready for production runtime engines. Our pipeline utilizes a low-cost, single-light, single-view capture setup designed for accessible and practical appearance acquisition. Optimization is driven by a masked loss function targeting regions where subsurface scattering effects are dominant. We validate our approach on a real-world dataset of $45$ individuals across the Monk Skin Tone Scale, ensuring demographic generalization. Furthermore, we complement this evaluation with synthetic data, a multi-light setup validating our single-light assumption, and a tilted-view configuration confirming angular consistency. Results demonstrate that our method effectively recovers scattering parameters from lightweight inputs, yielding realistic skin appearance directly compatible with standard real-time shaders.

title: Revisiting the centrifugal breakout scaling relationship for H$α$ emission in light of $ρ$ Oph C, the coolest B-type star with an H$α$-bright centrifugal magnetosphere
abstract: The corotating magnetospheres of B-type stars are strongly affected by magnetic field strength and rotational velocity, which determine both the geometry and strength of visible and radio emission; however, H$α$ emission largely disappears below a bolometric luminosity of $\log{(L / L_\odot)} \sim 2.8$. The nearby B5 V star $ρ$ Oph C (HD 147932) is the least-luminous rapidly rotating magnetic B-type star to display magnetospheric H$α$ emission. While $ρ$ Oph C's radio magnetosphere has been extensively studied, its magnetic field and H$α$ magnetosphere have been constrained only via snapshot observations. We present a new dataset of high-resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetry covering the star's rotational period, which is revisited by combining Hipparcos, K2 and TESS photometry. We find that the star's magnetic field strength and geometry are consistent with the model inferred from radio data. As expected from the magnetic model, there is very little variability in H$α$. Comparison of the light curve to both equivalent width measurements from metallic lines and magnetospheric models suggests that the star's photometric variability is dominated by surface chemical abundance spots; however, there is complex rotationally modulated variability at about the mmag level which probably originates in the magnetosphere. $ρ$ Oph C is the least luminous B-type star in which magnetospheric H$α$ emission has yet been detected, and its emission is notably weaker than the predictions of the centrifugal breakout model. Its photometric eclipse depth is also much lower than predicted by the CBO model. However, its radio luminosity is consistent with CBO predictions. We speculate on this basis that $ρ$ Oph C may be a transitional object between effective temperature regimes with hydrogen-dominated and decoupled metallic winds.

title: Shifted Lagrangian structures and syzygies on Calabi--Yau varieties
abstract: In \cite{FMR25}, Fantechi--Miró-Roig show how to construct new Lagrangian subspaces of the moduli of simple perfect sheaves on a K3 surface from a given one. We reinterpret their construction using the tools and flexibility of derived algebraic geometry. This allows us to generalize from K3 surfaces to (possibly singular) Calabi--Yau schemes of arbitrary dimensions.

title: Solomonoff Induction with Reflective Oracles
abstract: We study predictive properties of a reflective variant of Solomonoff induction formulated using reflective oracles (Fallenstein et al. 2015, Wyeth et al. 2025). We show that the resulting optimal predictor succeeds against computable predictive strategies that specify only part of the data-generating process. The argument relies on the fact that hypotheses computable from the predictor's own conditional probabilities remain within the reflective hypothesis class. In particular, the predictor learns incomplete models specified by computable interval restrictions on next-bit probabilities. We also establish weighted forms of unbiasedness and calibration. Finally, we discuss whether an optimal predictor's conditional probabilities suffice to compute every hypothesis in the reflective class.

title: Gravitational radiation from a particle in circular orbit around a wormhole: the nonrotating case
abstract: In this paper, we have generalized Poisson's(1993) calculation for the case of gravitational radiation from a particle in a circular orbit around a black hole to the case of the wormhole. Considering the motion of a test particle around a Schwarzschild like wormhole and using Teukolsky formalism, we have obtained an analytical result of flux at infinity under the assumption of small velocities. Focusing on the 22-mode, we have found a novel 0.5PN order term beyond the quadrupole order, which vanishes in the black hole limit. On the other hand, all higher order terms are getting modified in such a way that they give correct correspondence in the black hole limit. We have further corroborated our results with the numerical investigations, which show that the two waveforms match well when the particle lies far from ISCO. Thus, our work provides one of the first attempts toward the study of the post-Newtonian waveforms involving wormholes (ECOs).

title: Connecting field-level and n-point function measurements of galaxy bias
abstract: Precise measurements of galaxy bias parameters are essential for extracting cosmological information from galaxy surveys. Field-level analyses infer bias coefficients at a finite cutoff $Λ$, typically related to the lattice resolution, while $n$-point function analyses typically adopt renormalization conditions defined in the low-$k$ limit. In this work, we use the renormalization group (RG) to relate field-level measurements at different cutoffs and connect them to $n$-point function measurements. We generate mock galaxy fields with a Lagrangian perturbation theory forward model and a galaxy bias expansion, and then measure the bias parameters across a range of cutoffs. We show that the RG predictions describe the measured running and, in the limit $Λ\to 0$, agree with the (tree-level) $n$-point function measurements of first-order $b_δ$ and second-order $b_{δ^2}, b_{{G}_2}$. We also measure the running on halo catalogs based on full $N$-body simulations and show that the RG prediction describes the measurements well within the predicted systematic errors. Our results establish the RG flow as a natural formulation for relating galaxy bias measurements at different cutoffs and connecting the schemes used in field-level and $n$-point function analyses.

title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

title: Quantum Thermal Transistor via Nonlinear Environmental Coupling
abstract: Thermal amplification enables sensitive control of heat currents, providing a basis for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices. For a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base thermal reservoirs, we recover the absence of thermal amplification when system-reservoir interactions permit only single-quantum exchange. A controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, supported by numerical stationary solutions, shows that two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification and predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at the emitter and collector, varying the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors. This changes the emitter and collector heat currents far more than the base current, enabling large thermal amplification. We propose a realization using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system and bath spectral filtering, specifying conditions for its elimination to yield the required oscillator dynamics. These results establish nonlinear system-reservoir coupling as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification.

title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.

title: Structure of correlations for the single-$j$ model using quantum information theory
abstract: We say that a system undergoes a quantum phase transition when the mean-field ground state of a given Hamiltonian spontaneously breaks its symmetries depending on the Hamiltonian parameters. It is a widely accepted view that this phenomenon enables the mean-field state to absorb the maximum amount of correlations without losing its mean-field structure. However, it is still uncertain how those correlations are incorporated within the mean-field state and how the correlation structure changes when we get closer to the exact ground state by restoring the symmetries. In this work, we answer these questions by studying the single-$j$ model, which is a realistic fermionic nuclear model with abelian and non-abelian broken symmetries. We find that both types of symmetries have very different effects for the correlations within the mean-field state. This makes unclear the concept of the symmetry breaking process as a mechanism to absorb the maximum amount of correlations. Moreover, the symmetry restoration redistributes existing `fake' correlations between paired orbitals to more complex subsystems.

title: Finite-Key Readiness and Authentication-Key Replenishment in QKD-Assisted UAV Edge Computing
abstract: A service that needs fresh quantum keys must wait for key release, and may be denied it, before protected computation starts. We quantify this cost for a trusted stationary UAV serving two ground gateways, each obtaining its keys from one finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with parameters fixed in advance. A count-level Monte Carlo model, reproduced by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, including failed attempts and hover energy. At 26~dB effective optical loss, with authentication hashing at its proxy-benchmarked, near-zero cost, fresh keys raise the 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 to 28.65~s; hover energy grows in proportion. The scalar rate models evaluated here miss the deadline limit on the block size. The pulse budget lies in a window bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; for a fixed source, channel, and acceptance model, the authentication debit shifts the floor, whereas hashing cost does not. At a 35-s deadline the largest tested loss with a non-empty window is 27~dB at 1\% misalignment and 22~dB at 2\%; at 3\% no tested setting has one. Conditional on the assumed acquisition probability, the selected configurations meet this deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9--97.3\% on held-out trials, at 26~dB and at 18--20~dB with 2\% misalignment. A high-cost stress reference that charges hashing in full narrows the window and lowers these loss limits to 26 and 20~dB at the reference processing capacity. A small rise in error rate or loss pushes the deadline probability well below its target and drains authentication keys, while the protocol's security parameter is unchanged.

title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
abstract: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.

title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.

title: Progression-free sets in class $2$ and arbitrary finite groups
abstract: We study progression-free sets in arbitrary finite groups. We transfer sharp upper bounds from abelian groups to nilpotent groups of class $2$, and from nilpotent groups to arbitrary groups. Combining a recent result of Raghavan with the author's theorem on large subgroups of class $2$ gives \[ r_3(G) \, \leq \, C \, |G|\exp\left( -c\frac{(\log|G|)^{1/6}}{(\log\log|G|)^{1/3}}\right) \] for every finite group as $|G|\to\infty$. This improves the estimates obtained by using the abelian subgroup supplied by Pyber's theorem.

title: One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
abstract: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUC$_π$, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting $π$ treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index $J(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) - \mathrm{FPR}(t)$ across cutoffs $t$, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid S]$; for AUC$_π$, the decision maker's probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUC$_π$ is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by $|π(s) - π(s')|$ is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUC$_π$, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUC$_π$ does not.

title: Newton non-degenerate holomorphic foliations and their separatrices
abstract: In this paper we study germs of holomorphic foliations in the complex plane that are Newton non-degenerate. This is an algebraic condition attached to the Newton polygon of the foliation, analogous to the one defined by Kouchnirenko for analytic curves and, more generally, hypersurfaces. As in this case, the condition of Newton non-degeneracy for foliations can be identified through the comparison of two numerical invariants: the Newton number - a computation involving simple geometric data of the Newton polygon - and the Milnor number. The Newton number is never greater than the Milnor number, and the foliation is Newton non-degenerate if and only if they are equal. The assumption that a foliation is Newton non-degenerate imposes conditions on its set of separatrices. We prove that, under this hypothesis, the foliation has no weak separatrices and, hence, all its separatrices are analytic. We also give a description of the set of separatrices of a Newton non-degenerate foliation, which is sufficient to characterize the foliation as Newton non-degenerate when it is of generalized curve type. This allows us to prove that the property of being Newton non-degenerate is topologically invariant for foliations of generalized curve type.

title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.

title: C$^2$-Routing: Complementary Cropping and Compression for Efficient Vision-Language Inference
abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.

title: TanCRAFT: Context-Reasoned Anticipatory Feedback for Assembly Tasks
abstract: Preventing human error in physical assembly tasks requires assistance systems that can intervene before mistakes are made. This is especially challenging in settings where users are free to choose the construction order and correctness depends on the evolving assembly rather than a fixed next step. We present TanCRAFT, a four-stage real-time predictive assistance system that tracks the scene state, reasons about the current partial assembly, forecasts the near-future motion of manipulated pieces, and intervenes when the predicted placement is incompatible with the target. We instantiate our framework and confirm its effectiveness in a controlled tangram assembly task through offline benchmarks and a within-subject user study. Our findings show that the predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes relative to unguided and reactive sessions, while yielding the lowest mean perceived workload and shortest mean completion time. Overall, these results demonstrate the value of predictive feedback for error prevention and provide a step toward cost-aware assistance for automation and human-robot workcells.

title: A note on the intractability of enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression
abstract: We show that, given a Horn expression and a family of inclusion-wise maximal satisfiable subsets of its clauses, deciding whether there exists another maximal satisfiable subset is NP-complete. As a consequence, unless P=NP, there is no output-polynomial time algorithm enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression.

title: r-Process Abundance Variations in Globular Clusters as Fossils of Turbulent Mixing
abstract: Several metal-poor Galactic globular clusters exhibit substantial star-to-star $r$-process abundance variations at nearly fixed [Fe/H], with the ensemble suggesting smaller variations toward increasing metallicity. We investigate whether this chemical structure can be inherited from incomplete mixing in the galactic environments in which the clusters formed. Using parsec-scale simulations of rare-element transport in a supernova-driven turbulent disk, we follow the redistribution of $r$-process ejecta and characterize the abundance structure of gas selected to trace star-forming environments. Rare enrichment events generate strong [Eu/Fe] inhomogeneities that persist across a range of physical scales. As chemical evolution proceeds, the available abundance variance decreases, while spatial averaging over larger regions reduces the differences between their characteristic abundances. The simulations provide substantial pre-collapse $r$-process variance at low [Fe/H] and show the same broad decline toward higher metallicity suggested by the globular-cluster measurements. Our results support an interpretation in which at least some of the observed $r$-process variations are inherited from pre-existing chemical structure in the natal environment, allowing globular clusters to preserve a fossil record of the mixing history between rare enrichment and star formation.

title: Running out of Field Range: Nonlinear Sourcing of Light Scalars
abstract: Light scalar fields coupled linearly to the Standard Model are constrained by equivalence-principle tests, fifth-force searches, clock comparison tests, and stellar cooling. These bounds assume that the coupling to ordinary matter can be expanded to linear order for all field values reached. For a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson with decay constant $f$ this fails as soon as the field value reaches $O(f)$. The field around a source then stops growing with the coupling, and in addition the linear coupling of a probe is suppressed depending on its location. We reanalyze all of these bounds for the couplings to photons, electrons and nucleons. Space-based tests are weakened by several orders of magnitude, whereas the terrestrial tests are suppressed far more strongly and lose their sensitivity at low masses. As a result, for each coupling, $f$-dependent windows in the parameter space open up. For a coupling to nucleons a window persists at large couplings even for $f\sim 100 \,\rm{GeV}$. In particular, no current experiment constrains couplings between the naive limit and the stellar-cooling bound in a window of masses above $\text{few}\times 10^{-12}\,$eV, a range of more than ten orders of magnitude in coupling. This presents a unique opportunity for a ground-space clock comparison test to probe uncharted territory.

title: Thin-film lithium niobate integrated photonics at 493 nm
abstract: Visible and near-ultraviolet light underpins applications from biophotonics to quantum computing, which demand fast control of optical amplitude and phase. Integrated photonics offers scalable control, yet most visible-wavelength platforms lack gigahertz-scale modulation. We demonstrate a thin-film lithium niobate platform at 493 nm integrating grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and modulators. Segmented traveling-wave modulators achieve a half-wave voltage--length product of 450 mV$\cdot$cm, $>$20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring resonators show $2.9 \pm 0.2$ dB/cm propagation loss and quantify the platform's photorefractive response. This enables agile visible beam delivery for trapped-ion systems, although photorefraction and substrate uniformity remain key challenges to scaling.

title: Explicit restricted isometries with $k=m^{2/3-o(1)}$
abstract: We construct an explicit family of real $m\times n$ restricted isometries with $m\to\infty$, $m/n\to 0$, $δ_k\to 0$, and $k=m^{2/3-o(1)}$. We combine Gershgorin's circle theorem with a flat RIP estimate to reduce the problem to choosing a large vertex set in a strongly regular graph with the property that every small subset spans few edges. We select this vertex set using an incidence geometric result due to Zahl. The proof only uses the entrywise absolute value of the Gram matrix despite the conventional wisdom that such proof techniques exhibit a barrier of $m^{1/2}$. We prove that this barrier is actually $m^{2/3}$, and we show that our particular construction exhibits the same barrier.

title: BoviShift: A Six-Year Multi-Attribute Audit of Visual Cattle Phenotyping Across Animals and Time
abstract: Computer vision offers a scalable, non-contact means of estimating livestock traits, but correlated images and video frames make reliable evaluation difficult. Image-random splitting can place views of the same animal in both training and test sets, while deployment further requires transfer to animals captured in future years. We introduce BoviShift, a corpus reconstructed from six consecutive annual cohorts of an operational cattle marketplace collected from 2021 to 2026. It contains 2{,}657 cattle, 10{,}610 still images, and 2{,}566 walk-around videos across nine recorded breed categories. We evaluate three splitting strategies through four configurations: image-random and pooled cattle-disjoint splits over the same development cohorts, followed by separate future-2025 and locked future-2026 evaluations. Using a fixed ResNet-50 multi-task baseline, we assess weight, age, height, breed, and coat color. Differences between image-random and cattle-disjoint splitting are task-dependent rather than a universal leakage penalty. Future-cohort behavior is also attribute- and cohort-specific: breed declines relative to pooled evaluation; mean weight and age performance fails to beat constant baselines in 2025; height remains above baseline; and color transfers well to 2025 but degrades in 2026. Multi-task training improves all five point estimates in a single-seed ablation, still-view aggregation helps selectively, and zero-shot video-frame aggregation exposes a still-to-video domain gap. To our knowledge, BoviShift is the longest-spanning cattle-vision resource combining consecutive annual cohorts with physical and visual attributes.

title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

title: Non-local phase transition models for partial singularities
abstract: We study $Γ$-convergence, under appropriate scalings, of the energy functionals \[ F_\varepsilon(u) := [u]_{H^s(Q)}^2 + \int_{Q} W_\varepsilon(u)\,dx, \] where $s \in (0,1)$, $[\cdot]_{H^s(Q)}$ denotes the $H^s$-seminorm in $Q\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$, and $W_\varepsilon$ is a multi-well potential featuring infinitely many equally spaced wells together with additional intermediate wells whose height vanishes at a prescribed rate. Depending on this rate, different limiting behaviors emerge, ranging from classical models to new intermediate regimes.

title: Learning a model of non-stationary nuisances with non-local correlations for object detection
abstract: We tackle the problem of detecting faint objects in multivariate data corrupted by a strong and spatially correlated nuisance component in the low-sample regime. Standard covariance-based models often yield unstable or ill-conditioned estimators of the nuisance statistics, severely degrading detection performance. We propose a data-driven approach based on sparse precision matrix modeling, where the precision matrix is approximated through a pivoted sparse Cholesky factorization whose non-zeros coefficients are learned by maximum likelihood. This yields a low-complexity yet expressive statistical model of the nuisance. Building on this model, we derive a generalized likelihood ratio test for faint source detection enabling direct control of the false alarm rate. The approach is evaluated on an astrophysical application: the detection of exoplanets by high contrast imaging, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Pterodactyl: Pushing the Limits of Efficient Automated Translation Evaluation
abstract: In this paper, we present 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated quality evaluation. Our system, Pterodactyl, was engineered specifically for subtasks 2 and 3, that is, segment-level quality score prediction and the detection of error-free segments. Pterodactyl is a highly customizable, ultra-low cost system optimized for binary classification in translation triage and data curation. It is based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach, with prompt engineering and model selection guided by ROC analysis. We also developed several variants of Pterodactyl that were specifically adapted for subtasks 3.

title: Divisor Folding and Finite-Group Trace Obstructions
abstract: For a symmetric integer frequency set of size $n$ with Fourier floor $K$, we study a positive trace weighted by the reciprocal of the regularized Fourier multiplier. If restriction to frequencies divisible by $p$ leaves $n/p+O(K^2)$ frequencies, then for $n\ge K^4$ and $p\ll n/K^3$ the original trace differs by $O(n)$ from $p$ times the core trace at the inherited regularization. The transfer reaches cores of size $\asymp K^3$ and preserves vanishing triple density with diverging normalized triple count. We construct exactly regular finite abelian spectra at these scales for which the linear core trace bound fails by a power. The examples use unions of classical semiprimitive cyclotomic classes and also give obstructions in both reflection parities in odd characteristic. Finally, we bound the overlap of lifts of a core by its smallest positive Fourier height and the symmetry of the lifts. These bounds exclude balanced lifts of the binary examples in a range of cyclic extensions and quantify the asymmetry required in odd prime split extensions.

title: Singustars: Between Black Holes and Compact Stars
abstract: The Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff equations admit singular solutions in which a negative point mass is surrounded by a self-gravitating fluid. For a $Γ$-law polytropic equation of state, these solutions, which we call singustars, are thick shells bounded by two zero-pressure surfaces around a naked, repulsive, negative-mass singularity, with a Schwarzschild exterior. They form a two-parameter family, labeled by the mass $M$ and the compactness $C\equiv M/R$. Singustars join regular polytropes as the central negative mass vanishes and reach compactness beyond the Buchdahl bound. From exact equilibria and their radial modes, we find that singustars with $Γ= 2$ are stable only for $M\lesssim0.63$ and $C\lesssim0.25$, a region that nonetheless contains configurations more compact than any stable regular polytrope, although none with a light ring. In the numerically resolved parameter space, unstable singustars have a single unstable radial mode; many are energetically unbound. Nonlinear evolutions in ingoing null coordinates show that the end state depends on the perturbation. For the collapsing models studied, backward tracing of outgoing null rays identifies an event-horizon generator with a past endpoint on the singularity, before the first trapped surface appears. Outward perturbations disperse unbound shells and leave the singularity naked, while a bound shell migrates toward, and oscillates about, a stable configuration with the same conserved masses.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.

title: A fourth-order dimensionally split exponential time differencing scheme with real and distinct pole rational approximation for non-linear reaction-diffusion systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel fourth-order, L-stable exponential time differencing (ETD) Runge-Kutta type scheme incorporating a dimensional splitting integrating factor method for the numerical solution of nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. The method, ETDRK4RDP-IF, is obtained by approximating the matrix exponential operators in the classical dimensionally split ETDRK-IF scheme with an accurate fourth-order, L-acceptable rational function with real and distinct poles. The L-acceptability of the rational approximation guarantees effective damping of spurious oscillations arising from nonsmooth initial and/or boundary data and further eliminates complex arithmetic in the solution of the associated linear systems, thereby enhancing computational efficiency and making the scheme well-suited for parallel implementation in low-level programming languages such as Fortran and C++. Numerical experiments confirm the fourth-order accuracy for a range of reaction-diffusion problems with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, and demonstrate that it outperforms existing standard ETD methods in serial and parallel implementations, yielding CPU time reductions of up to a factor of 20.

title: The distribution of small gaps between zeros of the Riemann zeta function
abstract: Let $0<γ_1\leq γ_2\leq \cdots$ be the ordinates of the non-trivial zeros $ρ_n$ of the Riemann zeta function in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity. Selberg proved unconditionally that there exists $λ_0<1$ such that a positive proportion of the zeros $ρ_n$ satisfy $γ_{n+1}-γ_n\leq 2πλ_0/\log γ_n$. Simonič, Trudgian and Turnage-Butterbaugh were the first to obtain an explicit value in Selberg's theorem, showing that $λ_0=1- 10^{-3\cdot 10^{13}}$ is admissible. This was considerably improved by Zhao who showed that $λ_0= 1-2.36\cdot 10^{-6}$ is admissible. In this paper, we use a different approach, based on an unconditional variant of Montgomery's pair correlation method, to obtain a substantial improvement of these results, showing unconditionally that $λ_0=0.7892<4/5$ is admissible.

title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
abstract: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.

title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.

title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.

title: Automatic Continuity for projective clone homomorphisms
abstract: We show that every projective clone homomorphism from a closed function clone containing the automorphism group of a countable homogeneous Ramsey structure $Δ$ in a finite relational language is uniformly continuous. This answers, for such structures, open questions previously raised by Barto, Bodirsky, Marimon, Pongrácz, and the second author in several papers (Bodirsky, Pinsker, Pongrácz, J. Symb. Log. 2021; Barto, Pinsker, SIAM J. Comput. 2020; Marimon, Pinsker, arXiv:2512.01086). Consequently, the polymorphism clone of a first-order reduct $Γ$ of $Δ$ admits a projective clone homomorphism if and only if $Γ$ primitively positively interprets all finite structures; in other words, this ability of $Γ$ is characterised by the absence of non-trivial identities in its polymorphism clone, a purely algebraic condition.

title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows.
