abstract: Early detection and follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are crucial, as some of their subtypes, such as mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, carry a significant risk of malignant transformation. Although most AI studies investigating PCLs rely on computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue contrast, making it highly suitable for PCLs assessment. In this work, we propose an anatomy-aware two-stage deep learning framework for automated PCLs segmentation on abdominal MRI scans. First, a publicly available pancreas segmentation model is used to localize the pancreas. Then, we introduce the anatomyaware PCLSegNet, which incorporates anatomical priors as guidance for pancreas and PCLs segmentation. To address the class imbalance problem, we develop a Class-Specific ErrorWeighted (CSEW) loss function. Postprocessing is applied through anatomical constraints.Our proposed method outperforms multi-organ segmentation models such as TotalSegmentator, achieving substantially higher Dice scores for pancreas segmentation. Moreover, it also achieves a superior normalized surface Dice (NSD) and recall for PCLs segmentationcompared to other state-of-the-art models like nnU-Net, while also notably reducing the false negative rate, facilitating the automatic early detection and the noninvasive imaging-based assessment of PCLs.

title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
abstract: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.

title: Autonomous Trail Racing with a Bicycle Robot
abstract: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

title: Priority-Based Network Access with Strict-Priority Scheduling in PLCA Multidrop Networks
abstract: Shared-medium Ethernet is gaining renewed attention across industrial domains, driven by the adoption of 10BASE-T1S. In such multidrop networks, collision-free and deterministic medium access is achieved through Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA). However, PLCA follows a node-based cyclic access structure that does not account for traffic priority, leading to high access latency for time-sensitive traffic and limited scalability with increasing network size. Existing PLCA extensions improve latency for selected devices but remain restricted to node-based access and do not support network-wide traffic differentiation. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a priority-based network access and scheduling mechanism for multidrop networks. The proposed approach decouples medium access from node-based ordering and enables class-based prioritization, allowing high-priority traffic from any device to be transmitted ahead of lower-priority traffic. It further supports a configuration that emulates Strict Priority (SP) scheduling, providing low and bounded access latency for highest-priority traffic. Analytical bounds on the worst-case access latency are derived, validated, and shown to be tight. Performance evaluation demonstrates that the proposed mechanism reduces the maximum observed access latency for high-priority traffic by over 65% compared to PLCA, with latency increasing by less than 1% as the network grows from 8 to 40 devices.

title: Sharp Liouville theorems for the Hardy-Hénon p-Laplace equation and classification of positive solutions for the critical Hardy p-Laplace equation
abstract: We prove subcritical nonexistence for $-Δ_pu=|x|^au^q$ in $R^N$, with $1<p<N$ and $a>-p$, in the positive locally bounded weak class. Continuous Steiner symmetrization of a nonlinear auxiliary potential yields a directional pressure inequality; a localized Pohozaev identity and scaling give the Liouville theorem. At criticality, for $N\ge3$ and $-p<a<0$, we classify all positive entire weak solutions in $W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(R^N)$, without assuming local boundedness, symmetry, stability, finite energy, or decay at infinity.

title: Device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality for GHZ states and Bell-pair tree
abstract: We derive and compare device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) and genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) for GHZ states and trees of Bell pairs. A binary-outcome family using four global measurement contexts has the tight biseparable bound independent of the number of parties. We distinguish these GME bounds from Svetlichny-hybrid bounds, which permit arbitrary communication within either side of a bipartition. For GHZ states, we also give a $2N$-context GMNL witness and compare it with MABK and Svetlichny tests. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL, respectively, with explicitly specified input protocols and multi-bit local outputs. Separately, we prove the sharp four-context network bound $I_λ\leq2$ for every $N\geq3$ and $λ\geq2$, and bound the MABK scores of quantum networks assembled from bipartite sources. We successfully benchmark MABK, four-context, and Svetlichny witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations up to $10$ parties, under the local-measurement and sampling assumptions.

title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
abstract: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

title: Multi-Band Indoor MIMO Channel Measurements Across Sub-6 GHz, Mid-Band and mmWave: Comparing 2.55 GHz, 12.75 GHz and 25.5 GHz
abstract: Future wireless systems for indoor applications are expected to extend their operating frequencies from sub-6 GHz to mid-band and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies to support higher data rates. To characterize the frequency-dependent propagation behavior across these bands, multi-band channel measurements are essential. In this work, we conduct double-directional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel measurements in an indoor environment to enable a consistent comparison across three frequency bands. Measurements are performed using a 16x16 MIMO configuration at center frequencies of 2.55 GHz, 12.75 GHz and 25.5 GHz, covering both line-of-sight (LOS) and obstructed line-of-sight (OLOS) conditions. The measured channels are processed using the space-alternating generalized expectation maximization (SAGE) algorithm to extract multipath parameters, which are subsequently used to characterize the angular power distributions across the three frequency bands. The results show substantial angular-domain similarity across all three bands in both LOS and OLOS conditions, while also highlighting frequency-dependent variations.

title: Multi-Label Classification with Constrained Search for Inverse Design of a 16x16 Reconfigurable Pixel Antenna
abstract: In this paper, an inverse design method is presented for a 16x16 reconfigurable pixel antenna with 480 binary switches, giving 2480 possible patterns, far beyond what full-wave simulation can explore. Given a target frequency between 1 and 6 GHz, the method searches for a switch configuration whose simulated resonance lies close to the target. A forward surrogate model is trained on 22,152 full- wave simulated patterns to predict where a given switch pattern resonates. The forward task is formulated as multi-label classification over 100 frequency bins rather than reflection-coefficient regression, because a curve-fitting objective is dominated by the flat baseline around the narrow resonances of this structure. The inverse design is a simulated annealing search over the switch state, with a connectivity constraint maintained at every step so that every pattern generated is a valid antenna. The proposed methodology combines resonance-focused surrogate modelling with connectivity-constrained discrete optimization, enabling candidate generation without full-wave solver calls during the search. The pipeline is verified in CST Microwave Studio by simulating 220 predicted candidates, ten for each of 22 target frequencies. For each request, the best of the ten candidates reached a median frequency error of 23 MHz across the 22 targets, compared with 35 MHz for a solver-guided search using 200 simulations for each target. The proposed methodology therefore enables automatic switch configuration to achieve a requested resonant frequency, eliminating solver calls during the search and manual redesign of the antenna geometry.

title: Track4D: Representing Dense 3D Tracking for Video Diffusion Models
abstract: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d

title: FineSpeaker: Reliable Speaker Representation Learning at Fine Temporal Resolution
abstract: Speaker representation learning is fundamental to speech processing tasks such as speaker verification and diarization. Although long-context speaker encoders can produce stable and discriminative embeddings, short-duration verification and diarization require finer-grained temporal representations. Short temporal contexts limit the available speaker evidence and make speaker identity difficult to disentangle from phonetic and acoustic variability. This creates a temporal resolution-representation reliability trade-off: speaker representations should maintain local within-speaker consistency, between-speaker discriminability and remain sensitive to speaker changes at fine temporal resolution. Accordingly, we propose a framework for reliable speaker representation learning at fine temporal resolution. FineSpeaker first constructs resolution-controllable frame-wise speaker representations through mean pooling over an adjustable n-frame window, enabling flexible control of representation granularity. It then introduces a speaker encoder with local temporal modeling that exploits short-range speaker context to improve the stability and discriminability of short-duration and frame-wise representations. Furthermore, we develop a generative disentanglement strategy for optimizing frame-level speaker representations, combining VAE-based probabilistic modeling with flow matching to characterize speaker-related variation and suppress non-speaker interference. Experiments demonstrate competitive full-utterance performance, improved fine-grained speaker verification on VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb, and strong zero-shot diarization results, highlighting the benefits of balancing temporal resolution and representation reliability.

title: Fundamental Limits of Data-Driven Predictive Control
abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) has attracted substantial interest, and many variants have been proposed; however, comparatively less is known about the statistical closed-loop performance of these methods and the fundamental limits they are subject to. In this contribution, we apply the statistical decision framework developed in our earlier work to study fundamental limits of DDPC. The performance of a data-driven controller is measured by its risk, the expected deterioration in control performance relative to an oracle model-based controller at a given system, and by its total risk that measures the overall performance across all systems of interest. Lower bounds on these risks are derived using the bias-variance decomposition and the Cramer-Rao inequality. In particular, a lower bound on the total risk is obtained by a calculus-of-variations method. This bound applies to any DDPC design, thereby quantifying unavoidable performance limitations and providing a benchmark for assessing existing DDPC methods. In an illustrative example, we compare the risks of certainty-equivalence model predictive control, subspace predictive control, and data-enabled predictive control with the derived lower bounds, providing a quantitative performance assessment of these methods and some guidance on tuning regularization parameters in DDPC.

title: Hypersonic Flow Over an Axisymmetric Open Cavity: Effects of Segmentation Angle and Reynolds Number
abstract: This study investigates the influence of cavity segmentation angle ($ϕ$) on the flow characteristics of a cavity mounted on a cone under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. Four segmentation configurations, corresponding to $ϕ= 360^\circ$, $48^\circ$, $32^\circ$, and $16^\circ$, are examined for cavity length-to-depth ratios ($L/D$) of 1 and 6 over a range of Reynolds numbers ($Re_D = 23000$--$74000$). The flow field is characterized using surface pressure and heat flux measurements, complemented by planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization. The results indicate that, for $L/D = 1$, the downstream Strouhal number ($St$) and mean pressure remain largely unaffected by the segmentation angle and closely agree with those of the axisymmetric configuration. In contrast, the flow parameters within the cavity are larger than in the axisymmetric case, which is attributed to the three-dimensional bounding effect. For $L/D = 6$, the mean pressure distribution exhibits a similar trend across the segmentation angles, whereas the downstream $St$ increases with increasing $ϕ$, approaching the axisymmetric value. Flow-mode transitions are observed across all segmentation angles, consistent with the axisymmetric configuration. However, both the transition Reynolds numbers and the corresponding flow modes vary with the segmentation angle.

title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
abstract: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

title: Performance Analysis of a Dual-Polarised Bowtie Antenna in the Low RF Band: A Low-Cost Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment
abstract: We have set up a simple experiment to characterise a dual-polarised bowtie dipole antenna at St. Stephens College as part of undergraduate radio astronomy experiments. The antenna provides two orthogonal linear polarisation responses, allowing us to investigate the polarisation properties of radio-frequency signals using a simple and affordable experimental setup. In this article, we present our analysis of the performance of the antenna and demonstrate its use through polarisation-rotation measurements. This antenna is part of the Sky Watch Array Network (SWAN) and this analysis helps us understand the response of each individual array element in the setup.

title: Cross-channel amplification of frequency-distinct scattered waves in multibeam stimulated Brillouin scattering
abstract: Multibeam stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) can be amplified when one side-scattered wave draws energy from several pumps, each through a separate ion-acoustic-wave (IAW) branch. This is not common-daughter-wave coupling: scattered waves from different parent pumps may occupy nearly the same wave-vector region yet remain distinct optical modes because their frequencies differ. We examine this process with local-growth and finite-width-gain models, three-dimensional coupled-mode calculations and two-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. Adding the extra branches increases temporal growth and spatial gain across the tested crossing angles. In three dimensions, direct branches alone give weak, localized side scatter; with the cross branches present, a strong field fills much of the interaction region even though the incident beams, direct channels and initial seed are unchanged. The distinction persists at fixed total power. The coupled response remains strong as the power per beam falls, whereas the direct-only response drops rapidly. PIC spectra contain nearby scattered-light features accompanied by several pump-specific IAW branches, and the fixed-power scans yield a strong, non-monotonic response. These results support cross-channel feedback through separate IAWs as a multibeam SBS amplification mechanism that may help predict and control SBS losses in laser-fusion plasmas.

title: On shared responsibility, fish, and the strong law of large numbers
abstract: We give a new, short, and intuitive proof of the strong law of large numbers for i.i.d. random variables.

title: Statistical Characterization of CME Interaction Responsible for Successive Type II Solar Radio Bursts
abstract: Successive type II solar radio bursts are often considered as diagnostics for the evolution of CME-driven shocks and their interaction with the structured solar corona. However, the physical mechanisms driving these successive type II emissions are not well understood, with prior studies mostly limited to single event. In this work, we provide the first statistical analysis of successive type II radio bursts over Solar Cycles 23, 24 and the ascending phase of Solar Cycle 25 (1997-2025). We have constructed a catalogue of 73 independent successive type II events using radio dynamic spectra and SOHO LASCO coronagraph observations. The events were divided into three observational classes, based on the inferred physical interaction mechanisms: CME-Streamer interaction, CME-CME interaction and Single-CME. Statistical analyses were performed on the 56 events with clear physical classification. CME-streamer interactions constitute the largest class among the physically classified event, highlighting the potential importance of the ambient coronal environment in shaping successive type II radio emission. Comparative statistical analyses indicate that the CME linear speed has marginal differences among the physical classes, but the CME angular width is significantly different between the CME-CME and CME-Streamer populations. Other factors, such as shock evolution and the ambient coronal environment, are important for the production of successive type II radio burst. The catalogue presented here provides a statistical framework for the investigation of CME-driven shock evolution.

title: APG-Planner: Learning Vision-Based High-Speed Trajectory Planning via Analytic Policy Gradient
abstract: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.

title: Periodic Trends in Oxygen Vacancy Formation Energies Across Binary Main-Group Metal Oxides
abstract: The function of oxide materials, from solid-oxide fuel cells to solar thermochemical fuel production, depends on their oxygen vacancies. Their formation energetics have been mapped systematically for ternary perovskites, but reported values for the binary oxides, their conceptual and thermochemical building blocks, remain scattered across studies with differing computational methods. Here we report a systematic r$^2$SCAN density functional theory survey of neutral oxygen vacancy formation energies across 39 binary main-group metal oxide polymorphs spanning groups 1, 2, 13, 14, and 15, using the ShakeNBreak method to locate reconstructed defect ground states. The formation energies span 8 eV and decrease down each group and, for most multivalent cations, with increasing oxidation state. Both trends follow the reducibility of the cation. An interpretable crystal feature model is fit to these energies; its inputs are properties of the pristine bulk, with the reduction potential alternatively taken from tabulated thermochemistry. Retaining only its two dominant descriptors, the crystal reduction potential and the band gap, the model reproduces the formation energies with a held-out mean absolute error of 0.31 eV, lower than that of its four-descriptor parent model for transition-metal perovskites. The bond-breaking and stability terms of the full Born-Haber fit prove statistically null for the binary oxides, and the largest residuals identify the hosts where electron accommodation departs from the cation-reduction picture that the descriptors encode. The dataset provides a benchmark for machine-learning interatomic potentials, and the model estimates vacancy formation energies of main-group oxides from bulk properties alone.

title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures for Financial Time Series Prediction
abstract: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.

title: Small classes have linear neighbourhood complexity
abstract: A hereditary graph class is small if it contains at most $n!c^n$ labelled graphs on $n$ vertices for some constant $c$. Small classes include proper minor-closed classes and classes of bounded twin-width. We prove that every small class has linear neighbourhood complexity, that is, in every graph in the class, vertex neighbourhoods intersect any $k$-vertex set in only $O(k)$ distinct ways. This resolves a conjecture of Bonnet, Duron, and the first two authors (ITCS 2025) and makes the algorithmic, structural, and representation consequences of linear neighbourhood complexity available for every small class. In particular, every small class admits an adjacency labelling scheme with $O(\log^2 n)$-bit labels, improving the previous $O(\log^3 n)$ bound.

title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
abstract: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

title: The Distant Milky Way Halo from the Southern Hemisphere: Spatially broad and closer stellar debris associated to the Magellanic Stream
abstract: The Magellanic Stream (MS) is a gaseous structure extending over $150^\circ$ across the sky, likely formed through interactions between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) as they fell into the Milky Way (MW). Its predicted stellar counterpart would provide a collisionless record of these interactions, but few candidate members have been identified. To expand this sample, we constructed a catalog of 87,763 distant K-giant candidates using DELVE DR2 and VHS DR5 photometry and Gaia DR3 astrometry, and analyzed VLT and Magellan spectra of 51 targets along the trailing MS. Combining radial velocities, spectrophotometric distances, and proper motions, we identify five new MS candidates at 58--95 kpc. Their metallicities are consistent with the outskirts of the SMC, while orbit integrations in a time-dependent MW--LMC--SMC potential support a possible Magellanic origin. Combined with previously identified candidates, these stars span a substantially broader range of Magellanic latitude than predicted by existing models, suggesting an extended debris field rather than a narrow stream. The candidates also lie predominantly closer than the simulated debris. More recent, less eccentric SMC orbits may help explain this distance discrepancy, although new simulations are required to test their implications for the stellar debris, along with larger spectroscopic samples.

title: Browser Immune System (BIS): Innate and Adaptive Threat Detection in the Browser with a Cybersecurity Transformer
abstract: Security decisions about a web page are best made where the page is: in the browser, before anything leaves the machine. We present the Browser Immune System (BIS), a browser extension that screens navigation with a cybersecurity transformer running entirely on the user's GPU, and alias-web, the model that powers it: a 4B-parameter model that starts from the dual-regime cybersecurity transformer (CT0), extends its public release alias3-micro with a context-category sensor, and is quantised to 4 bits and compiled to a 2.44 GB graph for WebGPU. alias-web is the first in-browser realisation of that model's typed decision mode, System 1, with its official pieces: the marker-token mapping, the complete pointer head and the final normalisation that the exported graph omits. It answers a typed security question in about 150 ms on a laptop GPU, and the same weights generate explanations at 10.5 tokens/s on demand. BIS treats the model as an immune system: an innate response, one System 1 question per threat class, runs on every page; an adaptive response, System 2 text, explains a verdict only when the user asks. On BISBENCH-8, eight synthetic sites of which six execute real but harmless malicious behaviour and two are adversarial controls, BIS returns the expected page verdict on 7/8 sites with both controls green and a class-level micro-F1 of 0.71, scans a page in 0.9 to 6.4 s, and gives identical verdicts across samples and across Chrome and Firefox. Single-variable diagnostics trace both benchmark errors to what the model was shown and, with a first pass over eleven real public pages, show that two of the seven questions answer yes on ordinary scripts and login forms: specificity on the real web is the open problem. We report every error, the engineering obstacles between a research checkpoint and a working extension, and what the evidence does not yet support.

title: VISTA Magellanic Clouds deep observations of Classical Cepheids: Precision distances and a collision-driven SMC
abstract: The central regions of the Magellanic Clouds are crucial for understanding galaxy interactions and calibrating the cosmic distance scale, yet they remain observationally challenging due to extreme stellar crowding. We utilised deep VISTA observations (VMCDeep) to determine the highest-precision near-infrared Period-Luminosity (PL) and Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations to date for Classical Cepheids (delta Cep class, DCEPs) in the dense central regions of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC). We analysed J and Ks time-series data covering the central 1.77 deg^2 of each galaxy. Utilising approximately 40 epochs per filter and PSF-based photometry, we derived high-quality light curves for 573 and 2090 DCEPs in the LMC and SMC, respectively. We derived exceptionally precise PL and PW relations, exhibiting the lowest photometric dispersion published so far for the Magellanic Clouds. Fourier parameters calculated from the light curves indicate that pulsational models incorporating a mildly non-canonical mass-luminosity relation and a mixing-length parameter of alpha = 1.7 best reproduce the observations. Age derivations confirm a bimodal star formation history in the SMC centre. Crucially, we discovered a striking line-of-sight spatial dichotomy within the young SMC DCEP population (t < 116 Myr), which is bifurcated into two distinct structures separated by ~4 kpc. This provides independent stellar evidence tracing a recent direct collision with the LMC. Finally, by unifying fundamental and first-overtone pulsators, we derived a highly constrained relative distance between the Clouds. Comparing this to detached eclipsing binary distances, our data suggest a moderate metallicity correction for the Leavitt Law with gamma ~ -0.2 mag/dex.

title: Cumulants of Operator Semigroups for Hierarchies of Many-Particle Evolution Equations
abstract: The paper presents a brief overview of recent advances in the mathematical theory of evolution equations for quantum many-particle systems. The structure of expansions representing non-perturbative solutions to the Cauchy problem for hierarchies of fundamental evolution equations for many quantum particles is outlined. It has been shown that the concept of cumulants of operator semigroups forms the basis for non-perturbative representation of solutions to hierarchies of evolution equations that describe the state and observables. It is proven that the constructed dynamics of correlations underlie the description of the evolution of the state, both for finitely and infinitely many particles, governed by the BBGKY hierarchy for reduced density operators or by the hierarchy of nonlinear evolution equations for reduced correlation operators. In fact, it is demonstrated that the behavior of particle correlations governs the dynamics of states in quantum systems with an infinite number of particles.

title: Directed Domain Wall Motion by Radio-Frequency Currents
abstract: Magnetic domain walls (DWs) are central to emerging spintronic technologies for memory, logic and neuromorphic computing, where their controlled displacement is a key functionality. While current-induced DW motion driven by spin-orbit torques is well established under direct currents, it remains unclear how radio-frequency (RF) currents couple to DWs and whether they can generate directed motion under a symmetric periodic drive. Here we show that RF currents drive DW oscillations, which can be rectified into directed motion through symmetry breaking. Using time-resolved and static magneto-optical Kerr microscopy, we demonstrate that RF spin-orbit torques efficiently excite low-frequency DW oscillations well below the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. Whereas these oscillations remain symmetric in the absence of perturbations, symmetry breaking by a transverse magnetic field produces self-propulsion, while symmetry breaking by an initial current pulse gives rise to sustained DW motion. We further show that in initially uniform magnetic states, RF-driven expansion of a pulse-generated edge domain ultimately results in efficient RF-assisted magnetic switching. Together, these results establish a general framework for understanding how RF-driven DW oscillations are rectified into directed motion, providing new opportunities for their high-frequency control.

title: Beyond the Explicit: Benchmarking and Detecting Implicit Harm in Short Videos
abstract: Short videos have become a dominant online medium, where harmful content is increasingly conveyed in implicit and fragmented forms. Prior work largely focuses on explicit categories, such as violence and hate speech, and often fails to detect videos that subtly promote misleading values through narrative context, emotional framing, or cross-modal cues, partly due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks for implicit harm. To bridge this gap, we construct DeepHarm-7K, a large-scale harmful short-video dataset comprising 7,110 samples annotated according to a fine-grained harmful-content taxonomy. The dataset systematically covers implicitly harmful videos across diverse real-world scenarios and is constructed through a rigorous multi-stage quality-control process. Building on this dataset, we propose DeepHarm-VL, a multimodal detection framework that integrates visual, audio, and cross-modal reasoning. The framework employs a two-round reasoning strategy to progressively identify surface-level evidence and infer latent harmful implications. Experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both explicit and implicit harmful short videos.

title: Floating-point, exact and certified computation for control: paradigms, pitfalls, and how to combine them
abstract: Many questions in linear systems theory have a discrete answer: is a polynomial Hurwitz, is a 2-D system structurally stable, is the peak gain finite, which solution of a Riccati equation is stabilizing? Algorithms implemented in floating point usually answer such questions, but often with a limited, or even no, guarantee on the result, which depends on a tolerance fixed a priori. Computer algebra and interval arithmetic provide other ways of computing, which give guarantees on the result, but usually at a higher cost. In this paper, we propose a short guide to these approaches: floating-point, exact, multiprecision and interval arithmetic, certified root isolation and certified Newton methods. Using small examples from control theory (each of them runs in a few seconds), we show what each approach guarantees and in which situations it fails, and how several approaches can be combined, for example by certifying a numerical solution, or by reducing a problem exactly before solving it with certified real solving. We then revisit the structural stability of 2-D systems (with and without parameters) and the computation of the $H_\infty$ norm, and we list the available implementations. The main examples are given as reproducible worksheets based on the PACE ecosystem.

title: Path complexes with concatenation and their relation to digraphs
abstract: The path homology theory is based on the notion of path complex and is a part of GLMY-theory created and developed by Grigor'yan, Lin, Muranov, and Yau in a cycle of papers in 2012-2014. In this paper we define a path complex with concatenation ($PC$-complex) which is a particular case of a path complex. We define a natural topology on a set of vertices of any $PC$-complex, and describe properties of this topology and its relation to the discrete topology of Alexandroff. We prove the existence of functorial relations between some categories of $PC$-complexes and digraphs. These relations allow to transfer covering, homotopy and various versions of homology theory from digraph theory to $PC$-complexes.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
abstract: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

title: Arbor: When Labels Are Not Coarsened at Random
abstract: Merging datasets labelled at different levels of a taxonomy leaves some images with only a coarse label, and some classes with no fine-grained label at all. Standard training scores a coarse label by the total probability of the classes under it. Coarse labels name superclasses, and the standard objective is exact only when every class within a superclass is equally likely to receive a coarse label. We call a class novel if it is never labelled finely, and known otherwise. A novel class violates the assumption, and the classifier assigns its images to a known sibling. We propose Arbor, which models how labels become coarse. In each superclass with a novel class, Arbor adds a virtual novel class, and a logistic gate divides the superclass's probability between it and the known classes. The gate is trained with the likelihood of the observed labels under this model, the coarsening likelihood. We prove that at its population optimum the gate equals the Elkan-Noto correction of positive-unlabelled learning, and show that training the correction into the classifier improves on applying it after training. Across Cars, CUB and Aircraft with 90% coarse labels, Arbor correctly assigns 76-85% of novel-class images to their superclass, more than hierarchical classifiers, hierarchical novelty detection and the Elkan-Noto correction. Its top-1 accuracy over the leaf classes on known-class images is within 1.6 points of the best baseline, although its final predictions return the superclass more often. On the more challenging iNaturalist-2019 benchmark, Arbor improves novel-class accuracy from 46% (uniform target, the strongest baseline) to 68%.

title: Nonabelian Hodge theory in positive characteristic for rank-2 vector bundles over curves
abstract: We describe the Nonabelian Hodge Theory correspondence in positive characteristic between nilpotent Higgs bundles and flat bundles with nilpotent p-curvature, as constructed in the seminal paper by Ogus-Vologodsky, in the special case of rank-2 vector bundles over a smooth projective curve. In this set-up we can rephrase this correspondence as a shift of the extension class of a rank-2 vector bundle by a cohomology class encoding a W_2-lift of the curve. As an application, we obtain that a general rank-2 vector bundle of degree 0 admits a connection with non-zero nilpotent p-curvature.

title: Influence of Assortativity on the SICP Spreading Process in Hypergraphs
abstract: Many real-world systems involve group interactions that cannot be captured by pairwise graphs. They can be better represented by hypergraphs where each hyperedge could connect an arbitrary number of nodes. The Susceptible-Infected Contact Process (SICP) has been proposed to model the spreading of information and epidemics on hypergraphs. However, how higher-order topological properties of a hypergraph influence the SICP spreading process remains understudied. In this paper, we examine the impact of hypergraph assortativity based on the Neighborhood Coefficient (NC)-the average size of hyperedges incident to a node-on the SICP spreading process. By introducing a low-complexity measure of hypergraph assortativity grounded in analysis of variance, we apply hyperdegree-preserving rewirings to real-world networks and synthetic hypergraph models to tune their assortativity. We find and explain why lower NC assortativity yields higher average epidemic prevalence and lower prevalence variance across different seed selections. This phenomenon is evident when hyperdegree-preserving rewirings are applied to real-world networks with heterogeneous topological structures, but it is largely absent when comparing synthetic random hypergraphs to their rewired counterparts.

title: AcrossPlace: Do Vision--Language Models Recognize Places Beyond Their Source Views? A Comprehensive Benchmark
abstract: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models
abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis
abstract: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.

title: BiPOP: Partial-Order Planning for Long-Horizon Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Code: https://github.com/Kchu/BiPOP

title: Weak null singularities for the Einstein--Vlasov system
abstract: We study the formation and stability of weak null singularities for solutions to the massive and massless Einstein--Vlasov systems without symmetry assumptions. Extending previous results of Luk in the vacuum setting, we establish the existence of spacetimes arising from characteristic initial data that develop a singular null boundary while remaining extendible with a continuous metric. For both massive and massless particles, the energy-momentum tensor and Ricci curvature remain bounded and extend continuously to the singular boundary. For genuinely singular initial data, the Christoffel symbols in the original double-null coordinates fail to be locally square integrable near the boundary. We introduce new commutator vector fields that avoid both derivative loss and the most singular curvature component. Under additional curvature assumptions, we also prove Lipschitz inextendibility across the singular null boundary.

title: Polynomial approximations to Calabi--Yau metrics on quartic K3 surfaces and quintic threefolds
abstract: On the Fermat quartic K3 surface and the Fermat quintic threefold, we construct Kähler metrics from explicit rational polynomial potentials and bound their differences from the Ricci-flat metrics in integral tensor norms. For specified compact families of smooth quartic and quintic hypersurfaces near the Fermat hypersurfaces, we give a terminating algorithm that constructs polynomial Kähler metrics with prescribed pointwise bounds on their differences from the Ricci-flat metrics and on their Ricci forms. The resulting metrics converge to the Ricci-flat metrics in every $C^r$ norm, uniformly in the parameter.

title: Delaunay-Based Nearest Neighbor Search with Grid-Accelerated Queries and Parallel Construction
abstract: Nearest-neighbor search is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, with applications in distance field computation, surface reconstruction, and point cloud registration. In many graphics applications, data points lie on a surface manifold embedded in 3D space, whereas queries are distributed throughout the surrounding volume, a setting in which spatial partitioning structures such as k-d trees and grids can become inefficient. Dynamic-programming-based nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) offers an alternative: it traverses a successor DAG that records the history of incremental Delaunay construction and often outperforms spatial partitioning structures. However, its sequential construction is slow, and naive parallelization degrades query performance, limiting its practical adoption. We accelerate both queries and construction in DP-NNS. For queries, we introduce a grid-based initialization strategy that precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG, shortening search paths while preserving exactness and enabling a twofold speedup. For construction, we analyze how parallel insertion affects query cost and develop a parallel algorithm that preserves logarithmic expected query cost under stated geometric assumptions. Our parallel construction algorithm achieves a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline while maintaining nearly the same query cost. We further reorder query points to improve cache locality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms widely used libraries in nearest-neighbor query performance.

title: Conserved gravitational-wave Stress-Energy Tensor in General Metric Theories
abstract: We construct a gravitational-wave (GW) stress-energy tensor for general metric theories and show that it is conserved after averaging in the wave zone. In metric theories involving a vector field, we find that the conventional GW stress-energy tensor is generally not conserved. Combining the diffeomorphism identity, we identify the vector-field contribution required in addition to the conventional GW stress-energy tensor. On this basis, in a flat vacuum wave zone with constant background fields and after short-wavelength averaging, the perturbed field equation, perturbed action, Landau-Lifshitz, and Noether current methods yield equivalent tensors. In this setting, the completed tensor is generally nonsymmetric and satisfies $\partial_μτ^{μν}=0$, with energy flux $cτ^{i0}$. It also does not depend on whether a covariant or contravariant vector is chosen as the fundamental variable. Applying this framework to Einstein-æther theory, we derive the orbital energy losses of an adiabatic quasicircular compact binary, and provide a possible explanation for the discrepancies among previous results in this theory. These results establish a consistent radiation balance that allows additional gravitational degrees of freedom to be connected to the evolution of astrophysical systems and to observational tests of gravity.

title: On the domain of the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in quantum markovian dynamics
abstract: The GKLS representation of the unbounded generator of a quantum Markov semigroup crucially depends on an unbounded operator $G$, generating a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on the underlying Hilbert space, which is formally the sum of a negative self-adjoint operator $G_0$ and $-\mathrm{i}H$ with $H$ symmetric. In many situations it is useful to know the relationships between the domains of the three operators, in particular whether $\Dom(G)=\Dom(G_0)\cap\Dom(H)$ when both $G_0$ and $H$ are unbounded. In this note we show that this happens when $G_0$ and $H$ are self-adjoint quadratic polynomials in annihilation and creation operators in a finite-mode bosonic Fock space and $G_0\leq0$ or assuming a certain half bound on the commutator of $G_0$ and $H$. A counterexample shows that the conclusion does not hold in general situations.

title: Surface evolution under conformal map and linearized energy-stable parametric finite element methods
abstract: In this paper, we aim to develop a linearized, energy-stable, second-order-in-time parametric finite element method without Lagrange multipliers for surface evolution equations on surfaces with or without boundaries, including (volume-preserving) mean curvature flow and surface diffusion. We first reformulate the original equations into a new unified form in which the tangential motion is determined by requiring the flow map to be conformal. Based on this new formulation, we present a family of parametric finite element schemes that employ a linearized Euler or Crank-Nicolson discretization in time. We prove the existence and uniqueness of the resulting linear system, as well as the energy stability of the schemes. Our discrete methods can be applied to general surfaces although the second-order scheme may degenerate to first-order accuracy in certain cases. Numerical results verify the robustness of our method and demonstrate its ability to preserve mesh quality.

title: Hyperexponential Stabilization of Nonholonomic Systems by Oscillating Controls
abstract: We address the problem of designing time-varying feedback controls that stabilize a given equilibrium of a nonholonomic system at a faster than the exponential rate. We consider systems with an arbitrary degree of nonholonomy and prove a theorem on practical hyperexponential stabilization under a suitable assumption on the parameterized dither signals. The convergence proof is based on a comparison equation with a prescribed power of logarithmic terms. We apply this result to stabilize a model of a car with two off-hooked trailers.

title: CaseScope: A Multi-Field Benchmark for Case-Level Pathology Diagnosis with Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Wenchuan-Zhang/CaseScope.

title: Analytical Characterization of Radial Resolution at Oblique Angles for Near-Field Communications
abstract: Exploiting radial resolvability in near-field communications requires analytical expressions that directly map physical beam parameters to resolution-controllable focal regions. However, beam characterization at oblique angles produces complex algebraic expressions that mask these critical interactions. In this work, we introduce an electromagnetic-aware analytical model built upon a tight upper bound of the spatial power density. This approach yields compact, closed-form solutions for the peak intensity position and radial focal extent, enabling the design of contiguous multi-user focal regions with controlled radial resolution. Performance evaluations confirm that the framework closely tracks exact solutions while facilitating system dimensioning and inter-beam interference management across varying steering angles.

title: The maximum product of nontrivial cross $t$-intersecting families
abstract: Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty families of $k$-subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $|A\cap B|\ge t$ for all $A\in\mathcal A$ and $B\in\mathcal B$, and suppose that each family has fewer than $t$ common elements. For $k\ge t+2\ge4$ and $n\ge(t+1)(k-t+1)$, we prove \[ |\mathcal A||\mathcal B|\le\max\{h_t(n,k)^2,b_t(n,k)^2\}, \] where \[ h_t(n,k)=\binom{n-t}{k-t}-\binom{n-k-1}{k-t}+t,\quad b_t(n,k)=(t+2)\binom{n-t-2}{k-t-1}+\binom{n-t-2}{k-t-2}. \] The bound is sharp, and we characterize all extremal pairs, whose families have equal sizes but need not coincide. The proof combines clique lifts, exchanges of generating families and a density inequality for cross-intersecting uniform layers. This gives a product version of the Hilton--Milner--Frankl theorem throughout the Erdős--Ko--Rado range. In particular, it answers a question of Wen and Lv on whether a threshold of order $kt$ suffices for the sharp product bound.

title: Vision-Grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment for Scalable Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval
abstract: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/ViSeLA

title: TabOmics: A Small, Open Tabular Foundation Model for Wide Omics Data
abstract: Omics studies often produce tables with thousands to tens of thousands of molecular features and few samples. Tabular foundation models use diverse strategies to predict labels for such tables, with some relying on in-context learning, while approaches to wide tables may involve subsampling, grouping, or compressing features. We present TabOmics, a small, open family of tabular foundation models with 7.3M parameters, pretrained exclusively on synthetic tables. TabOmics processes all features retained after preprocessing jointly and derives predictions, attention-derived feature-importance scores, and test sample embeddings from the same forward pass. On 46 classification tasks from three benchmarks of high-dimensional, low-sample-size tables, TabOmics v2.5 with eight ensemble members achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) among the evaluated models (0.943), outperforming TabPFN-3.5 with eight members on 32 tasks despite having about 30 times fewer parameters. With a single member, TabOmics v2.5 reaches a mean AUROC of 0.941, versus 0.942 for TabPFN-3.5 with eight members, with no significant paired difference under the reported task-level analysis. On synthetic tables, its feature-importance scores achieve feature recovery similar to that of TabPFN-Wide, and its predictions remain above chance at 30,000 features. On breast cancer tasks, the top ranked genes include PAM50 genes, which define the subtype labels, indicating concordance with the label definition rather than independent biological validation. The code, model weights, training recipes, and experimental artifacts are publicly available.

title: K-stable Fano varieties can have obstructed deformations
abstract: We exhibit examples of K-stable Fano varieties with obstructed qG-deformations; more precisely, their miniversal qG-deformation spaces can be non-reduced. As a consequence, we show that both the K-moduli stack and the K-moduli space can be non-reduced, and hence non-smooth, at points corresponding to K-stable Fano varieties.

title: FOORT: Flexible Object-Oriented Ray Tracing
abstract: We present FOORT (Flexible Object-Oriented Ray Tracing), an open C++ code for ray-tracing images of black holes and other compact objects in arbitrary spacetimes. FOORT is designed to offer flexibility and can handle horizons, naked singularities and numerical metrics, allowing it to ray-trace numerous different metrics including Kerr and other black holes, as well as horizonless objects such as fuzzballs and boson stars. New metrics, analytical or numerical, can be added with minimal effort, and geodesics are initialized at the camera without reference to conserved quantities, so no special structure of the metric is required. Besides the intensity observed from a geometrically and optically thin equatorial disk, FOORT is set up to track a number of diagnostics along each geodesic, such as the number of equatorial crossings and the radius of closest approach. Its adaptive mesh can refine the image on any of these diagnostics, efficiently resolving narrow features such as higher-order photon rings. Accompanying Python tools convert the output into images and interferometric visibility amplitudes. We describe the main features of the code, validate it against analytic results in the Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes, demonstrate it on several non-Kerr metrics, and characterize its scaling with the number of OpenMP threads. FOORT is lightweight, requiring only C++17 and OpenMP, and has already been used in a number of studies of black hole and compact-object imaging. The code is publicly available in a GitHub repository.

title: $2$-blocks with defect group of rank $2$
abstract: We classify all controlled $2$-blocks with defect group of rank $2$ up to Morita equivalence. This provides a proof of Donovan's Conjecture for resistant $2$-generated $2$-groups.

title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
abstract: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

title: Duality and hidden symmetries for time-inhomogeneous Markov processes
abstract: We study the notion of duality in the setting of time-inhomogeneous Markov processes. We define duality with time-dependent duality functions. We establish the connection between duality and time-dependent symmetries and intertwinings. We illustrate the abstract results with examples from interacting particle systems and diffusion processes.

title: Discrete Supernovae and the Limits of Continuous Models in Low-Mass Dark Matter Halos
abstract: Many galaxy formation models represent supernova feedback by a continuous energy injection rate averaged over the stellar initial mass function (IMF). This approximation can fail in low-mass dark matter halos, where single, discrete supernovae can unbind more gas than the reservoir holds. We investigate this using a one-zone model that characterises continuous and discrete supernova feedback at redshifts $z\geq5$. Both feedback modes inject the same expected energy per unit stellar mass formed. In the discrete model, individual supernovae are resolved and energy is injected instantaneously; in the continuous model, supernovae are IMF-averaged and energy injection is spread over a finite time interval. Once stars form, a supernova can unbind 1.5-2.7 times the gas present. Continuous feedback begins removing gas after $\sim 4$ Myr, whereas the first discrete supernova occurs after $\sim 10$ Myr, which produces a stellar mass excess before feedback takes effect. The excess persists because the reservoir responds nonlinearly: an event removes at most the gas present, and star formation halts once it is empty. It depends strongly on halo mass: from 135 per cent at $10^7\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to 15 per cent at $10^8\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to negligible at $10^9\, \rm{M}_\odot$ by $z=5$. Fixing the number and timing of supernovae does not remove the stellar excess, which indicates that it is not caused by stochastic IMF sampling. Instead, it vanishes when the same energy is divided among more, smaller events. Matching the energy released per unit stellar mass therefore does not guarantee equivalent feedback in halos that retain gas until the first supernova.

title: Classification of G-g.o. metrics on compact homogeneous spaces G/H with G simple
abstract: We classify the $G$-g.o. metrics on compact homogeneous spaces $G/H$, where $G$ is a compact connected simple Lie group and $H$ is an arbitrary closed subgroup. We give the complete list of nonnormal metrics, including their parameter conditions and the possible mixing between equivalent isotropy summands.
