We derive a unified master equation using Lewis-Riesenfeld dynamical invariants, accommodating arbitrary driving within Born-Markov theory. We demonstrate the applicability of the unified master equation to constant-Rabi-coupling (continuous-wave), periodically-modulated-Rabi-coupling, and nonperiodic (ramped and chirped) driving protocols. Fluorescence spectra of a periodically driven three-level $Λ$ system reveal signatures missed by conventional descriptions. We trace the limitations of the conventional descriptions to inaccurate bath-frequency sampling and the neglect of nonsecular dissipative couplings, and map out the parameter regimes that require a unified treatment. The fluorescence spectra provide experimentally accessible signatures, which serve as a spectroscopic guide to reliable modeling of dissipative processes that can inform quantum control, simulation, sensing, and information processing.

title: Stability Conditions on Twisted Derived Categories I: Existence and Full Numerical Support
abstract: We prove that for every nonempty smooth projective variety $X$ over an arbitrary field and every Brauer class $α$, the twisted derived category $D^b(X,α)$ admits a Bridgeland stability condition with full numerical support. Based on Chunyi Li's construction and its extension to arbitrary fields, we establish uniform phase control under tensoring by an Azumaya algebra and calibrate the resulting slicing to the induced central charge. We further show that the constructed stability condition is geometric and satisfies a mass--Hom bound, which persists throughout its connected component.

title: On real-analytic non-degeneracy of left-symmetric algebras in dimension 3
abstract: In this paper, we show that any three-dimensional differentially non-degenerate left-symmetric algebra over $\mathbb R$ is non-degenerate both in the formal and real-analytic categories via the correspondence with Nijenhuis operators.

title: A Disease-specific Retinal Aging Biomarker for Predicting Progression to Late Age-related Macular Degeneration
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults. While chronological age is a primary risk factor, it inadequately reflects individual variations in retinal aging, limiting effective AMD risk stratification and timely intervention. Here, we propose and validate fundus-based AMD age (FAA), which quantifies disease-specific retinal aging in AMD and captures accelerated AMD-related retinal aging, thereby improving prognostic precision over chronological age. Trained on 36,782 images from 2,192 participants in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) dataset and validated across AREDS and AREDS2 cohorts, our model demonstrates significant improvements over traditional chronological age-based approaches. Specifically, integrating the proposed FAA into Cox proportional-hazards models significantly enhances prediction performance. FAA improved the C-index from 0.836 to 0.888 and reduced the 5-year Brier score from 0.050 to 0.046 in AREDS, with consistent gains observed in AREDS2 (C-index 0.715 to 0.756; 2-year Brier 0.078 to 0.076). FAA showed improved prognostic performance across the two datasets and under different phenotype definitions (reading center-defined vs. specialist-defined grading), supporting its potential utility for AMD risk stratification. These findings highlight the advantage of incorporating FAA into AMD risk prediction frameworks, supporting further evaluation of FAA for AMD risk stratification.

title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea
abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

title: Ramsey numbers of loose triangles versus cliques
abstract: An $r$-uniform loose triangle $C_3$ consists of three edges that intersect pairwise in exactly one vertex and have no vertex common to all three. For graphs, this is the usual triangle, and the Ramsey number $R(C_3,K_t)$ has order of magnitude $t^2/\log t$ by celebrated results of Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi and of Kim. Kostochka, Mubayi, and Verstraëte proved that $R(C_3,K_t^{(r)})=O_r(t^{3/2})$ for every fixed $r\ge3$ and showed that this bound is sharp up to a logarithmic factor. Motivated by the logarithmic saving in the graph case, they conjectured in 2013 that the upper bound could be improved to $o(t^{3/2})$.This conjecture has since received significant attention and has been reiterated in several papers. We prove the conjecture by showing that, for every fixed $r\ge3$, \[ R(C_3,K_t^{(r)}) =O_r\left(\frac{t^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log t}}\right). \]

title: Monolayer MoSe2 as an Attenuator of Spintronic Terahertz Emission
abstract: Understanding ultrafast spin-to-charge conversion at ferromagnetic/2D interfaces is critical for developing THz-frequency spintronic devices such as ultrafast memories, sensors, and compact THz sources. We investigate this by studying spintronic THz emission (STE) from Py/Au heterostructures capped with transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayer MoSe2 using time-domain THz spectroscopy. We observe a pronounced reduction in emitted THz amplitude when a monolayer MoSe2 flake covers Py/Au or Py/Pt emitters compared with uncovered regions. A consistent, approximately fourfold attenuation occurs for both systems, despite an order-of-magnitude larger THz radiation from the bare Py/Pt emitter. These results indicate that the suppression is independent of emitter strength. We attribute the attenuation to THz absorption by free charge carriers and trions that are either present due to charge transfer from the metallic layer or photoexcited by the laser pulse, which can significantly diminish the detectable STE signal. This finding provides an explanation for the discrepancy between weak STE signals from FM/TMD heterostructures and magnetotransport reports of sizable spin-orbit torques in similar systems, and highlights the need to account for photoinduced THz attenuation when interpreting ultrafast spin-to-charge conversion measurements in 2D TMD heterostructures.

title: An algorithm for solving the Burgers equation based on rational approximations and the collocation method
abstract: We propose a numerical method for solving initial-boundary value problems for the Burgers equation that takes into account the presence of singularities of the analytic continuation of the solution into the complex plane. The algorithm uses rational approximations, a collocation method and a new scheme for time discretization combined with the relaxation method. An adaptive strategy is developed to account for the location of the singular point of the solution. Solutions to the well-known benchmark problem with a sine-shaped initial condition are obtained for the values of the viscosity as low as nu = 10^-8. Verification of the numerical results in such an extreme parameter regime makes it necessary to modify a classical formula for the exact solution so as to avoid floating-point overflow during its computation. The developed method is compared with an algorithm employing the Runge-Kutta scheme, and the conditions under which each approach yields superior results are outlined. An important feature of the proposed method is its capability to track the singular point of the solution. To verify this, we consider a problem whose solution has a simple analytical form and demonstrate that the exact and approximate coordinates of the singular point of the solution agree with high accuracy, even when the singularity comes extremely close to the domain of the problem. Taking the location of the singular point into account yields significant gains in both accuracy and run time relative to other methods.

title: Non-existence of closed embedded magnetic geodesics
abstract: We give a counterexample to S. Novikov's 1982 conjecture that every Riemannian $2$-sphere contains a closed embedded curve of curvature $c$ for every $c>0$.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

title: Higher-Group Statistics on Lattices
abstract: Crossing a domain wall can permute anyons, and intersecting strings can create a particle. These couplings between defects of various dimensions are specified by higher groups. We develop a lattice framework defining higher-group statistics as Berry phases of closed sequences of hopping operators, invariant under local modifications of the operators. Our central example is a closed Majorana chain, a 1-dimensional topological superconductor, embedded in 3 dimensions. We construct a loop-flip process with phase $+i$, refining the usual $\pm 1$ loop-flip invariant through intermediate transfer of fermion parity between the chain and physical fermions. In two dimensions, charge-wall statistics distinguish two $\mathbb Z_4$ toric codes enriched by $\mathbb Z_2$ charge-conjugation symmetry, with identical anyon statistics but distinct gauged theories: the quantum doubles of the dihedral group $D_4$ and the quaternion group $Q_8$. We provide two complementary constructions of statistical processes. The first extends the Smith normal form algorithm in [Phys. Rev. X $\textbf{16}$, 011010 (2026), arXiv:2412.01886] to higher groups, generating processes from lattice geometry and prescribed local moves. For a finite higher group $\mathbb G$, we prove that statistical processes on a $d$-sphere are classified by $H_{d+2}(B\mathbb G,\mathbb Z)$. The second constructs processes directly from homology classes without examining exponentially many defect configurations, enabling us to study statistics for complex higher-group structures where the previous method is computationally prohibitive. These processes detect boundary anomalies of higher-group symmetry-protected topological phases. For example, we distinguish 2-group anomalies in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions. Higher-group statistics provide new invariants for characterizing coupled defects in quantum many-body systems.

title: A completely decomposable modular Jacobian of dimension $1777$
abstract: We exhibit a congruence subgroup $Γ\subset\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ of level $120$ and index $23040$ whose modular curve $X_Γ$ has genus $1777$ and whose Jacobian is isogenous over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ to a product of elliptic curves. This surpasses the previous record of a completely decomposable complex Jacobian of dimension $1297$ found by Ekedahl and Serre in $1993$.

title: Bayesian determination of structural ensembles from single-particle X-ray scattering images
abstract: Single-particle X-ray scattering with free electron lasers records snapshots of individual molecules with femtosecond time resolution and is therefore ideally suited to study structural heterogeneity or molecular motions. Current approaches to determine structural ensembles rely on prior classification of the scattering images, which is error-prone and becomes infeasible for single macromolecules, whose images contain too few coherently scattered photons. Here, we present a Bayesian approach that samples weighted ensembles of electron densities directly from the posterior probability distribution given all scattering images, thereby avoiding classification altogether. We demonstrate our approach in the low signal-to-noise high heterogeneity regime using synthetic scattering data of a small and flexible protein, as well as on published experimental scattering images for the coliphage PR772 virus.

title: Asymptotic Dimension of Persistence Modules of Bounded Presentation
abstract: We compute the asymptotic dimension of spaces of multiparameter persistence modules of bounded presentation under the interleaving distance. The $d$-parameter modules with at most $n$ generators and $m$ relations have asymptotic dimension, and Assouad-Nagata dimension, exactly $d(n+m)$, the number of coordinates of their generator and relation grades, over every field; for two parameters this is $2(n+m)$. The space has continuous moduli, already for two parameters and $n,m\ge2$: over an infinite field it contains, at every scale, infinite uniformly separated families of pairwise non-isomorphic modules with one fibered barcode, so it is not doubling even at a fixed fibered barcode; already for $m\ge1$ it is not coarsely equivalent to a proper metric space. The proof is an induction on the number of distinct grade coordinates: an interleaving small compared with the gaps between these coordinates moves each of them by at most twice its size and preserves the induced grid representation, so the continuous moduli are invisible at large scale. Each class of modules at finite distance therefore embeds coarsely into Hilbert space; for $n,m\ge2$ over an uncountable field, the classes that contain these families admit no such embedding into a separable Hilbert space. Under the two-parameter matching distance $2(n+m)$ is a lower bound, attained for one generator and for two generators with at most one relation; on a finite net of $S$ slices the asymptotic dimension is at most $2nS$.

title: A PTAS for Constraint Satisfaction Problems on Interval Graphs and Bounded Rank-Width Graphs
abstract: We present a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for all Boolean arity-two maximum constraint satisfaction problems (Boolean Max-2-CSP) where the constraint graph is either interval or has bounded rank-width. This class of problems includes, for example, Max-Cut, Max-DiCut, Max-2-Lin(2), and Max-2-SAT. In particular, this settles the approximability of Max-Cut on interval graphs. To achieve these results, we show the following. 1. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an $n^{\mathcal O(r \varepsilon^{-2})}$-time $(1 - \varepsilon$)-approximation for Boolean Max-2-CSP on graphs of rank-width at most $r$. 2. There is a polynomial-time algorithm that, for any interval graph $G = (V, E)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, finds a subgraph $H = (V, F)$ of $G$ such that $|F| \geq (1 - \varepsilon) |E|$ and $H$ has rank-width at most $\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon^{-1})$. Our techniques additionally extend to all bounded-alphabet arity-two max CSPs.

title: Lorentz Boosts and Governing Equations of the Quantum Geometric Tensor in 4D Energy-Momentum Space
abstract: In solids, the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), $Q_{μν}=g_{μν}-\frac{i}{2} Ω_{μν}$, combines the quantum metric and Berry curvature. Its imaginary part governs anomalous velocity and quantized Hall transport, while its real part determines the quantum weight and geometric contributions to flat-band superfluid stiffness and dielectric response. Here, we extend the QGT to four-dimensional (4D) energy-momentum space ($ω/c,k$), treating frequency and momentum as independent coordinates. Invariance of the real-spacetime plane-wave phase fixes their Lorentz transformation in energy-momentum space. Lorentz boosts of static Dirac and Weyl systems then generate frequency metrics, quadrupolar frequency-momentum shear metrics, and electric-like Berry-Maxwell fields. We identify five Lorentz-invariant contractions and derive the governing field equations and flow conservation laws for both the quantum metric and Berry curvature from static Weyl geometry and Lorentz covariance. We further connect Gaussian spectral amplitudes of the QGT to localized Gaussian events in 4D spacetime. Finally, we discuss experimental realizations in spacetime crystals or time-varying media and clarify how this unified quantum geometry of a gravitational-like metric and electromagnetic-like gauge fields connects geometric self-consistency with physical event dynamics.

title: Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech
abstract: Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT

title: Characterizations of Pettis Integrable Multifunctions in Locally Convex Spaces
abstract: In this paper, we present characterizations of Pettis integrability in $bcc(X)$ and $cwk(X)$ of a multifunction $Γ: Ω\to cc(X)$, where $(Ω, Σ, μ)$ is a complete finite measure space and $cc(X)$ $(bcc(X), cwk(X))$ is the family of all nonempty convex closed (bounded convex closed, convex weakly compact) subsets of a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space $X$. Incidentally, a convergence theorem for scalarly integrable multifunctions is proved. As an application, we are going to prove full characterizations of Pettis integrability for fuzzy maps defined on $Ω$ and taking values in the generalized fuzzy number hyperspace $\mathcal{F}_{cwk}(X)$.

title: Rainbow matchings in non-uniform hypergraph systems
abstract: Let $s\geq 1$, $r_1, r_2,\dots, r_{s+1}$ be given positive integers and $r=\max\{r_1, r_2,\ldots, r_{s+1}\}$. We prove that if $\mathcal{F} = \{\mathcal{F}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{F}_{s+1}\}$ is a family of hypergraphs on a ground set of $n$ vertices, $n\geq 4r^2(s+1)$, such that $\mathcal{F}_i\subseteq \binom{n}{r_i}$ and $|\mathcal{F}_i|>\binom{n}{r_i}-\binom{n-s}{r_i}-\binom{n-s-r}{r_i-1}+1$, for all $i \in [s+1]$, then $\mathcal{F}$ admits a rainbow matching of size $s+1$ or there exists $W \in \binom{[n]}{s}$ such that $W$ is a vertex cover of $\mathcal{F}_i$, for all $i \in [s+1]$. This improves upon the previously known range $n>2r^3s$ to $n>4r^2(s+1)$. Moreover, for a given family $\mathcal{F} = \{\mathcal{F}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{F}_{s+1}\}$ of hypergraphs $\mathcal{F}_i\subseteq \binom{n}{r_i}$, we give a best possible Ore-degree condition for $\mathcal{F}_{i}$'s that guarantees the existence of a rainbow matching of size $s+1$ for $\mathcal{F}$.

title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
abstract: We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise. Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values. We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.

title: Kac lemma on noncommutative probability spaces
abstract: We prove non-commutative Kac's formula for actions of countable groups. We replace the return time functions by suitable projections in von Neumann algebras. Moreover, we prove a generalised Kac's formula in the non-commutative setting which extends the allocation construction of Meyerovitch and Weiss and is motivated by the random Kac inequality of Aaronson.

title: Interfacial Structure and Dynamics of Active-Passive Fluid Mixtures
abstract: We investigate the interface between an active and a passive fluid using molecular dynamics simulations of active Brownian particles in contact with a passive Lennard-Jones fluid. We compute the surface tension via two independent routes, pressure anisotropy and capillary-wave analysis, and find that they disagree systematically once activity is switched on. Static density and orientation profiles reveal three distinct activity regimes, with particles preferentially oriented toward the interface. Going beyond these static properties, we characterize the interface dynamics: a threshold activity above which mixing becomes irreversible, coinciding with the onset of the mixing regime, and a transient overshoot in interfacial width before relaxation to steady state.

title: Exploring the Pion Vector Form Factor Beyond the Physical Sheet
abstract: Using analyticity and unitarity, we parametrise the pion vector form factor on the first and second Riemann sheets, below the inelastic $πω$ threshold. We fit this model-independent parametrisation to the available $τ^-\toπ^-π^0ν_τ$ data from ALEPH, Belle, CLEO and OPAL, together with spacelike data from NA7 and JLab, and extract the pole position and couplings of the $ρ^\pm$ along with the pion charge radius and low-energy $ππ$ scattering parameters. Our results are independent of external scattering input and agree with the literature; in particular, we find $M_{ρ^\pm} = 762.07\pm 0.63$ MeV and $Γ_{ρ^\pm} = 143.62^{+0.79}_{-0.80}$ MeV. The parametrisation is publicly available in the EOS software.

title: A binomial-adjusted $θ$-trapezoidal tau-leaping method for chemical kinetic systems
abstract: In Hu, Li and Min (2011), the authors propose a weak second order accurate $θ$-trapezoidal method as an improvement to the classical tau-leaping method. However, for complex chemical kinetic systems their model's underlying analytical assumptions can fail to hold in practice, leading to a significant reduction in its computational effectiveness. Here we introduce a modification to the method which allows it to regain desirable convergence characteristics, both given the original and a relaxed version of the underlying assumptions. We confirm this improvement through a local error analysis and present numerical examples showing it consistently performs either better or comparable to the $θ$-trapezoidal method.

title: Non self-similar solutions to the Ricci flow coming out of metric cones
abstract: Given an asymptotically conical unstable expanding gradient Ricci soliton, we provide the existence of a family of Ricci flows starting at the same metric cone up to isometry. Moreover, the family of solutions we construct is shown to be parametrized by positive modes of the weighted Lichnerowicz operator associated to the background expanding gradient Ricci soliton. Each solution of this family is shown not to be induced by an expanding gradient Ricci soliton. If the background expander has no non-trivial infinitesimal deformations, we show furthermore that the solutions we provide are not self-similar. We finally prove that solutions are distinct up to isometries preserving the potential function of the background expanding gradient Ricci soliton.

title: Quantitative Junction Transport Modeling of RHIC Charge and Baryon Stopping
abstract: Charge and baryon stopping in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr isobar collisions are modeled by HIJING with junction. With realistic nuclear geometry and a tuned diquark splitting, it reproduces STAR's net-baryon yield, charge difference, and scaled baryon-to-charge ratio at midrapidity. Junctions set the ratio's magnitude while neutron skins drive its centrality trend. At the LHC, large asymmetric pair production in HIJING obscures junction effects, causing apparent tension with data. This tuned generator reproduces RHIC data and predicts O+O behavior, setting a quantitative benchmark for baryon transport.

title: Off-diagonal decay of capacitance matrices via Brownian motion
abstract: We establish upper and lower bounds for the off-diagonal entries of the capacitance matrix of infinite systems of spherical resonators in chain, screen and crystal geometries. Let $d$ denote the distance between two resonator centres. For chains contained in a cylinder of bounded radius and with bounded axial gaps, the decay is of order $d^{-1}\log^{-2}(2+d)$. For screens contained in a slab and relatively dense in the tangential directions, it is of order $d^{-3}$. For relatively dense three-dimensional configurations, we obtain exponential upper and lower bounds. No periodicity is assumed. Our proofs are based on the classical connection between the Dirichlet problem and Brownian motion, which enables us to relate the decay estimates to hitting probabilities of Brownian motion.

title: Cup and cap synchronization: higher-order node dynamics from topology
abstract: Higher-order node-based synchronization provides distinct mechanisms for discontinuous synchronization transitions. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework capable of encompassing existing models and revealing the role of higher-order interactions beyond triangles is still missing. Here, combining algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics, we introduce Cup and Cap Synchronization, a unifying theoretical framework for higher-order node-based dynamics that naturally incorporates the topological organization of the underlying higher-order network. We show that Cup and Cap Synchronization can display critical behavior belonging to the universality classes of two existing higher-order Kuramoto-like models, whose distinct critical behaviors were thought to originate from different mechanisms. Remarkably, we demonstrate that Cup and Cap Synchronization displays additional phenomenology not captured by the previously proposed models of higher-order node-based synchronization. Most relevantly, the inclusion of four-body interactions can fundamentally alter the critical properties of the synchronization transition, giving rise to collective phenomena that cannot be observed in models including only interactions mediated by edges and triangles. These findings reveal the importance of going beyond the commonly studied three-body terms and establish Cup and Cap Synchronization as a unifying theoretical framework for understanding collective dynamics in higher-order networks.

title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry
abstract: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

title: Certified Hierarchical Planning and Tracking: A Learning-Based Approach
abstract: In this paper, we develop a hierarchical control framework for nonlinear dynamical systems with safety constraints. Specifically, a low-fidelity model is introduced for trajectory planning, while a tracking controller is designed for the high-fidelity system. We first characterize the tracking error bound (TEB) using a storage function. Then, we formulate the synthesis of the tracking controller, the storage function, and the TEB as an optimization problem. Following that, we develop an offline learning approach to approximately solve the optimization problem, by incorporating behavior cloning and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver. We further integrate the learned controller and the TEB into online tracking of the high-fidelity system. This framework enables the control of high-dimensional nonlinear systems with safety guarantees, while maintaining computational efficiency for real-time implementation. Finally, experiments are provided for illustration.

title: Direct Search meets Frank-Wolfe: Inexact Derivative-Free Bilevel Optimization over Polytopes
abstract: In this work we propose BLDS-SIMPLEX, a derivative-free direct search method for the solution of bilevel optimization with polytope constraints at the upper level. The proposed method reformulates the feasible set using barycentric coordinates and explores it using Frank-Wolfe-type directions, relying on a fixed-accuracy black-box oracle for the upper-level objective function. We analyze its convergence properties and complexity in the case of smooth reduced objective; additionally, we analyze a variant for the case of nonsmooth objectives and show its convergence to a specific kind of stationary point that we introduce as a natural generalization to the classic stationarity notions in this setting. Numerical tests on modified instances from BOLIB support the viability of our new approach.

title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

title: Lurkers at the Threshold: GWTC-4.0's near-threshold events
abstract: We present the first systematic parameter-estimation analysis of 42 candidate gravitational-wave signals identified in GWTC-4.0 with a probability of astrophysical origin $p_\mathrm{astro} \geq 0.5$, but a false-alarm rate of at least $1\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, which were therefore not selected for parameter estimation in the catalogue. We use a catalogue-style analysis workflow and publicly available strain data to obtain posterior samples for these candidates, of which 29 pass our validation criteria. Of the remaining 13 candidates, seven are consistent with noise or impacted by instrumental artefacts, while six yield results that cannot be reliably interpreted. We identify several interesting candidates: a possible neutron star-black hole merger, GW230920_064709, and two candidates with evidence for non-zero effective spin: GW230902_172430 and GW230823_142524. The latter also shows mild evidence of precession, although further analysis is needed to establish the robustness of this result. We quantify the information gained from these observations using the Kullback-Leibler divergence, finding that the inferred spin parameters are generally only weakly constrained. We present a reproducible analysis workflow that uses publicly available data and software, without access to LVK collaboration resources, and incorporates automated posterior-validation tools. We also provide a data release containing results in a format compatible with those from GWTC-4.0. Our results demonstrate that useful parameter constraints can be obtained for many candidates below the catalogue's parameter-estimation significance threshold, while highlighting the challenges of analysing marginal signals and the importance of careful validation.

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
abstract: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

title: A lift of Baxter's cyclic summation identity with applications to quantum topology
abstract: While studying the chiral Potts model Baxter discovered a cyclic analogue of Ramanujan's ${}_1ψ_{1}$ summation identity. This identity was subsequently interpreted by Faddeev and Kashaev as a pentagon relation for the quantum dilogarithm function, a key ingredient in cyclic quantizations of Teichmüller theory. Existing forms of the identity involve multivalued functions so one must either accept overall phase ambiguities or keep track of branches on a complicated covering space. In this paper we show how to remove the phase ambiguities with a much simpler choice of covering space. As an application we compute the Fourier transform of the holonomy $R$-matrices of the author and Reshetikhin. A corollary is a simpler proof that Kashaev's $R$-matrix is a specialization of the colored Jones $R$-matrix, which was first shown by Murakami and Murakami.

title: Unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a triangular lattice: deconfined fermions in a vison crystal and superfluidity
abstract: We investigate an unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory coupled to fermions on the triangular lattice at half filling, using auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The triangular geometry gives rise to a global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that acts as an Ising symmetry on the plaquette fluxes. At weak transverse field $h$, this symmetry is spontaneously broken, stabilizing a vison crystal. We argue that this phase is deconfined: fermions, charged under an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge field, propagate in an ordered $π$-flux background and form a Dirac semimetal. Increasing the transverse field triggers a first-order quantum phase transition to a confined $s$-wave superfluid, at which confinement and global symmetry breaking occur simultaneously. This contrasts with the square lattice, where the corresponding transition is continuous. We extend our analysis to finite temperature and determine the thermal phase boundaries of both ordered phases. The superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, whereas the vison crystal undergoes a thermal Ising transition. Together, our results establish the $T \times h$ phase diagram and demonstrate how the triangular geometry leads to qualitative changes in both the phases and the criticality of the model.

title: $NΩ$ Dibaryon near Unitarity from Physical-Point Lattice QCD
abstract: The $NΩ$ system is a promising dibaryon candidate because its constituents share no valence quarks and therefore avoid valence-quark Pauli repulsion. We determine the $^{5}S_{2}$ $NΩ$ interaction in (2+1)-flavor lattice QCD at physical quark masses ($m_π\simeq137~\text{MeV}$) using the HAL QCD method. The interaction is attractive over the resolved range and supports a shallow state near unitarity. A direct $T$-matrix pole analysis gives $B_{nΩ} = 0.61\,(^{+0.41}_{-0.30})\,(^{+0.60}_{-0.18})~\text{MeV}$; including finite-charge-size Coulomb attraction yields $B_{pΩ} = 1.25\,(^{+0.46}_{-0.39})\,(^{+0.69}_{-0.25})~\text{MeV}$. These results provide a first-principles benchmark for future $NΩ$ femtoscopy and dibaryon searches.

title: How to arrange four points in the plane
abstract: Arranging points in the plane appears to be an elementary geometric problem, yet it is deeply rooted in statistical physics. As a toy model, we consider the configuration of four points. We completely classify the minimal configurations of four points interaction energy in $\R^2$ under the general Lennard-Jones potentials $V(r)=r^{-p}-br^{-q}$, where $p>q>0$ and $b\in\R$. We find that there is a threshold curve \[ D_{p,q}=2^{-(p-q)/2}\Bigl(1+\frac{p-q}{q+2}\bigl(1+2^{-(q+2)/2}\bigr)\Bigr) \] to determine the minimal shapes. The main results can be stated concisely as follows: consider $\min\sum_{1\le i<j\le4}\bigl(|x_i-x_j|^{-p}-b|x_i-x_j|^{-q}\bigr)$. For $b\le0$, the minimizer does not exist. For $b>0$, the minimizer is unique up to rotation and translation. Furthermore, the minimizer is \[ \begin{cases} \text{a square},&\hbox{if}\;\; D_{p,q}\ge1, \text{a rhombus with angle }θ\in(π/3,π/2),&\hbox{if}\;\; D_{p,q}<1. \end{cases} \]

title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
abstract: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
abstract: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.

title: Identifiability and partial identification under spatial confounding in additive risk models
abstract: In spatial risk attribution, continuous environmental exposures and unmeasured background factors often co-vary across broad geographic scales, making it difficult to separate true exposure effects from spatial confounding using finite disease counts. Existing remedies typically project out or penalize shared spatial trends, leaving unclear whether estimation instability stems from the overall capacity of the latent random field or from its directional alignment with exposure. By decomposing the Fisher-weighted smoothing operator of an additive Poisson point process model, we show that while effective degrees of freedom measure total smoothing capacity, the relative loss of Fisher information for the exposure coefficient is governed solely by a distinct directional quantity that we call penalized collinear overlap. Rotating the spatial kernel alters this information loss while holding total capacity fixed, implying that no single smoothing scale is universally optimal. Because real-world confounding combines smooth regional trends with sharp local jumps that escape any moderate basis dictionary, point identification remains fragile. We therefore develop a partial identification framework that bounds residual confounding bias using an observable benchmark covariate. Projecting a joint spatial confidence ellipse yields valid intervals even under weak benchmarks, while incorporating a negative control outcome sharpens the bounds and flags assumption violations. Simulation studies and an analysis of childhood respiratory mortality across England demonstrate the method.

title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
abstract: We develop score-based generative models for time series and standard finite-dimensional data, building on the analytical computation of the expected signature of a new class of jump-diffusions, called entire sig-jump-diffusions. These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

title: Channel-Chart-Driven Antenna Activation for Energy-Efficient Cell-Free Massive MIMO
abstract: Cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) can provide uniformly high system performance across the coverage area through distributed cooperation. However, keeping all antennas active leads to high circuit and fronthaul power consumption. This paper studies energy-efficient uplink reception through antenna activation, where only a subset of distributed antennas is selected to serve the users. To enable network-wide activation with low signaling overhead, each access point (AP) maps its locally estimated channel state information (CSI) into a lowdimensional channel-chart (CC) embedding and forwards this representation to the central processing unit (CPU) instead of the full CSI. Based on the received embeddings, we formulate a binary antenna-activation problem for network EE maximization and propose three low-overhead strategies: (i) direct embeddingdomain activation using a proxy EE metric without CSI reconstruction, (ii) nearest chart-point CSI approximation, which estimates CSI from a reference chart database for greedy EE optimization, and (iii) decoder-based CSI reconstruction using a pre-trained autoencoder. The proposed approaches further enable a systematic comparison of antenna activation techniques in terms of achieved performance, computational complexity, and signaling overhead. Numerical results show substantial EE gains over the all-active baseline, with only a minor degradation in sum spectral efficiency and a significant reduction in signaling overhead. Moreover, the proposed greedy framework achieves EE performance close to that of the simulated annealing baseline, confirming its effectiveness for low-complexity antenna activation.

title: The Brown--Shields Conjecture: Two Approximation Theorems and a Counterexample
abstract: We construct an outer function in the classical Dirichlet space whose radial zero set has logarithmic capacity zero, but whose polynomial multiples do not approximate the constant function $1$. This disproves the Brown--Shields conjecture. The proof rests on two approximation theorems for canonical generators of invariant subspaces. The first shows that every proper outer canonical generator can be approximated in the Dirichlet norm by canonical generators associated with singular inner functions determined by finite positive atomic measures. The second shows that each fixed finite-atomic canonical generator can be recovered as a strong Dirichlet limit of outer canonical generators whose radial zero sets have arbitrarily small logarithmic capacity. We then combine these approximations using two techniques: a complete metric that controls boundary logarithms and a nested-ball construction that preserves outerness and noncyclicity while ensuring that the radial zero set is polar. In fact, we show that every proper outer canonical generator can be approximated arbitrarily closely by such counterexamples, both in the Dirichlet norm and in the $L^1$ norm of their boundary logarithms.

title: Achiral-Chiral Dissociation and Structural Zero of the Current in the Spinterface Model of CISS
abstract: We study the transport sector of the spinterface model of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) under spin-resolved dissipation, extending the quantum non-equilibrium Green's function formulation of Ref.~\cite{Alwan2026QSpinterface} to spin-resolved lead broadenings. The spin current decomposes into an achiral part, driven by the interfacial moment, and a chiral part, driven by the Rashba spin flip. Under increasing lead spin asymmetry, the achiral part grows linearly while the chiral part follows the geometric-mean suppression, so the two sectors dissociate; they also peak at different coupling scales along the lead broadening. The coupling and bias optima are operating points of the reference configuration, not universal scaling laws. A structural zero appears at $λ_R\sin(ϕ/2)=t_{\mathrm{mol}}$ in the collinear-lead configuration, where the chiral signal collapses to machine precision universally across chain lengths, frequency resolutions, and twist angles; the zero originates from the rank-one singular bond matrix, whose null eigenvector traps an electron in a spin-superposition dark state that does not hop. With non-collinear ferromagnetic leads, the zero is broken in a controlled way: the residual is generically linear in the transverse polarization, arising from a single coherent spin flip at a boundary, and becomes quadratic at a tuned cancellation angle where two boundary contributions interfere destructively, with the scaling exponent jumping sharply from one to two. These results establish the spinterface model as a transport platform with a two-axis dissociation structure, non-scaling operating optima, and an exact structural zero whose non-collinear deformation is a clean linear-plus-quadratic hierarchy.

title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
abstract: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.

title: Macroscopic $L^\infty$ bounds for the homogeneous Landau--Coulomb equation
abstract: We establish an instantaneous global $L^\infty(\R^3)$ bound at positive times for smooth, rapidly decaying solutions to the three-dimensional spatially homogeneous Landau equation with Coulomb potential, where the upper bound depends solely on the initial mass, momentum, energy, and entropy. This resolves an open problem posed by Golding, Gualdani, and Loher \cite{GGL} without requiring any initial higher velocity moments, Fisher information, or Lebesgue integrability. The proof builds on two main analytical ingredients. First, we establish the instantaneous generation of the negatively weighted Fisher information with weight $\la{v}^{-1}$. On the lifted two-particle phase space, we compare the separable weight matrix against a collision-invariant pair weight and control the rotational commutator near the diagonal via the quadratic local mass decay supplied by the conserved energy, closing a Riccati differential inequality at the second-moment threshold. Second, to overcome the $\la{v}^{-3}$ radial degeneracy of the diffusion matrix at large velocities, we prove a truncated anisotropic mixed Nash inequality on upper level sets of the density that recovers longitudinal regularity from two transverse Fisher directions and the nonlinear high-density part of the Coulomb entropy dissipation. Localizing this functional inequality to radially aligned velocity cells with the critical weight $\la{v}^{3/2}$ and coupling it with a weighted truncated entropy identity across nested exterior domains yields a superlinear De Giorgi recurrence that bounds the velocity tail uniformly in $\R^3$.

title: Reflection Zeros Set the Scattering Invariant of Finite Majorana Wires
abstract: Majorana modes, zero-energy excitations of superconducting wires that are their own antiparticles, could store quantum information protected from local noise. In transport experiments, however, ordinary bound states mimic their signature, a conductance peak at zero voltage, and whether Majorana modes have been observed remains debated. A sign, $Q$, of the electron reflection at zero energy marks the topological phase of a long wire, but what $Q$ certifies in a finite device has been unclear. Here we show for the first time that $Q$ counts reflectionless states, waves that enter through one contact and leave entirely through the other: $Q=-1$ when an odd number of them lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means that the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of $Q$, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point at which two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, $Q=-1$ exactly when the zero-bias conductance measured at a contact exceeds $e^2/h$. These results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the invariant from conductance.

title: Hausdorff measures of planar Brownian level sets
abstract: For any Hausdorff gauge \(h\), we prove that all level sets of planar Brownian motion have zero \(h\)-measure almost surely if and only if \(\liminf_{r\to0^+}h(r)\log(1/r)=0\). This resolves Taylor's question for arbitrary Hausdorff gauges. The proof yields \(0<\HH^{h_0}(L_x)<\infty\) for some \(x\) almost surely, where \(h_0(r)=1/\log(1/r)\). The Hausdorff dimensions of the spatial mass superlevel sets form a deterministic, strictly decreasing bi-Lipschitz spectrum. For each fixed positive mass below the supremum, the exact-mass set almost surely has the same dimension as the corresponding superlevel set.

title: Maturity$^2$: Assessing the Maturity of Crypto Agility Maturity Models
abstract: Crypto agility maturity models aim to support organizations in preparing for cryptographic transitions, such as migrating to post-quantum cryptography. Recognizing the importance of measurable maturity, NIST references several such models in its guidance. Given NIST's influence on cybersecurity practice, these models may shape organizational planning and governance mechanisms. However, their design quality has not been systematically evaluated. In this work, we assess three industry-driven maturity models against established design principles. Our analysis reveals recurring weaknesses, particularly the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance for improving crypto agility. At the same time, we highlight individual strengths that can assist practitioners in choosing among the models and derive concrete recommendations for strengthening future crypto agility maturity models.

title: Real log canonical tresholds and real log canonical tresholds with signs
abstract: In this paper, we study the properties of the real log canonical threshold $\text{rlct}(X,Y)$ associated with a pair $(X,Y)$ and the real log canonical thresholds with signs $\text{rlct}^{\pm}(f)$ associated with a polynomial function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$. In particular, we relate these invariants to other invariants arising from the theory of motivic integration. We also show how to compute these invariants in several particular cases, including the Newton non-degenerate case and the case of analytically irreducible plane curve germs.

title: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control
abstract: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) \emph{self-informed sampling (SIFS)}, a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4~Hz to 1~kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.

title: Infinite spin superparticles
abstract: We obtain infinite spin representations of the super-Poincaré algebra from a higher-derivative superparticle action on a super-Minkowski background in 3, 4, 6 and 10 dimensions. Super-twistor transforms are performed, and used to deduce first-quantised spectra.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
abstract: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.

title: Modelling redshift-space distortions with tracer-centred split densities
abstract: Analysing galaxy clustering in split environmental densities has been demonstrated to offer an advantage over standard two-point clustering for extracting cosmological information. A major challenge to realising this potential with the density-split (DS) technique is that the observations are in redshift space. This complicates its modelling, primarily because the density-split centres may not be conserved between real and redshift space. We develop a modelling framework that splits on the tracer-centred density PDF, rather than the volume-weighted density PDF commonly used in previous studies. We derive the linear bias associated with the threshold density in redshift space, enabling us to connect large-scale DS clustering to the density PDF. We find that the threshold density field consists of doughnut-like structures, which we term `Island(s)'. We propose an empirical model, analogous to the halo model framework, that comprises linear, non-linear, and stochastic terms and accurately reproduces the anisotropic redshift-space clustering of tracers in each DS bin. Using this model, we confirm that DS clustering can provide tighter constraints on cosmological parameters than the standard two-point statistic. Furthermore, we show that the gain in cosmological information from DS analyses relative to standard two-point statistics arises primarily from knowledge of the density PDF, which incorporates small-scale perturbation modes below the smoothing scale.

title: Observation of the $Λ(1520)$ suppression in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV
abstract: A suppression of the baryonic $Λ(1520)$ resonance yield relative to the $Λ$ ground state by $0.589 \pm 0.015^{\rm stat} \pm 0.086^{\rm syst}$ is observed in central relative to peripheral Pb-Pb collisions, with a significance of $6.8σ$. The $Λ(1520)$ production at midrapidity is measured in six centrality classes in Pb-Pb collisions for the first time at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV with ALICE. The $Λ(1520)$ is a sensitive probe of late-stage hadronic interactions since its lifetime is comparable to that of the hadronic phase in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. Statistical hadronization model calculations, predicting yields at chemical freeze-out, overestimate the measured ratio. The transverse-momentum spectra and the centrality dependence of the suppression are reproduced by the MUSIC hydrodynamic model only when coupled to the SMASH hadronic transport afterburner, which implements rescattering and regeneration in the late hadronic stage. The measurement, which represents the first observation of resonance suppression within a single collision system, provides a stringent test of the late-stage dynamics and evidence that hadronic interactions substantially modify reconstructible resonance yield.

title: Random Exploration is Random
abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA
abstract: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.

title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
abstract: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real--synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91--0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.

title: Poincaré polynomials of nilmanifolds associated with path graphs
abstract: We give explicit and recursive formulas for the Poincaré polynomials of Dani--Mainkar nilmanifolds associated with path graphs. We also prove that these polynomials are unimodal, and we calculate a range of Betti numbers asymptotically. As an application, we derive a sharp lower bound for the dimension of the total de Rham cohomology of a Dani--Mainkar nilmanifold.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

title: Control Variates to reduce the variance of the empirical Moment Generating Function: an extreme value perspective
abstract: Accurate estimation of Moment Generating Functions is fundamental in many applications, but empirical estimators have high variances. Within a control variate setup, Extreme Value Theory is leveraged to identify how extreme values affect the variance reduction method's optimality.

title: Continuum space hierarchical Cannings process: II. Genealogies and ancestral web
abstract: The present paper is the second in a series of three papers in which we consider a \emph{spatial multi-type population model} arising as the many-individuals-per-site limit of individual-based models. The evolution mechanisms in this model are: migration, Fleming-Viot resampling, $Λ_0$-Cannings resampling, and $(Λ_k)_{k \in \N}$-Cannings block-resampling. This evolution leads to a collection of \emph{measure-valued} processes indexed by a continuum geographic space $Ω_N^\infty$, called the \emph{continuum hierarchical group}, obtained as the limit of a discrete hierarchical group $Ω_N^L$ as $L\to\infty$, where $Ω_N^L = \oplus_{k \geq -L} Z_N$ with $Z_N$ the cyclical group of order $N$. On this geographic space, each component is a probability measure on a type space $\K$. In the first paper \cite{gh1}, we \emph{constructed} the measure-valued process on $Ω_N^\infty$ describing the type frequencies in the population and identified its main properties.
